title: Are the Texans in panic mode following an 0-2 start? ESPN weighs in
description: The Houston Texans would love to avoid the slow starts under the DeMeco Ryans regime, but the bigger storyline has been the way they've overcome the adversity. Still, is it time to panic?
fullText:
The Houston Texans would love to avoid the slow starts under the DeMeco Ryans regime, but the bigger storyline has been the way they've overcome the adversity.

The Texans once again are sitting at 0-2 following back-to-back losses to the Buffalo Bills and Cincinnati Bengals. Credit: All-Pro defensive end Will Anderson Jr. called both rosters "AFC Championship-level teams," but that doesn't take away the sting of another slow start with questions on both sides of the ball.

But should there be a panic meter yet for Houston? Last season, the Texans started off 0-3 before rattilng off nine wins to tie the franchise record in victories before advancing to the divisional round for a third season.

ESPN's Bill Barnwell isn't buying into the slow start derailing the Texans' season. In his latest article, he ranked all eight winless teams by their chances of making the postseason.

To no one's surprise, Houston led the charge with a 41.8%, which ranks 16th among all 32 rosters.

"A win against the Colts on Sunday in what amounts to a de facto playoff game would calm concerns in Houston," Barnwell wrote. "And after what happened in 2025, there isn't the same sort of panic after an 0-2 start that there would typically be for a team with championship aspirations. Given those expectations, though, starting the season by losing to a pair of teams that the Texans would expect to see again in the postseason picture is a disappointing start. And if the Texans do fall to the Colts next week, their margin for error would grow perilously thin."

Barnwell mentioned consistent quarterback play as a reason to not entirely panic just yet for Houston's postseason chances. Josh Allen, through two weeks of the regular season, has played at MVP level, totaling over 350 yards and four touchdowns in a 36-31 victory.

Burrow, who only threw two touchdown passes, has been one of the league's more efficient passers since 2021. Coming up in the next three weeks are matchups against Indianapolis' Daniel Jones and Tennessee's Cam Ward, two passers still looking to find a rhythm entering winless starts.

"Consider, though, that the Texans finished second in scoring defense last year," Barnwell wrote. "If we take the second-best scoring defense for each season since 2002 and see where they ranked the following year, their average rank fell to 12th. I would be surprised if the Texans were outside the top 10 by the time we looked at the end of the season, but it would hardly be a surprise or unreasonable to expect something closer to the bottom half of the top 10 than a return to the top two."

The one concern remains the offense overall, most notably in the running game. David Montgomery finished with three touchdowns in his debut, but also averaged just over 3.0 yards per run. Last week, he and Woody Marks combined for 1.4 yards per carry and less than 30 yards on the afternoon.

"Through two weeks, that running game hasn't been present. The Texans are 28th in success rate, 29th in EPA per snap and 30th in yards per carry on designed runs. Montgomery scored three touchdowns in the opener, but he has found space hard to come by, averaging 2.7 yards per attempt on the ground. Part of the problem has been availability. Ingram missed the loss to the Bengals, and [Braden] Smith is on injured reserve because of a foot injury.

The run issues materially impacted the Texans against the Bengals. Despite Caserio expressing his confidence that coach DeMeco Ryans had confidence in the running game after Week 1, Ryans quickly pivoted in the other direction one week later."

To read the full article and see where teams like the Colts, Titans and Los Angeles Chargers rank, click here.

The Texans take on the Colts this Sunday at Noon.

title: New York Giants vs. Tennessee Titans: NFL experts make Week 3 picks
description: Experts from around the NFL make their picks for a Week 3 game between the New York Giants and Tennessee Titans.
fullText:
The New York Giants (1-1) host the Tennessee Titans (0-2) at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, in Week 3.

Opening the week, the Giants were listed as 6-point home favorites, but that line has dipped to -3 following a slew of injuries, including a season-ending knee surgery for quarterback Jaxson Dart.

Let's take a look at who some of the experts and insiders around the league are taking in the Week 3 matchup:

Bill Bender (The Sporting News)

Vinnie Iyer (The Sporting News)

Even in the absence of Jaxson Dart and Brian Burns, most experts and analysts believe the Giants can upend the struggling Titans. However, far fewer believe it will come in a high-scoring affair, with most predicting under 42 combined points.

title: Barcelona want to renew 17-year-old versatile La Masia gem, have high hopes on him
description: For some time now, there has been talk of FC Barcelona’s need to strengthen at centre-back.The Blaugrana explored the possibility during the summer, especially after Ronald Araujo and Alvaro Cortes�...
fullText:
For some time now, there has been talk of FC Barcelona's need to strengthen at centre-back.

The Blaugrana explored the possibility during the summer, especially after Ronald Araujo and Alvaro Cortes' exits, but no reinforcements arrived.

The sporting department, led by Deco, continues to monitor the market closely for options. At the same time, the Catalans are also keeping a close eye on the development of players coming through the academy.

And, according to Carlos Monfort of SPORT, one of the names generating particularly positive reports within Barcelona is Baba Kourouma.

Within Barça there is a belief that the 17-year-old starlet possesses some very interesting qualities and that, if he maintains his current development, he could become a player to watch in the future.

As such, they are now planning to renew the La Masia prospect's contract in the near future.

Kourouma did not start out as a centre-back. The teenager, brother of former Barcelona star Ilaix Moriba, began as a defensive midfielder before gradually being converted into a central defender.

He can also play at left-back or move back into midfield, or in advanced positions on the flank. The youngster is also capable of playing as a No. 10, a role he has filled with the Catalan national team.

Kourouma has just received a call-up to the Spain Under-18 squad after recently completing the necessary paperwork to make him eligible.

Last season, he already showed glimpses of his potential. In his first year at the Juvenil level, he made 43 appearances and was also entrusted with the captain's armband, reflecting the confidence placed in him.

He was also called up to train with the first team by Hansi Flick last year.

As such, Barcelona want to renew him. Kourouma's contract runs until 2028 and the club's intention is to extend his deal.

The player, for his part, dreams of succeeding in the Blaugrana shirt. Over the past few years, he has received several approaches from other clubs, including some significant offers, but he has always chosen to remain at La Masia.

Even as search for a centre-back continues, the La Liga champions are also closely watching Kourouma's development within the academy.

title: Puka Nacua injury status: Here's the latest update on Rams' WR
description: Rams WR Puka Nacua (hip) seems to be trending toward not playing against the Broncos on SNF.
fullText:
It sounds like the Los Angeles Rams will likely be missing a key player when they face the Denver Broncos on Sunday Night Football in Week 3.

Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua (hip) is "not making great progress" in his recovery, L.A. coach Sean McVay said during an interview with ESPN Los Angeles (via Rams Wire). After sitting out Monday Night Football in Week 2, Nacua did not participate in L.A.'s light practice on Wednesday.

Following that comment from McVay, NFL Network's Ian Rapoport said he "would be surprised" if Nacua suits up for SNF against the Broncos. So it certainly sounds like Nacua is trending toward not playing in Week 3.

Meanwhile, in Denver, running backs J.K. Dobbins (hip) and RJ Harvey (hamstring) were limited on Wednesday, while rookie Jonah Coleman (ankle) was held out.

"I think we're good at that position. ... I think we're going to be alright," Broncos coach Sean Payton said on Wednesday when asked about the running back room.

Denver and L.A. will practice again on Thursday and Friday before releasing final injury reports with game statuses.

title: Red Sox's Aroldis Chapman Is Fan Of This National League Pitcher
description: The Boston Red Sox and Milwaukee Brewers are both headed to the postseason
fullText:
Aroldis Chapman has made a name for himself by lighting up the radar gun throughout his career.

Chapman holds the record for the fastest pitch thrown in the Statcast era at 105.8 mph. He also holds the No. 2 spot with a 105.7 mph pitch. Chapman is ninth all-time in saves and has more strikeouts than any reliever in the history of baseball. Chapman has left his mark on the game, and the 38-year-old is still playing like an All-Star.

Chapman has been around for a while, so there's not much he hasn't seen. However, he, like everyone else, is in awe of Jacob Misiorowski. Chapman's fastball has been one of the best pitches in baseball for years, but to see that kind of velocity from a starter is special.

"He's unbelievable," said Chapman, per The Athletic's Jayson Stark. "I love to watch him."

Looking for the perfect gift for a baseball player in your life? Check out our brand-new baseball lifestyle brand!

The third fastest pitch thrown in the Statcast era belongs to Ben Joyce, at 105.5 mph. However, this year, Misiorowski tied him with a 105.5 mph fastball to Pete Crow-Armstrong. It is the fastest pitch ever recorded by a starting pitcher in the Statcast era.

Chapman has been amazing fans with his velocity for years, but now there's a player who's able to match him on the radar gun as a starter. What makes Misiorowski so impressive is the fact that he maintains his velocity late into games. While Chapman comes in for an inning and blows his fastball by hitters for one inning, Misiorowski is doing it for six innings every five days.

title: Stephen A. Smith thinks Giants should pursue Browns quarterback
description: Stephen A. Smith has an idea for the New York Giants regarding their quarterback situation.
fullText:
The New York Giants will be without starting quarterback Jaxson Dart for the rest of the regular season.

Head coach John Harbaugh confirmed the news on Wednesday. Dart has damage to his MCL, PCL, and meniscus. Per ESPN's Adam Schefter, the meniscus is the main issue.

MORE: 4 potential Jaxson Dart replacements as Giants assess QB situation

Jameis Winston will be the Giants' starting quarterback for now, but ESPN's Stephen A. Smith has a better idea. He thinks the team should go after Cleveland Browns quarterback Shedeur Sanders since he's behind Deshaun Watson on the depth chart.

"I would tell the Giants to go and pursue Shedeur Sanders," Smith said on "First Take." "That would be what was on my mind, personally."

Jun 5, 2026; San Antonio, Texas, USA; Stephen A. Smith looks on before the game between the San Antonio Spurs and the New York Knicks in game two of the 2026 NBA Finals at Frost Bank Center. Mandatory Credit: Scott Wachter-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Even though Watson is the Browns' starting quarterback right now, they likely won't deal Sanders. They still see him as part of their future, and they'll likely need him at some point this season.

The Giants will likely have to look at other options, like Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Flacco. He's a bit older, but still has a ton of starting experience in the NFL.

In the meantime, Winston will start for the Giants this Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. They'll need him to play much better than he did on Monday against the Los Angeles Rams, when he completed 11-of-27 passes for 111 yards and an interception.

Kickoff will be at 1 p.m. ET on CBS.

title: 6-foot-7 Tyten Wedig helping to lead Columbia football's turnaround season
description: Columbia hosts South Glens Falls on Friday night in Class A play.
fullText:
EAST GREENBUSH - He was nearly named for someone most kids today know from the title of a popular football video game.

And, given that Tyten Wedig has come to excel at football, a first name of "Madden" - after Pro Football Hall of Famer John Madden - certainly would have fit.

His parents, though, "really liked Titan." And, since his mother wanted the option to call him "Ty," the family made the slight tweak to the spelling of the name, which has proven quite apropos.

"They didn't know," Wedig joked, "I would get this big."

Only a junior at Columbia High, Wedig stands 6-foot-7.

And, now, the Oklahoma native who moved to East Greenbush with his family when he was in the second grade, is becoming one of Section 2 football's top linemen and generating plenty of Division I interest.

Columbia coach Jake Preston first met Wedig at a youth football banquet.

"He was not that coordinated then - but he was so much bigger than the rest of them," said Preston, who is now in his fourth season leading the varsity. "I heard his name was Tyten, which I thought was incredible."

Over the years, Wedig has grown into his body. Now in his second season with the varsity, he is a two-way starter for the Blue Devils.

"He has been awesome for us," Preston said. "He has worked his tail off."

Following Columbia's Week 1 victory over Queensbury, Wedig did a game-day visit to Syracuse University. He also has future visits lined up with the University at Buffalo and Marist, plus has drawn interest from other Division I programs.

"It has taken off for him this summer and fall. It is still very early for him in the recruiting process," Preston said. "He went to a ton of camps and has been in contact with a ton of coaches."

At the moment, Wedig's attention is dialed in on helping to lead the Blue Devils to a winning 2026 season after the team finished 2-8 overall last fall. Ranked No. 21 in the state's Class A poll, Columbia (3-0 overall, 3-0 Class A) returns to action Friday when it hosts South Glens Falls (0-3, 0-2) as part of the district's homecoming weekend.

"That (winning) is what I am focused on right now. I want to make it into the playoffs and do some damage. I think we can go out there and show people we're the real deal," Wedig said.

Wedig, who wears jersey No. 52 in honor of former Green Bay Packers linebacker Clay Matthews III, cited a number of factors that have helped him to elevate his skills as an offensive tackle and as a defensive player who splits time between tackle and end. One of the biggest helps to Wedig has been teammate Adam Burek, a senior captain who also is a two-way starting lineman for the Blue Devils.

"I could go on for hours about how much he has helped me," Wedig said of Burek. "He has taken me under his wing. I met him in modified. He has helped me so much. I really can't say it in words. He has helped with power, speed and how to block a guy. He has provided constant advice and he is a great leader for our team. I wouldn't be where I am without him."

Preston called Burek "an incredible ambassador for our program," and credited the senior's example for helping Wedig become "married to the weight room." Burek said he's enjoyed watching the strides Wedig has made.

"From the time when I was a sophomore and he was a freshman, it was very fun to watch him grow as a player and a person," Burek said of Wedig. "I would say he was very physically mature for his age when he was younger - but, mentally, he wasn't there (with football). He took a very big step going into his sophomore year, starting on varsity, and an even bigger leap going into his junior year."

An honors student who served as the varsity basketball team's starting center this past winter, Wedig also shows great emotional intelligence on the football field. There have been times this season when opponents, unable to deal with Wedig's size, tried to bait him into a penalty after the whistle.

Each time, the junior walked away.

"I like to let my game speak for itself. I am not going to let another kid get into my head," Wedig said.

"He is very good at keeping his emotions under control," Burek said. "He is good at using his emotions at the right times, and good at being aggressive when he needs to be."

During the offseason, Wedig added 15 pounds of muscle to his frame through weight training. He also worked on his skills with Burek and Co., as the Blue Devils looked to turn the page from their disappointing 2025 campaign.

"I worked a lot on strength and conditioning. Coach (Tom) Libardi has helped me so much. He has me keeping track of everything. I owe a lot to him," Wedig said. "I feel like I am 10 times the player I was last year; I wasn't as physical and my feet were a lot slower last year. I focused on those two things the most."

When it comes to a potential major in college, Wedig intends to pursue either aerospace or mechanical engineering.

"He is incredibly smart. Just talking to him … you realize he is brilliant," Preston said. "The sky is the limit for him, and I love the fact he has the academics. The biggest thing he says all the time is that there is life after football."

Wedig said his love for football grew incredibly when he made his first varsity start last year at Union College vs. Brewster. He said the feeling that came over him during introductions convinced him he wants to pursue playing the sport in college.

"I want it more than anything in the world," Wedig said. "I love the feeling of going out there, working as hard as I can - the feeling of being in pain - and being better than I was last week. … I like improving and looking back on how much I have grown as a person, a player and as a man."

Right now, though, the focus is on helping Columbia improve to 4-0 after this week's homecoming game.

"The feeling of winning with your brothers beside you is better than anything," Wedig said.

There's more to Albany with the Times Union. 

This article originally published at 6-foot-7 Tyten Wedig helping to lead Columbia football's turnaround season.

title: Josue De Paula Earns Rave Reviews From Dodgers Leadership Despite Demotion
description: Dodgers top prospect Josue De Paula is no longer on the active roster, but the major league team had nothing but positive things to say.
fullText:
Los Angeles Dodgers top prospect Josue De Paula is no longer on the active roster after getting sent down to Triple-A, but the major league team had nothing but positive things to say.

De Paula played just 11 games with the Dodgers, but he delivered outstanding offensive production and quickly earned the fanbase's adoration as a young presence at the plate.

However, he was demoted as Shohei Ohtani neared activation from the injured list. Fans who bought into what the 21-year-old showed were disappointed, but the organization seemed just as reluctant to see him go.

After the move was announced, manager Dave Roberts said De Paula, as the team's default designated hitter, was set to lose at-bats now that Ohtani returned.

Still, De Paula earned a postseason look, and the team will factor him into its plans.

"We had a runway to give him, which we gave him, and he performed more than admirably. He's a part of the conversation, and he's earned that, and that's what I told him last night," Roberts said to the media, including Dodgers Nation's Noel Sanchez.

In terms of skill set, Roberts sees all of De Paul's traits — the plate approach, swing decision, and vision to deliver in the postseason.

"He's just a special hitter," Roberts added. "Hitters don't see the ball that quickly out of hand; it's a gift. Just the ability to [limit] chase, I think that lines up in the postseason. And no moment is going to be too big for that kid."

Through 11 games in the big leagues, De Paul is hitting .323/.500/.545 with a 1.081 OPS. He is getting on base during half of his plate appearances, and he is really making hitters work.

Andrew Friedman, the president of baseball operations, had been following De Paula closely, and despite the otherworldly production, the Dodgers executive was not surprised.

"It's what you expect, but you never really know until you see it," Friedman said to the media, including Dodgers Nation.

"But it obviously really stood out, and he's done everything he can to put himself in a position to be in the conversation for us as we're making our postseason roster."

Meanwhile, Josue De Paula gets the chance to show what he can do defensively in Triple-A while the Dodgers decide.

title: Xi says China and US must ensure AI ‘is always under human control’ as Trump touts ‘great friendship’ before White House talks – live
description:
Xi arrived at the White House on Thursday morning ahead of major talks, which are expected to cover trade, AI, Taiwan and more
In the first row in front of the leaders sit US vice-president JD Vance and his wife Usha Vance, Trump’s daughter Ivanka Trump and her daughter Arabella, US secretary of state Marco Rubio, treasury secretary Scott Bessent, defence secretary Pete Hegseth and commerce secretary Howard Lutnick.
Donald Trump is speaking now. He notes that Xi is the first Chinese leader to make a second formal visit to the White House, and says the two have “forged a truly great friendship” since Trump was first elected in 2016.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Here is brief recap of the remarks made by Donald Trump and Xi Jinping just now on the Chinese president’s landmark state visit to Washington.

Trump touted their “truly great friendship” and that they had made “tremendous strides on the issues facing our countries” as he welcomed Xi to the White House. He kept his remarks vague and focused on their personal relationship, of which he said he is “very proud”. Trump said the two leaders would focus on security, technology and artificial intelligence at their summit today, and are working towards “a more balanced trade relationship”.

Xi, meanwhile, struck a very different tone, acknowledging that he and Trump have built a “personal rapport” but concentrating his remarks on geopolitical concerns. Xi called for continued dialogue and the building of mutual trust, understanding and peaceful co-existence between the two countries and to avoid conflict. He stressed that Chinese and US interests are “deeply intertwined” and that they “stand to gain from co-operation and will both lose in conflict”. He also stated clearly his hope that Chinese companies would be “treated fairly” in the United States.

The Chinese leader also emphasised their joint, historic responsibility as leading nations in artificial intelligence. Both the US and China have the capability and responsibility to manage AI for good, he stressed, and must “ensure the development of AI is always under human control and serve the wellbeing of the people”.

The two men are meeting now in the Oval Office, where they will discuss the fragile trade-war truce, Taiwan, AI and China’s support for Iran and for Russia’s war in Ukraine. A breakthrough is unlikely today for the world’s two most powerful nations, but stick with us as we bring you all the latest out of the meeting.

fullText:
US consumers are starting to opt out of the streaming world as several services raise prices without offering many perks

It may not be quite as politically buzzy as the price of gasoline or eggs, but another household expense is going up for millions of people. Disney has brought the price-gouging experience of its theme park home again by raising the prices of most iterations and bundles of its Disney+ and Hulu streaming services. Whether you pay to watch them with or without ads, separately or bundled together, you’re probably getting a price hike of a couple of bucks per month. The few bundles that will remain the same price feature ad-supported versions of both services (plus ESPN). Don’t worry, though; paying extra to avoid the ad-supported versions of those services won’t mean that you’re missing out on some cross-promotional opportunities. Disney’s terms of service note that they reserve the right to insert ads before and after programming on whatever subscription tier they want, regardless of what you’re paying for. True magic!

This particular magic isn’t reserved for Disney, though. Price hikes among streaming services have become so common that The Verge has a dedicated page aggregating the news of them, which tends to arrive every few months. Apple, apparently high on Emmy fumes, has raised its prices four times in four years, keeping pace with many of its competitors despite a vastly smaller dedicated catalog. Depending on which version of Peacock subscribers use, they’ve seen their bills padded by five or six dollars a month just since the summer of 2025, including another increase last month. Netflix, meanwhile, hasn’t gone up since March 2026. That’s not a reprieve; that’s a sign another hike must be around the corner.

Consumers have noticed. Reportedly an estimated 39% of Americans canceled a streaming service in the past six months due to what’s been dubbed “streamflation”. Another survey indicates that a majority of people Access to the six big streaming services (Netflix, Disney+/Hulu, HBO Max, Paramount+, Apple TV, Peacock) will boost that number somewhere in the neighborhood of $120, on top of which subscribers need broadband internet for the services to actually work. For the total price, you might as well call the whole thing Cable+, in that it’s like your old cable bill, only there’s more of it. No wonder cancellations are rampant.

To retain subscribers without putting the screws directly to them, it might be viable for streaming companies to stabilize annual prices – typically a discounted lump-sum payment covering a full year of a service – even when raising monthly costs. Some, like Netflix, don’t offer this option. While those that do have kept annual subscriptions cheaper than the a year’s worth of month-to-month, companies don’t seem interested in maintaining bargain levels. The annual price for Disney+ at launch was $70. Now it’s $190, an increase of 170% – presumably to stay competitive with eggs. Amazon Prime, whose streaming service began as a perk for members already paying an annual membership fee for unlimited shipping and other benefits, has also risen while inserting more ads into its programming and downgrading the picture quality. You want higher resolution and fewer ads? That’s another $50 a year.

The reasons for all this shameless gauging are pretty simple: Wall Street doesn’t just demand profits (though those have sometimes been scarce in the streaming world) but endless growth, and some services don’t have all that much more room, realistically, to sign up more users any more. Netflix has 325 million subscribers worldwide. What’s their reach goal? 500 million? Three billion? What happens when everyone on Earth with an internet connection and a credit card already has Netflix?

Not every service is so close to a saturation point (unless you count electricity as a streaming service). But it’s notable that even a supposedly lower-tier streamer like Peacock commands over 40 million monthly subscribers, equivalent to more than 10% of the United States population. (It’s a heavily US-skewing service, so unlike Netflix those users aren’t especially global.) By comparison, the biggest magazine in the US has a subscriber base of around half that (and that’s the AARP magazine, an outlier in that it’s distributed to paying members). The New York Times, considered an especially successful recent example of the subscription model, has 13 million subscribers. The AMC Stubs A-List program that allows moviegoers to see four films a week has about 1 million.

That’s all to say that streaming has unprecedented reach, which means the only realistic way to boost profits is to either raise subscription prices, or make less stuff. The latter might sound ridiculous, especially given that we’ve been living in the post-boom age for streaming shows for a while now. Then again, that’s worked out well for the catalog-based Tubi, whose original works are lower-profile and lower-budget than its competitors. One of several free streaming services, Tubi outstrips some of those paid competitors in market share and turns a profit based only on its ads.

Watching a movie or a show on a free service isn’t exactly an optimal experience; there are those ad breaks, sometimes the transfers aren’t top-notch, and the content churn tends to be a little faster than the subscription streamers. It’s definitely not a place where you can catch much of anything nominated for an Emmy in the past five or six years (though some Oscar movies or second-tier popular hits from that period might turn up). On the other hand, free streamers often manage to under-promise and over-deliver; at a time when paid subscriptions seem eager to offer less than ever, especially in the quite broad field of films made before 1995, Tubi, PlutoTV and their ilk always have at least a couple dozen stone-cold classics on hand that more than make up for not including the latest big-name time-wasters (looking at you, Matthew McConaughey/Woody Harrelson sitcom where they play themselves!). And the price always stays the same.

Still, some free streaming services with surprisingly robust and shifting catalogs aren’t exactly the dream of cord-cutting that was fed to consumers throughout the 2010s. The initial idea was to shed the bloat from all-or-nothing cable services that hold monopolies, or something close to it, in plenty of geographic areas. Competition for subscribers would keep good deals in the offing. Instead, what’s been happening over the past five years or so is a redistribution of that money from one set of giant companies to another. There’s slightly more consumer control over the size of the bills, in the sense that, yes, it’s possible to cancel a couple of services in a way that picking and choosing individual cable channels wasn’t possible outsidea few premium subscriptions. But there’s also far less clarity about how to catch the best shows and movies of any given year. For ages, it was mostly a simple formulation: have cable, add HBO. Now even the prestige of HBO seems a little more niche – a Game of Thrones spin-off; a well-liked Green Lantern show – than in the past.

There’s also a strange sense that this scramble of greed isn’t paying off as well as it should; many streaming services feel like they’re in far more precarious financial positions than most cable companies or channels were at their peak. It’s a dystopian development: corporations still want consumers on the hook for endless subscription payments, but also seem to want them to share in the nervous stock-checking of a shareholder, without any particular upside. Each month, you check your streaming holdings and see if you’re about to be charged even more, and whether you need to pick one to divest (cancel, whether for good or for now). You can toggle some of them on and off timed to the occasional appearance of a major series like Severance or The Pitt, but the onus for keeping track of erratic streaming schedules is on the subscriber. None of these shows are as necessary as basic groceries. But the ability to relax and watch TV after a long day is still in danger of becoming another budget-related stressor – an unholy combination of cable bloat and the endless doomscroll.

title: Climate protesters say tech companies, not AI, are the real ‘danger to humankind’ – and the planet
description:
Activists gathered outside the OpenAI offices on Monday during climate week in New York City
On Monday evening, protesters gathered outside the unmarked Manhattan offices of OpenAI, maker of ChatGPT, holding signs calling to “Eat the rich, save the planet”. Over the next two days, groups also picketed outside the offices of fellow tech giants Google and Amazon; other protesters, including clergy, were arrested while disrupting a closed-door AI health summit in the city. Tonight, protesters will target a Brooklyn gas power plant that was set to close – until it was purchased to power AI datacenters.
The protests come on the heels of an Anthropic employee quitting his job with a warning that intensified an already-growing AI panic: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Activists gathered outside the OpenAI offices on Monday during climate week in New York City

On Monday evening, protesters gathered outside the unmarked Manhattan offices of OpenAI, maker of ChatGPT, holding signs calling to “Eat the rich, save the planet”. Over the next two days, groups also picketed outside the offices of fellow tech giants Google and Amazon; other protesters, including clergy, were arrested while disrupting a closed-door AI health summit in the city. Tonight, protesters will target a Brooklyn gas power plant that was set to close – until it was purchased to power AI datacenters.

The protests come on the heels of an Anthropic employee quitting his job with a warning that intensified an already-growing AI panic: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Though it was far from the first time an AI expert had issued a doomsday message about the threat the tech poses, this time it dominated public attention, arriving as trust in big tech has hit an all-time low and communities across the country are trying to stop the building of datacenters. From 2024 to 2026, at least $64bn in proposed datacenter buildout was blocked by local organizing. Today, bans have been passed in at least 18 states at the local or county level, and New York passed a statewide moratorium this summer.

“They are claiming that they have the power to end humanity, but at the same time can’t get AI to do a lot of major things that they’re pushing for,” said Jonathan Westin of Climate Defenders and the Stop Funding Billionaires campaign, which organized the “unplug AI” week of action.

Like Westin, many of the protesters at the anti-AI protests this week were part of climate organizations, in town for New York’s climate week, a global gathering of elected officials, policy experts and advocates timed to the meeting of the United Nations general assembly. Datacenters require significant amounts of water to function and an immense amount of energy to power, often using fossil fuels, bringing pollution into communities. Organizers are calling for more datacenter moratoriums and stronger commitments to protect water access and to block fossil fuels. They say tech companies’ greed is the real threat to the environment.

Even Wall Street has warned the AI boom could cause another economic bubble to burst – one that, protesters say, will be carried on the backs of working Americans. “Regular people shouldn’t be left holding the bag for a bunch of billionaires and trillionaires to play Monopoly with our economy,” Westin said.

Other groups at this week’s protests, like the anti-war organization Code Pink, called attention to how many big tech corporations work with the US military: the US has used tech made by Palantir, xAI and Anthropic to establish targets and rain down bombs in the war in Iran – all with far-from-perfect accuracy.

Alex Hanna, director of research at the Dair Institute, an AI research organization centering communities facing environmental damage and extraction from AI, said the doomsday prophesying from tech companies and former employees are a distraction amid “the climate and ecological crisis, the rising fascism that is borne out of climate politics, the making of climate refugees, and the growing inability of people just to get by from day to day. It’s such a disconnect from what seems to be actually happening.”

Some protesters outside the OpenAI offices Monday had traveled from New Mexico, where a planned datacenter threatens the already-sapped Rio Grande and a community facing a 20-year drought. Oracle’s Project Jupiter, which is contracted to OpenAI, was pitched as a job creator for the community, but organizers say the companies aren’t talking about how it would drain the area’s limited water resources.

“There’s just so much misinformation that’s being sold, not only to the elected [officials], but to the community, and I think it’s really a disservice to the people of New Mexico for these companies to come in and just basically lie about what they’re going to do and how these projects are going to benefit communities,” said Daisy Maldonado, a resident of Doña Ana county, the planned site of the datacenter.

At an AI sustainability conference elsewhere in the city on Tuesday, five protesters were arrested for disrupting a keynote on using AI to solve the energy grid crisis. Activists called out the conference framing as “greenwashing”, or using misleading descriptions to brand something as eco-friendly or less harmful. “We do not want to greenwash these datacenters that are being built,” said Adrosto de Silva, who also traveled from New Mexico to the OpenAI protest. “There is no way that you can do harm reduction in any sort of datacenter whatsoever.”

At Monday’s protest, attendees – including the Tennessee state representative Justin Jones, who dropped in while in town for climate week – emphasized that many of these fights are happening in communities of color and poor communities, where the companies thought they wouldn’t face local backlash.

“This building behind me is a danger to humankind,” said Jones, gesturing at the OpenAI offices. “The confluence of this techno oligarchy is a threat to us all. I’m here because if they come for one of us, they’re coming for all of us.”

title: Global bond sell-off piles new pressure on UK borrowing costs before budget
description: Rising cost of 10-year gilt to near 19-year high hikes upfront cost of government investment and limits chancellor’s room for...
fullText:
Rising cost of 10-year gilt to near 19-year high hikes upfront cost of government investment and limits chancellor’s room for manoeuvre

International bodies warn of rising debt and borrowing risks

Burnham stands by claim UK is ‘in hock’ to bond markets

A global sell-off in government bonds has put fresh upward pressure on UK borrowing costs, before a tough budget for John Healey next month.

The yield – effectively the interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds, known as gilts, had risen to 5.38% by mid-morning on Thursday, approaching the 19-year high set last week.

Higher interest rates raise the upfront cost of government investment and feed through into Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts of whether the chancellor is on course to meet Labour’s fiscal rules.

Analysts believe recent increases in yields have wiped out more than half of the £24bn “headroom” against the rules that the former chancellor Rachel Reeves had built up at the time of the spring statement in March.

Healey, her successor, has repeatedly promised to meet the rules with a “buffer against uncertainty” but this is widely expected to be significantly lower than £24bn.

Rebuilding it to that level would be likely to require large tax increases or spending cuts; but Treasury sources insist the budget will be “focused”, with important spending decisions postponed to a review next year.

Investors across the main markets have been ditching bonds in recent weeks in a wave of selling prompted by fears of higher inflation and interest rates as the conflict in the Middle East rumbles on.

The Bank of England chief economist, Clare Lombardelli, said in a speech on Thursday that the longer oil prices remained elevated as a result of the war, the more likely it was that UK interest rates would have to rise.

“The longer higher energy prices persist, the greater the risk that indirect effects build and that inflation expectations, wage bargaining and price-setting behaviour begin to adjust in response,” she told an economic conference in Warsaw, Poland.

“On that basis, policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation or weaker activity.”

Higher rates would mean increased mortgage costs for homeowners, at a time when Andy Burnham’s government has promised to offer consumers a “breathing space” against the rising cost of living.

The Bank is also expecting an eye-watering 24% rise in the quarterly energy price cap that determines household utility bills in January, if oil prices remain high.

Lombardelli’s message echoed that of the Bank governor, Andrew Bailey, after the nine-member monetary policy committee left interest rates on hold at 3.75% last week.

She stressed that high oil prices had had less impact on other prices across the economy than the Bank had feared; but the longer they remained high, the greater the risk of inflation becoming entrenched.

As the bond sell-off continued to worsen on Thursday, yields on 30-year US Treasury bonds surged to 5.444% – the highest level since 2004.

Alongside higher inflation, investors appear to be concerned about the risks of uncontrolled US government spending. Some analysts also suggest large-scale bond issuance by AI firms is undermining demand for treasuries.

title: AI hack of Medicare exposes Australia’s vulnerabilities and experts warn ‘there is more of this to come’
description: Council on AI Strategy chief says incident unlikely to be isolated and country should enhance capability to detect and report...
fullText:
Council on AI Strategy chief says incident unlikely to be isolated and country should enhance capability to detect and report incidents

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Technology experts have warned revelations an artificial intelligence agent hacked Medicare’s internal systems will not be the only dangerous breach of government data and have called for Australia to boost its protections against the growing risk.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, challenged the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, on Thursday after the company’s agent infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.

OpenAI alerted the government earlier this month to the June hacking via an email to a public-facing address, a situation Albanese called “obviously unacceptable”.

But the Australian Council on AI Strategy chief executive, Anna-Maria Arabia, said the case was unlikely to be an isolated incident.

“All of the evidence shows that our operating systems are vulnerable,” she told Guardian Australia.

“Frontier AI now has capability to expose those vulnerabilities at a rate quicker than we can keep up, quicker than we can patch them.

“When the companies are undertaking tests in what they think are secure environments, and when there are breaches of those environments and these incidences do happen, whether it’s accidental or not, what we’re seeing is the frontier AI capability exposing these vulnerabilities.

“All evidence suggests that there is more of this to come.”

Arabia said Australia needed to quickly enhance capability to detect and report incidents, and the country should host AI training labs here.

Johanna Weaver, Australia’s former chief cyber negotiator at the United Nations, agreed more incidents were inevitable.

Weaver is a member of the advisory board to the minister for government services, Katy Gallagher, and the executive director of the Tech Policy Design Institute.

“Cybersecurity experts have been warning that frontier models and AI agents could expose vulnerabilities in critical systems. What we are seeing now is the tip of the iceberg.

“Governments need to draw a clear line: if companies cannot control their AI systems, they should not release them publicly.”

The US Studies Centre expert Olivia Shen warned AI companies should not be allowed to decide on their own disclosure obligations for hacks and breaches.

“We just don’t know how big the problem is. It could be the tip of the iceberg, but either way, we can’t be ignoring the risk.

“It’s all happening at a time when Australia is designing our national standards on AI. It hasn’t been entirely clear if those national standards were going to be very hyper-focused on datacentres and leave governance questions as a bit of a bolt-on.

“I think this strengthens the argument that you need to have some pretty clear standards, even just based on mandatory incident reporting, built in.”

Intelligence agency the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) is reviewing how prepared the government is to block and respond to hacking by AI. Officials will look at policies around how AI companies should report cyber-incidents to the government, and how cooperative companies should be during and after an attack.

It will also investigate whether the current laws and systems are adequate to stop AI, and how government systems can be strengthened.

The shadow industry minister, Andrew Hastie, called for Australia to develop its own domestic AI capability, instead of relying on the US.

“If there’s rogue AI agents out there, we need to have our own defensive AI agents protecting Australian government data, our private sector, and other things that are important to us,” he said.

The Greens demanded Labor call in the new US ambassador, David Brat, to establish what President Donald Trump knew about the attack.

“This breach by a foreign AI company on an Australian government database is deeply alarming and brings home the risks that these out-of-control tech corporations pose,” acting leader, Mehreen Faruqi, said.

“The fact that the government did not even know it happened is disturbing.”

fullText:
On the 31st August I got an email from a customer, telling me that they had found an imitation of my data wrangling software on Github. I’m not linking to it, but here is a screenshot:

It is using our product name and logo, without permission. I reported it to Github as an imitation on the same day. I got this reply:

A colleague scanned the Mac .dmg file from the repository using virustotal.com and got a whole load of malware warnings:

Using Isobuster he found out that they have also changed the background image of the .dmg:

The new image encourages downloaders to ignore any warnings about the malware!

I reported this additional information on the 10th September.

As of the 23rd September, I have had no response from Github support beyond the original automated email. 23 days without a reponse. This is pisspoor. Do better Github.

I’m not sure what my next line of attack is. A DCMA takedown request to Github?

title: Nine countries without internet that never disconnected
description: Nine countries out of range at once, and not one network disconnected. A case of contrasting signals.
fullText:
A case of contrasting signals · Observed State Index

Between the afternoon of 2 September 2026 and the morning of the 3rd, the system flagged nine countries as out of range at the same time in its internet section: Indonesia, Thailand, Japan, Singapore, Australia, Vietnam, Mexico, the Philippines and Hong Kong. The flag was correct, because the signal the system watches had left its range.

But that signal measures a single thing: how many networks answer a probe. Read on its own, it said something that did not happen. It was checked against three other measurements of a different nature, for the same countries and the same hours, and none of them moved. The networks did not disconnect: they stopped answering.

The lesson is not about this event but about what a single signal can claim on its own: a signal that crosses its threshold is a fact about that signal, not yet about the world.

For the internet, the system uses the ping-slash24 signal from IODA, the connectivity measurement project at Georgia Tech. IODA sends probes to blocks of addresses in each country and counts how many respond. The system compares that number with the previous 90 days for the same country, and marks it «out of range» when it moves five standard deviations away or changes by more than 50%.

In IODA's public series, the drop begins in the same ten-minute interval, at 13:40 UTC on 2 September, in eight of the nine countries; in Hong Kong, ten minutes later. It ends between 05:30 and 09:40 UTC on the 3rd. In the system's run at 09:22 UTC on 3 September, all nine were out of range.

Everything pointed to an event. The drops were large: at their worst interval, Indonesia lost more than half of the networks that responded, and Japan more than a third. Everything lined up: the countries formed a coherent geographic group, and the drop began at the same moment in all of them.

IODA's own detector flagged it. For Japan alone it issued seven critical alerts between 14:20 UTC on the 2nd and 09:00 on the 3rd. And a second copy of the system, running in parallel during a migration, flagged it too; that is how it was recorded in the internal documentation — as a confirmation.

It was not one. Both copies read the same IODA API. They were not two witnesses, but the same witness telling the same thing twice.

Besides the probes, IODA publishes other signals per country, and three of them measure different things. BGP counts how many address blocks are still announced in the internet's routing system: a network that disconnects stops being announced. Traffic to Google measures how many real people reach Google's services from that country. The network telescope picks up the background traffic that switched-on machines send, unintentionally, to a range of addresses nobody uses.

When a country loses the internet, all four fall together. Each one was compared over the event window, from 12:00 UTC on 2 September to the same time on the 3rd, against the same window the day before:

Routes did not move by even a tenth of a percent in any country. Traffic to Google repeated its daily curve, and in Singapore it was even higher than the day before. The telescope, a noisy signal, stayed between −7% and +3%, with no drop comparable to that of the probes. Aviation in the region's corridors stayed at its usual level, which makes a physical event unlikely.

During those hours, the networks of those nine countries stayed announced, kept serving their users and stayed switched on. The only thing that fell, for about twenty hours, was the share of networks answering IODA's probes.

That is a fact about the measurement, not about the connectivity of those countries. Anyone reading «internet out of range in Japan» would understand «Japan is having internet problems», and that did not happen.

The cause. With these data it is not possible to tell whether there was a problem on the path between the probes and that region, filtering of the responses, or a fault in the probes themselves. This document does not attribute the event to IODA or to anyone else. IODA's own method combines several signals precisely to tell cases like this apart.

The system stores BGP and the telescope as context signals alongside the probes. BGP was exactly the signal that would have refuted the outage that same day. And it was not being stored. In the run at 09:22 UTC on 3 September, BGP was empty for all 52 countries.

It was not a code error but a clock one. The process asks IODA for the hour that has just closed and was keeping the last interval of each signal. Twelve minutes after the hour closes, the probes are already published and BGP almost never is, so BGP was being stored empty. Nothing gave it away: an empty context value is a valid state, and no alarm was watching it.

It was fixed on 13 September. BGP and the telescope now keep their last interval that has data; the probes do not change. The first run after the fix was at 05:10 UTC on 14 September, at the same minute that used to leave it empty, and BGP arrived for all 52 countries. The earlier days cannot be recovered.

That a signal crossing its threshold is a fact about that signal. To claim something about the world, it takes another signal, of a different nature, saying the same thing.

That confirming with the same source read twice is not confirming, even when it looks as if two systems agree.

That a context signal is only useful if someone checks that it is being stored. This one was in the design, in the code and in the files, and it was empty.

All the figures in the contrast come from IODA's public API (api.ioda.inetintel.cc.gatech.edu), queried per country for 1 to 4 September 2026. Anyone can reproduce them. «Worst interval» is the lowest ten-minute interval against the median of the reference window; BGP and Google are averages over the whole window.

Malaysia also dropped (−23.5% at its worst interval) without reaching its threshold, because each country is measured against its own variability. Poland had a brief dip that afternoon that does not follow the pattern, and was left out. The aviation check covers three of the four time bands of the event: the one at 02:30 UTC on 3 September is not in the system's data. Cloudflare Radar, whose annotations of verified incidents the system uses as context, recorded no outage in those countries on those days.

title: Why Influence Is Deeply Human
description: A software engineer’s perspective on why influence is deeply human, plus reflections from LDX3 and an upcoming free workshop.
fullText:
~7 minute read | Read in browser​

Staff+ Career Coach | Former Staff Engineer

Quick note: I still intend to publish the edition with my thoughts on how AI is reshaping engineering careers, as promised in the last two editions. 🙂 It will go out in the next regularly scheduled edition on Sunday, October 4 at 4 p.m. Pacific.

The two weeks leading up to LDX3 disappeared into final talk preparation, travel, and the conference itself. I came home with plenty to think about, so I’m sending this shorter midweek edition for two reasons.

First, I’d love to invite you to a free interactive workshop on influence I’m hosting as part of the Uncharted Career Series: Build Influence Beyond Technical Expertise, on Thursday, October 1 from 12–1 p.m. Pacific.

Second, my experience speaking at LDX3 gave me a new perspective on influence that I’d like to share with you.

I learned fairly early in my engineering career that I was not especially influential.

I could have strong technical opinions and good reasons behind them. Sometimes those ideas made their way into the code I wrote or the design documents I authored. But they often did not travel much farther.

Other people did not necessarily buy into those ideas just because I thought the reasoning was sound.

That frustrated me for a long time.

At some point, I came across the idea that facts and evidence alone are usually not enough to change someone’s mind. I remember feeling quite irritated by it.

I valued intellectual honesty and rigor. I believed that if we researched a problem carefully, gathered the relevant evidence, and made a strong argument, reasonable people should be persuaded by the quality of the reasoning.

If that was not enough, what exactly were we supposed to do?

The more important realization came years later.

Even after learning that technical correctness alone was insufficient, I was still trying to solve my influence problem through more technical knowledge and better technical arguments.

Looking back, I was treating influence primarily as an intellectual problem: if the reasoning was sound, I assumed people would eventually see what I saw.

But influence is also a deeply human problem.

Once I began taking that seriously, the questions I asked changed.

Before trying to persuade someone, I needed to understand what I was actually trying to influence. What was the current state? What did I want to change? Was I trying to change someone’s understanding of a problem, the priority we gave it, a technical decision, or the action we took next?

I also needed to understand the people involved. What did they already believe? What did they value? What incentives and constraints were shaping their position? What context did they have that I did not? And what kind of relationship existed between us? Or did one need to be built first?

Then there was the ongoing work of advocacy. I had to make my reasoning clear in language that connected with the other person’s context, listen to what came back, incorporate information that changed my own thinking, and continue bridging the distance between our evolving positions.

Over time, these became the three ingredients I believe comprise influence: Clarity of Purpose, Thriving Relationships, and Skillful Advocacy.

None of them replaces technical depth.

But technical depth becomes far more useful when you know what change you are trying to create, understand the humans whose participation that change requires, and can advocate for an idea in a way they can actually engage with.

As my scope at work grew, this became increasingly important.

A technically sound design could not create that participation on its own.

That shift took me years to understand.

​
Today, I see many technically strong engineers get stuck here: when an idea is not gaining traction, they often respond by strengthening the technical argument instead of examining what else may be getting in the way.

That is why I wanted to make the next Uncharted Career Series session an Uncharted Lab focused on influence.

If you have an idea that keeps stalling, a technical concern that is not gaining traction, a difficult stakeholder relationship, or a decision you want to shape, this workshop will give you a practical framework for examining where your influence may be breaking down.

We’ll start with a short lesson on the three ingredients of influence and the technical, organizational, and business contexts in which influence plays out.

Then you’ll apply the framework to a real influence challenge from your own work, followed by group discussion and open Q&A to help refine your thinking and identify one concrete influence move to try next.

​Join me Thursday, October 1 at noon Pacific.​

Last week, I spoke at LDX3 in New York on a very different topic: how working with legacy systems can build technical judgment.

I had spent months trying to create an intellectually rigorous talk. I wanted engineers who had inherited old systems, lived through migrations, and watched earlier technical decisions age to see what those experiences could teach them about judgment.

The talk was incredibly well received, despite a conference schedule with plenty competing for people’s attention. I was speaking at the same time as Charity Majors on the other stage, and my office hours later ran at the same time as Jez Humble’s.

But the strongest signal came afterward.

As soon as my office hours started, one person arrived with a question about designing an interview loop that would hold up in the age of AI. Then more people trickled in.

One engineer wanted to brainstorm how to position years of legacy-heavy experience at a major technology company more favorably in interviews.

Another wanted to talk about how the schema ecosystem I had described in the talk had proliferated so much, and how I would solve the problem today.

Someone else wanted to know what eventually happened to the “magic phone” from one of my stories.

The conversation kept going for 45 minutes, until I finally had to excuse myself for a dinner for which I had already missed the provided transportation.

I also received several messages on LinkedIn and Slack from attendees I hadn’t met, telling me how much the talk had resonated with them.

As I reflected on those conversations, I realized that people had received more than an argument about technical judgment.

Many had recognized their own careers in the talk.

Work they may have considered unglamorous, dated, or even career-limiting could now be seen differently.

Living with imperfect systems had exposed them to decisions and consequences. They had learned things about tradeoffs, operational reality, failure, maintenance, and second-order effects that are difficult to learn from greenfield work alone.

In retrospect, I had been so focused on whether the talk would give people a useful intellectual framework that I had underestimated what can happen when an idea helps someone understand their own experience differently.

That brought me back to something I have written about before:

We can put a lot of care into an argument, a design document, a technical decision, or a conference talk.

But effective influence needs to take into account what another person understands, trusts, remembers, chooses to reconsider, or does differently.

Learning how to do that well takes a lot of practice.

If this edition resonated, I help engineers navigate these exact challenges through 1:1 coaching and a live course on behavioral interviews.

If you’d like more essays like this, you can read past editions here.

You’re receiving this email because we connected in some way: through coaching, a discovery or complimentary call, a 1:1 conversation, a community, a talk, or resources and workshops I’ve shared on behavioral interviews, career growth, and technical leadership. You can unsubscribe at any time.
