title: Netanyahu expected to criticize Mamdani in campaign-style U.N. speech
description:
Benjamin Netanyahu is expected to use his UN address on Thursday to berate New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani for calling him a war criminal, a feud that highlights the Israeli leader's growing isolation ahead of elections at home that he may lose. 
   Addressing the mayor directly ‌in a video statement this week, Netanyahu said he was going to New York "to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers" and "to tell the truth about you." He falsely accused ‌Mamdani of supporting Hamas militants. 
   Mamdani campaigned for office on a promise to have Netanyahu arrested for alleged war crimes should he visit the largest US city but later said he determined he lacked the legal authority to do so. This ​week, Mamdani described Netanyahu as "the architect of a horrific genocide against Palestinians.
fullText:
TEL AVIV, Sept 24 (Reuters) - Benjamin Netanyahu is expected to use his UN address on Thursday to berate New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani for calling him a war criminal, a feud that highlights the Israeli leader's growing isolation ahead of elections at home that he may lose.

Addressing the mayor directly ‌in a video statement this week, Netanyahu said he was going to New York "to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers" and "to tell the truth about you." He falsely accused ‌Mamdani of supporting Hamas militants.

Mamdani campaigned for office on a promise to have Netanyahu arrested for alleged war crimes should he visit the largest US city but later said he determined he lacked the legal authority to do so. This ​week, Mamdani described Netanyahu as "the architect of a horrific genocide against Palestinians."

Netanyahu, who rejects war crimes allegations, will be making his first visit to New York since Mamdani took office in January. Israelis opposed to Netanyahu's right-wing government are planning to protest in New York.

Ahead of his speech, Netanyahu's government paid to place 500 pro-Israel and anti-Iran billboards and dozens of trucks carrying messages in support of Israel across Manhattan, Netanyahu's office said in a statement.

"Freedom doesn't defend itself. America and Israel stand together against terror," one of the billboards states. Under it appears the subtext: "Paid for by the State of Israel".

NETANYAHU ADDRESS TO RESEMBLE 'CAMPAIGN SPEECH'

Israel ‌holds a general election in five weeks that opinion polls suggest could ⁠end Netanyahu's long hold on power.

The campaign is unfolding amid mounting criticism of Israel's Gaza war and without a planned meeting with US President Donald Trump.

"He's not really speaking to the UN, he's speaking to the Israeli public," said former Israeli Ambassador Michael Oren, who expects Netanyahu's address to resemble a "campaign speech."

"Maybe ⁠he's thinking, 'If I can attack Mamdani and attack the Iranians, somebody who was wavering between voting for me and voting for (Gadi) Eisenkot may decide to vote for me,'" Oren said, referring to former military chief Eisenkot, Netanyahu's leading rival.

NETANYAHU NOT EXPECTED TO MEET TRUMP

Netanyahu is making an unusually short visit to the US for his UN address. He arrived in New York around 9 a.m. ET (1300 GMT) and is expected to fly back the ​same ​day after delivering his speech in the afternoon.

The Israeli leader is to meet with the presidents of Argentina, ​Bolivia, Ethiopia, Panama and Paraguay and the vice president of Colombia, and with the ‌prime ministers of Greece, Papua New Guinea and Slovenia, Netanyahu's office said. His office did not say if meetings were planned with US officials.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, two Israeli officials earlier said Netanyahu's team was discussing potentially holding meetings with senior US officials including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, though nothing had been set.

Netanyahu is not expected to meet Trump. The two men jointly launched a war on Iran on February 28, but they found themselves on a collision course after the US and Iran agreed to an interim ceasefire that Netanyahu opposed.

Many Israelis were angered by that deal, and opinion polls showed they questioned Trump's commitment to Israeli security, even as his administration proceeds with billions of dollars in arms sales to Israel's government.

"A lack of any encounter with the president, a month ‌before an Israeli election, will indicate that Trump is keeping a distance from him and will be negative for ​Netanyahu's campaign," said Nimrod Goren, president of Mitvim, an Israeli think tank focused on the country's foreign policy.

The election ​is scheduled for October 27.

ISRAEL CONFRONTS INTERNATIONAL CRITICISM

Israel's longest-serving prime minister, Netanyahu has in the ​past made a visual spectacle of his UN appearances, using charts, diagrams and props to warn of Iran's nuclear program, which Tehran says is for civilian ‌purposes.

Last year several delegations walked out as Netanyahu approached the lectern while supporters ​in the gallery cheered.

Goren said Netanyahu's speech would likely ​follow a familiar script: defending Israel, confronting its critics and warning about Iran while arguing that Israel's opposition to Tehran serves the interests of the wider international community.

He will also likely tout what he sees as his own achievements and close ties to Trump and the US, Goren said.

Israel has faced deepening diplomatic isolation since launching its war in Gaza in ​response to the Hamas-led attacks on Israel nearly three years ago.

Netanyahu ‌is unable to travel to many countries because of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant, issued against him and his former defense minister as well as the then-military commander ​of Hamas in 2024.

Earlier this month, once-steadfast allies Britain, France and Canada announced sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which drew a muted response from ​Washington.

fullText:
Hurricane season is showing no signs of slowing down, with three storms brewing in the Pacific.

Powerful Category 5 Hurricane Polo is sending bands of heavy rain and strong winds across Mexico's southwestern coast, while Tropical Storm Nolo is forecast to intensify into a hurricane late Thursday, threatening Hawaii's Big Island with potentially catastrophic flooding.

Some areas of Hawaii are expected to see up to 35 inches of rain, according to the National Hurricane Center.

A third storm, Hurricane Odalys, is churning over open water far from land.

Polo is forecast to remain a powerful major hurricane for the next few days, with its core expected to stay offshore before moving farther out to sea, according to the NHC. Nonetheless, the storm could produce up to eight inches of rain in parts of Guerrero, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides.

Hurricane conditions caused by Tropical Storm Nolo are possible as early as Friday night in Hawaii County, the NHC said. The National Weather Service said Tropical Storm Nolo would likely strengthen before closing in on the Big Island on Friday or Saturday.

John Bravender, a weather service warning coordination meteorologist, said during a news conference Wednesday afternoon that the heavy downpour "could cause catastrophic flooding," adding, "but when you put that on top of grounds that we've been raining off and on for the last couple of months … that rain could cause even more damage."

Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda told residents, "This is a very serious situation. We do believe that the rain is going to come. It's coming already."

Activity in the Pacific Ocean is being fueled by a "supersized" El Niño climate pattern.

El Niño affects hurricane severity in both the Atlantic and the Pacific. This year's particularly powerful  El Niño conditions, which could become the strongest on record, have led to fewer hurricanes in the Atlantic (particularly the Caribbean) and 

Weather changes fast. Get real-time alerts for your area on the new Yahoo Weather app.

Here's the location, path and status of each of the storms:

According to the National Hurricane Center, Hurricane Polo is a Category 5 storm and is expected to remain a powerful major hurricane for the next few days.

Polo was located about 160 miles south of Manzanillo, Mexico, and about 175 miles west-southwest of Zihuatanejo, Mexico.

It had maximum sustained winds of 160 mph.

It was moving northwest at 9 mph.

A tropical storm warning is in effect from Tecpan de Galeana to Manzanillo, and a tropical storm watch extends west of Manzanillo to Playa Perula.

Coastal parts of Guerrero could see 4 to 6 inches of rain, with isolated totals up to 8 inches, through Thursday.

Coastal parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco could get 2 to 4 inches. The rainfall could produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain.

Swells from Polo will affect southwestern Mexico over the next couple of days and spread toward west-central Mexico and Baja California Sur on Friday and into the weekend, bringing life-threatening surf, rip currents and coastal flooding.

The National Hurricane Center said Tropical Storm Nolo was forecast to strengthen into a hurricane late Thursday and could become a major hurricane by the weekend.

A hurricane watch is in effect for Hawaii County, where hurricane conditions are possible by Friday night.

Nolo is expected to move north or north-northeast through Friday before making a sharp turn west near the Big Island by Saturday.

Nolo was located about 285 miles south of South Point, Hawaii, and about 460 miles south-southeast of Honolulu.

It had maximum sustained winds of 50 mph.

The Big Island could see 15 to 20 inches of rain, with a handful of places seeing up to 35 inches. The conditions may produce catastrophic, life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in steep terrain.

Maui could get 5 to 10 inches of rainfall, with up to 20 inches in some areas, and the rest of the Hawaiian Islands could see 1 to 3 inches of rain, with up to 6 inches possible.

Storm surge could raise water levels 1 to 3 feet above ground in parts of Hawaii County.

Swells from Nolo are expected to reach the Big Island's east- and south-facing shores by Friday, building through the weekend and bringing life-threatening surf and rip-current conditions.

The National Hurricane Center said Hurricane Odalys posed no threat to land. There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.

Odalys is expected to strengthen further over the next day or so before weakening later this week.

Odalys was located about 1,145 miles west-southwest of the southern tip of Baja California.

It had maximum sustained winds of 85 mph.

It was moving east-northeast at 8 mph.

fullText:
Xi Jinping called Thursday for the United States and China to manage their superpower rivalry and keep AI under human control as President Donald Trump gave his Chinese counterpart a lavish welcome at the White House

Trump shook hands with Xi at the start of a day full of pomp and pageantry, but their talks will focus on tense issues -- particularly how to handle the rising challenges posed by artificial intelligence.

The 80-year-old US president hailed what he called his "truly great friendship" with the Chinese leader, with whom he has met three times since returning to power last year.

"Working together, President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries," Trump said.

"During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and super intelligence -- SI."

But while billionaire Trump has repeatedly dismissed fears that AI could pose a threat to humanity, Xi took a more measured tone on the issue.

"We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control," he said at the White House.

Xi added that the two countries had a "historic responsibility of advancing human development and progress" and should "strengthen communication."

The Chinese leader also announced that a pair of pandas -- a traditional symbol of Beijing's diplomacy -- would be heading to a US zoo in a few days.

Few breakthroughs are expected during Xi's state visit. Instead the trip is likely to be more about pomp and pageantry as the world's two biggest economies seek to manage their rivalry.

Trump kicked off things by personally greeting Xi at the airport on Wednesday -- the first time in more than six decades that a US president welcomed a foreign head of state in person at Joint Base Andrews near Washington.

A formal welcome and a handshake on the White House South Lawn launched Thursday's events, which include a military flyover, talks in the Oval Office, and a state dinner.

Trump had earlier said that the 73-year-old Xi looked "strong, vibrant, and fit," following recent rumors about the Chinese leader's health.

But the warm welcome masks deep tensions over thorny topics including the trade war between the world's top two economies, and Beijing's diplomatic and economic support for Iran.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Wednesday announced a two-month extension of a trade truce that was due to expire in November.

Both sides are keen to avoid plunging back into the trade war sparked by the US president's sweeping global tariffs last year.

Trump confirmed on Wednesday that he would discuss his stalled Iran war with Xi, despite earlier playing down reports that Beijing was giving Tehran intelligence.

"I'll be talking about that and many other subjects -- but it's all coming along well," Trump said.

Taiwan will also be on the cards, with Trump's words likely to be watched for any sign of diminishing US support for the self-governing island that Beijing claims as its territory.

Xi's visit will wrap up on Friday morning when the two presidential couples have tea at the White House and then visit the National Archives, home to the US Declaration of Independence.

In his 8-page ruling, U.S.
fullText:
A federal judge in Washington, D.C., issued a temporary restraining order on Thursday, ordering the White House to restore access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters who had been banned by President Trump.

In his 8-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, ordered the White House to "immediately return, reinstate, and restore" access to the news outlets for a period of 14 days, saying their lawsuit against the president was likely to succeed in showing that their press passes were revoked without due process.

But hours after the ruling was issued, some reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were still denied access to the White House grounds, and the outlets requested an immediate hearing.

"This morning journalists from each of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO attempted to enter the White House and were turned away, and Secret Service agents confiscated the hard pass of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated," the outlets said in a court filing early Thursday. I

Kelly ordered the Trump administration to respond to the accusations of non-compliance by midday on Thursday. It was not immediately clear when a hearing might take place.

Trump announced the ban on reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Sept. 18, saying the outlets "constantly write or report fiction or lies" about his administration.

The three news organizations filed a lawsuit in federal court Monday, alleging that Trump had violated their First Amendment rights by retaliating against them for coverage he didn't like.

"President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration," the complaint stated. "But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting."

The organizations argued that their reporters were not afforded due process and are asking a federal judge to quickly rule that Trump's ban is unconstitutional. The filing cites a 1977 ruling by the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which found that the White House cannot arbitrarily deny a journalist a press pass without due process.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the filing stated.

Dozens of media organizations signed an amicus brief in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

The Trump administration filed a response to the suit on Tuesday, arguing that "access to the White House is a privilege — not a right."

It said that Trump concluded that the three news outlets violated "the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."

Trump had previously indicated that he would appeal any ruling against him.

On Friday afternoon, Trump announced the ban in a Truth Social post, saying it was not prompted by any particular stories but was "a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," Trump said at an Oval Office event an hour later while explaining his decision to enact "the ban on the free press."

"There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories," the president said. "If they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house."

According to CNN, Trump's close aide Natalie Harp showed him clips of media coverage shortly before he announced the ban.

On Saturday, reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were turned away from the White House by members of the Secret Service and had their credentials — so-called hard passes needed for access — confiscated.

The journalists — CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett — are listed as plaintiffs in the court filing.

The news outlets are longstanding members of the White House press pool that provides rotating coverage of the administration and travels with the president.

The White House Correspondents' Association condemned the move, saying it violates the First Amendment.

"The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably," Jacqui Heinrich, Fox News senior White House correspondent and WHCA president, said in a statement. "That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."

In response to the ban, four major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — refused to participate in the White House pool, the rotating group of reporters, photographers and videographers that document the president's public events. CNN had been scheduled to serve as the television pool on Monday, including his trip to New York City for the United Nations General Assembly.

As a result, Trump was largely inaudible during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the White House's new helipad on Monday, where he gave a brief speech without the microphone that the pool would typically provide.

Speaking with reporters after arriving at the United Nations on Tuesday, Trump appeared to take issue with the presence of CNN's Kaitlan Collins, saying he was "surprised" to see the journalist.

"You should not be here covering me," Trump said. "You said you weren't going to be covering me."

In a post on X, Collins said she was credentialed by the United Nations to cover the General Assembly.

CNN is scheduled to serve as the television pool Chinese President President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House on Thursday night.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the ban in an appearance on NBC's Today show earlier Tuesday.

"We're not closing CNN," Rubio said. "There aren't a bunch of police officers or soldiers kicking down the doors of MSNBC or MS NOW, whatever it's called, and arresting people and unplugging it from the grid. They're just not allowed to work from the workspace at the White House."

U.S. presidents throughout history have complained about negative coverage of their administrations. In 2009, the Obama administration sought to exclude Fox News from a series of interviews with a Treasury Department official in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, but backed down when the other major television networks objected.

During his first term in office, Trump continued the Oval Office's adversarial relationship with the media, referring to the press as "fake news" and the "enemy of the people." It has escalated in his second.

In 2018, Trump administration officials revoked the press pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta after they said that he had interrupted the president during a news conference. The network sued, and Kelly, the D.C. federal judge, ordered Acosta's credentials restored.

A similar situation played out the following year when the White House revoked Playboy correspondent Brian Karem's press pass over a verbal argument between Karem and Sebastian Gorka, a former White House aide, at a Rose Garden event. A different federal judge ordered the White House to restore Karem's pass.

Last year, Trump barred Associated Press journalists from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some official events after the news service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing.

In December, the Pentagon announced new restraints on journalists, who were asked to sign a pledge affirming that they would not gather unauthorized information for publication. New organizations refused to sign the pledge, and temporarily lost their credentials. The New York Times filed suit, and in March, a federal judge ruled that the Pentagon restrictions were unconstitutional. The Pentagon restored press credentials to the journalists who refused to sign the pledge, while imposing a new rule that they can only enter the Pentagon with an escort. The Times again filed suit and the case is ongoing.

The White House has also made attempts to circumvent traditional broadcast television models. On Monday night, it launched a YouTube stream branded "TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station" that the White House said would showcase "the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place."

Since its launch, Trump TV has featured a rotating stream of Trump's speeches, Oval Office gatherings and other White House events from throughout the president's second term.

The first video showed Trump's remarks on July 3 at Mount Rushmore.

In March, the White House launched an official app that is now the No. 2 most popular news app in the App Store. "The American people are not waiting on those cameras," the White House said in a press release touting the app's ranking. "They are going straight to the Presidency."

In his first event without a network TV pool on Monday, Trump unveiled the White House's new helipad before departing for New York. His remarks were nearly inaudible on the White House video feed. Joe Reberkenny, a White House correspondent for the Washington Blade who was serving as the in-town pool reporter, said he couldn't hear Trump "over the sound of the helicopter."

fullText:
With six weeks to go until Election Day, and early voting already underway in a handful of states, the conventional wisdom is that Republicans may be in for some setbacks in the midterms.

As it defends its fragile House and Senate majorities, the GOP is fighting political history, which has traditionally seen the president's party lose congressional seats during the midterms. It's also battling high costs at the grocery stores and gas pumps tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran, as well as President Donald Trump's underwater approval ratings.

But Democrats are saddled with their own issues, from an ideological civil war between the party's left wing and the establishment that has handed Republicans plenty of political ammunition, to a brand image that's nothing to brag about. Add to that the Democrats' major disadvantage as the GOP floods the airwaves with attack ads.

Here are six forces that will likely determine whether Republicans can turn back a possible blue wave and hold power in Congress.

WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM ELECTION POLLING

Six weeks until Election Day, and just as the voting begins, fuel prices keep rising, with the national average for gas nearly $4.50 per gallon and diesel topping $6.50 per gallon, according to AAA.

Public opinion polls point to the economy, including the cost of living, as the top issue for voters in this year's midterms. That means that the issue that boosted Trump and Republicans to sweeping victories in 2024 is a major liability in 2026. And the rising prices in recent weeks, fueled by renewed fighting in the war with Iran and Ukraine and attacks on Russia's diesel industry, are doing the GOP no favors.

"Gas prices were much higher under Biden than under "TRUMP." So were almost all other prices," the president argued Monday in a social media post, as he referred to former President Joe Biden.

While Trump and Republican leaders point fingers at Biden, polls indicate voters increasingly place the blame for ongoing economic and inflation pressures on the current administration.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Democrats last week heavily criticized Trump and Republicans after the president argued that fuel costs were "a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done," as he pointed to the attacks on Iran's nuclear facilities.

Meanwhile, the latest Fox News poll indicated that by a wide margin, the Democrats are considered the party that would better handle inflation.

But when asked about the overall economy, recent national surveys from Reuters/Ipsos and NBC News had the GOP and Democrats all knotted up on which party would better handle the issue.

"My listeners are looking for prices to come down across the board," New Hampshire-based center-right talk radio host Jack Heath told Fox News Digital.

"People elected President Trump to lower prices and improve their situation and people are looking for that improvement," Heath, host of "Good Morning NH," emphasized. "They're looking for Trump to deliver on his promises."

"I'm asking you to just pretend I'm on the ballot just one more time," the president said last week during a campaign stop in battleground North Carolina.

It's a line Trump repeatedly used earlier this month, at the GOP's first-ever midterm convention.

Facing what polls indicate is an enthusiasm gap with Democrats, the president and Republican leaders are hoping to energize the MAGA base, which doesn't always vote when Trump isn't on the ballot. While the president's approval rating in the Fox News poll stands at 39% among all voters, it remains at a sky-high 98% among self-described MAGA Republicans.

But some longtime Trump allies are starting to break with the president as they face challenging re-elections.

GOP Rep. Maria Salazar won re-election two years ago by 20 points in South Florida's 27th Congressional District. But with Trump's negative poll numbers a potential anchor around her, Salazar last week released a TV ad criticizing the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement as having "gone too far," and that "Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

Meanwhile, on Monday two Trump allies who are in heated Senate battles - Rep. Ashley Hinson of Iowa and former Rep. Mike Rogers of Michigan, broke with the president as they a swift end to the war with Iran.

Watch whether vulnerable Republicans create more distance from the president, or move toward Trump to juice Republican turnout.

Republicans are aiming to turn what's normally a referendum on the party in power into a choice election, as they spotlight major Democratic primary victories this year by far-left and socialist candidates over more mainstream Democrats.

"In state after state, the Democrat establishment has been overthrown and replaced by crazed lunatics and radicals. They call themselves Democrat socialists, but actually, they’re communists," Trump charged at the midterm convention.

The messaging is pronounced in Michigan's crucial Senate race, where GOP nominee former Rep. Mike Rogers, as he referred to Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed, told Fox Business this week, "We don’t want this socialism nonsense in our state, and this guy is too extreme."

12 SENATE RACES THAT WILL DETERMINE WHO CONTROLS THE CHAMBER

Polling gives a boost to the GOP's "commonsense vs. crazy" messaging.

Fifty-five percent of registered voters surveyed in the latest Fox News national poll held an unfavorable view of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), while only three in 10 saw the DSA in a positive light.

The Fox News poll was the latest national survey to show that while the DSA has gained traction among Democrats, the group and the broader socialist movement in America face significant national skepticism.

While the GOP full court press continues, in hopes of swaying undecided voters, Democrats are divided on its effectiveness.

Ty Strong, founder and president of the Moderate PAC, warned that the GOP playbook "absolutely could be effective."

But Shannon Jackson, a key consultant and advisor to progressive leader Rep. Ro Khanna of California, argued that Republicans are "reaching for things. I think the DSA issue is something they’re trying to make something, but it is not."

Meanwhile, this year's primary surge by socialist and left-wing candidates isn't helping Democrats boost their brand.

The party's favorable ratings hit historic lows in the months following the 2024 election, and the latest Fox News poll indicates Democrats are still well underwater, with 55% of voters viewing the party in an unfavorable light.

Republicans enjoy a formidable cash advantage over the Democrats, and they're using it in the final stretch leading up to Election Day.

While Democratic candidates in many key races have outraised their GOP opponents, the Republican National Committee remains far ahead of the rival Democratic National Committee when it comes to cash-on-hand.

And GOP-aligned outside groups, including the Trump-allied MAGA Inc., are opening the floodgates when it comes to ad spending, in order to try and level the playing field by overcoming the difficult political environment.

Republican groups have outspent their Democratic counterparts by more than $83 million to run spots in ten crucial Senate races since the start of September, according to figures from AdImpact, a nationally known firm that tracks ad spending.

While a financial advantage is not always decisive, strategists say it can often move the needle in a close contest. And in the 10 Senate races spotlighted by AdImpact, a onetime Democratic ad spending advantage over the summer turned into a major GOP deluge.

While much of the ad dollars dished out by Republicans are to protect vulnerable seats, the money may help as the GOP works to flip open-Democrat-held Senate seats in Michigan and New Hampshire.

Thirteen months ago, Texas passed a new congressional redistricting map, giving Trump his first major victory in his push to give Republicans a big boost heading into the midterm elections by drawing more right-leaning districts.

Fast-forward to present day, and as they fight to hold their razor-thin House majority, Republicans were the big winners, with partisan redistricting netting them potentially 10 additional right-leaning congressional seats in time for the midterms.

But redrawing the maps and winning the seats are two different things, and some election analysts caution that the fierce headwinds facing the GOP could lead to Republicans falling far short of their original expectations heading into the redistricting wars.

There are 435 seats in the House of Representatives, but the Cook Report suggests the battle for the chamber's majority could come down to just 21 districts it rates as toss-up.

The Fox News Power Rankings list 17 seats as true toss-ups.

Decades of gerrymander, including this cycle's mid-decade redistricting, has made a major impact by narrowing the House battlefield, which may limit the number of pickups by the Democrats even if a blue wave forms.

While the number of competitive House seats stays historically small, the Senate map is widening, which is a positive sign for Democrats.

Democrats are feeling the heat in open-seat contests in Michigan and New Hampshire, two must holds for them as they try to win back a Senate currently controlled 53-47 by the GOP.

But Senate showdowns in red states, including Alaska, Kansas, Nebraska, and Iowa, are now considered very competitive.

Need proof: Vice President JD Vance campaigned in Iowa and Kansas last week.

But recent polling is also giving Republicans hope they can flip the Democrat-controlled open Senate seat in blue-leaning Minnesota.

title: The Best Power Tools to Gift Your Favorite DIYer
description: Whether they're a beginner or an expert, you can give them the ultimate gift this year.
fullText:
It can be hard to choose the perfect gift for that DIY enthusiast on your list who seems to already have every tool imaginable. If you’re looking for just the right thing for someone just starting out on their DIY adventure, or a seasoned weekend warrior, all of the options can be intimidating. As an experienced DIY home maintenance aficionado as well as an experienced carpenter and furniture builder, here are some of my favorite tools to give this year.

My favorite drill and driver set, the new Makita 18-volt LXT drill and driver set, is the best tool for anyone who likes DIY. These tools use an efficient battery system that gives you more work time per charge. The drill in this set can deliver about 70% more torque than its predecessors, and the impact driver has a speed control, allowing you to use more force on tougher materials and less on more delicate jobs. This set is a great gift because it comes ready to use, with an 18-volt hammer drill, an 18-volt impact driver, a 2-amp-hour battery, a 5-amp-hour battery, and a charger.

Makita is known for producing the best batteries on the market, with its first battery-powered drill launching in 1969. These drills are still coveted by pros even today because they were so well-balanced and easy on the wrists. This set builds on that reputation, with light batteries that give you more control over your tools.

The new 20-volt DeWalt oscillating multitool is a great gift for a DIYer of almost any persuasion because it’s so versatile. You can use an oscillating multitool for anything from DIY sink installation to DIY drywall repair. The big improvement for this tool over its previous model is that it has been re-engineered to vibrate less, making it more comfortable and safer to use. It also has a wider cutting radius and a brighter LED.

This set is a great gift because it comes with everything you need to use it right out of the box, including a 20-volt DeWalt oscillating multitool, a 20-volt MAX compact battery, a charger, a tool-connect chip adapter, a fast cut wood blade, a wood with nails blade, a sanding attachment, some sandpaper, and a depth guide.

DeWalt makes some of the best woodworking tools and is known for durable and precise cutting tools.

A Kreg Rebel 20-volt pocket hole joiner is a great gift to give a DIY woodworker because it allows you to make precise joints in half the time. Kreg is known for making quality jigs for making joints and cutting straight lines, but this tool integrates a power tool into the jig, allowing you to line up and drill a pocket hole much more quickly. It comes with the joint-making tool, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, an easy-set drill bit, and dust collection attachments.

I use Kreg jigs for cabinet-making, for quick hidden joints on frames, and for putting together shelving, and this tool is a game changer for all of those projects.

The new 20-volt sealed head DeWalt powered ratchet set is a good choice to give a DIY mechanic because of its unique adapter system. The interchangeable coupling allows you to use this powered ratchet set with both ⅜-inch and ½-inch sockets. The gear mechanism that drives the socket head is protected from metal dust and debris, so it’s more durable than its predecessors.

The set has what you need to use it right out of the box. It comes with a 20-volt cordless-powered ratchet, a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery, and a charger. This ratchet is compact enough to use for oil changes and vehicle maintenance but powerful enough for turning stubborn bolts like the ones on the outside of your HV/AC filter access panel.

The best place to begin a DIY tool set is with a cordless drill. The Ryobi 18-volt cordless drill set is a good gift for a beginner because it’s a decent-quality tool that comes with everything you need to get started, including a battery and bits. For everything from hanging pictures to changing air filters, a drill is an essential tool.

The set comes with an 18-volt drill, an 18-volt, 1.5-amp-hour battery, a charger, a 40-piece bit set, and a tool bag.

The DeWalt 20-volt cordless/corded wet-dry vac is a good gift for someone with a home shop because keeping your shop clean and organized is always its own project. Sawdust buildup can be a hazard because it can be combustible, so a shop vac is also a good gift for safety. This shop vac can tackle both wet and dry messes, so it’s good for cleaning your car or around the garage, as well as in the shop.

This is a tool-only deal, but it can be plugged into a power outlet and work without a battery. The shop vac comes with a hose, a crevice tool, and a HEPA filter.

The Klein digital laser level and angle finder can be used for everything from leveling a mounted TV to making precise cuts when doing woodworking. It’s a good gift for a DIYer at any skill level, and it can be a useful addition even to a well-appointed shop.

This tool uses an internal electric accelerometer instead of a spirit bubble to gauge angles and judge level. This allows you to measure angles based on numbers instead of a visual bubble, but also allows the level to find angles from any starting point you choose.

title: Walsh settles for bronze with semi-final defeat
description: Michaela Walsh will return from the European Boxing Championships in Bulgaria with a bronze medal as she loses out in her featherweight semi-final.
fullText:
Michaela Walsh will return from the European Boxing Championships in Bulgaria with a bronze medal as she lost out in her featherweight semi-final.

The 33-year-old Belfast woman lost on a 4-1 split decision by Kazakhstan-born Hungarian Vladislava Kukhta [29-28, 29-28, 29-28, 29-28, 28-29] after a technical bout of contrasting styles.

Walsh has now secured three podium finishes this year following silver medals at the Commonwealth Games and Strandja Tournament.

"It was very cagey and the tactics were to try and lead her on [into counters] but she is a great operator and it was always just how that first round was going to go as it would dictate the fight," Walsh reflected when speaking to Boxing Ireland.

"I'm proud of my performance and fought to the very end.

"2023 was the last time I was on an international podium [until this year]. I was going through a bit of a stale period, but never gave up, believed in myself and knew I could produce big performances.

"This isn't over, it's just a stepping stone, so onto next year for the Olympic qualifier."

Both took a while to settle and a quiet opener was shaded by southpaw Vladislava on three of the five cards.

The World Boxing Cup Brazil finalist found a home for some straight lefts, while Walsh enjoyed her own moments when quickening the feet to advance and land on the inside.

The pace increased in the second as they began to let their hands go, Vladislava opting for volume to Walsh's more measured approach to draw the lead and counter.

Accumulation would catch the eye as the Hungarian's work was rewarded on all five cards to help her into a healthy lead on three cards with two even.

Walsh needed a big final round and opened well with a right and while Vladislava was not content to coast home as she enjoyed further success with the left, the Belfast woman boxed superbly with consistent shots finding the target.

However, she needed more and although four of the five judges sided with her work, her tournament came to an end.

title: Injury rules Graham out of Scotland's autumn Tests
description: Scotland's record try-scorer Darcy Graham is to miss the autumn internationals against New Zealand, Australia and Japan with a ruptured bicep.
fullText:
Scotland's record try-scorer Darcy Graham is to miss the autumn internationals with a bicep injury.

The 29-year-old Edinburgh winger has 38 tries from his 57 caps but will not have the chance to add to that tally in home Tests against New Zealand, Australia and Japan.

Edinburgh head coach Sean Everitt revealed Graham is facing at least 12 weeks on the sidelines as he recovers from a rupture.

Describing the collision incident as "pretty freakish", Everitt, said: "That's not good news for us and not good news for him, especially with the autumn series coming up."

Scotland continue their Nations Championship fixtures against New Zealand at Murrayfield on 7 November, with Australia and Japan in Edinburgh on the following weekends.

The inaugural series will culminate with a finals weekend at Twickenham on 27 and 28 November.

In the summer, Scotland beat Argentina and Fiji either side of a 42-28 defeat in South Africa, which has Gregor Townsend's side sitting second behind France in the northern hemisphere standings.

title: Bradford 'reluctantly' let Preston talk to Alexander
description: Bradford City "reluctantly" give Championship strugglers Preston permission to speak to boss Graham Alexander about their managerial vacancy.
fullText:
Bradford City have "reluctantly" given Championship strugglers Preston North End permission to speak to boss Graham Alexander about their managerial vacancy.

Paul Heckingbottom was sacked after two years in charge of North End earlier this month following six defeats in their opening seven league games.

Alexander, 54, had two spells at Deepdale as a player and made 372 league appearances for the club.

He had a five-game spell in caretaker charge in 2011-12 before ending his playing career with the Lilywhites at the end of that season, aged 40.

"Bradford City AFC can confirm we have been approached by Preston North End to speak to Graham Alexander regarding the Championship side's managerial vacancy," the Bantams said in a statement., external

"Reluctantly, Bradford City has granted permission for Graham to speak to Preston North End."

BBC Radio Lancashire reports that Preston are down to their final two candidates for the role.

The Bantams are top of League One with five wins from their first seven games of the season.

Alexander took over at Valley Parade in November 2023 and led them to promotion from League Two in his first full season in charge.

They finished fourth in League One in 2025-26 before losing to Bolton Wanderers in the play-offs.

The former Scotland international, who has also had spells in charge of Fleetwood, Scunthorpe, Salford, Motherwell and MK Dons, is contracted to the club until the end of next season.

Preston are second bottom of the Championship with four points from eight matches and host Millwall in their first game after the international break on Saturday, 10 October.

title: Fox makes 'easy decision' to sign three-year Arsenal deal
description: USA international Emily Fox has described signed a new contract at Arsenal as "an easy decision".
fullText:
USA international Emily Fox has described her decision to sign a new contract at Arsenal as "an easy decision".

The 28-year-old has been a key player for the club since joining from North Carolina Courage in 2024 and is understood to have signed a new three-year deal.

She was part of the squad that won the Women's Champions League title in 2025 and the Women's Champions Cup trophy in 2026.

In her first season at the club, she won the Women's League Cup and has been named in the PFA team of the year in the last two campaigns.

Speaking to BBC Sport, she said: "I'm very pleased to be able to continue my journey with Arsenal and it was honestly an easy decision because of where I want to be now, and in a few years' time.

"When I think of how I'm going to grow, be challenged and be in an environment where it's like my second home, I think of Arsenal.

"It is a club that is wanting to continue to push the women's game, invest in it and focus on the community, the history of it, the culture, and wanting to excel."

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

BBC Sport reported in January that Fox had a year remaining on her existing contract but Arsenal were always confident she would stay at the club.

She has established herself as one of the best full-backs in the world and has made almost 100 appearances for Arsenal in all competitions.

However, despite helping Renee Slegers' side to European glory in 2025, Fox feels there is one important medal missing from her collection - the WSL title.

"There is definitely some unfinished business. We want to keep going, keep winning and maybe get some things that we've already won before too," said Fox.

"Being at Arsenal, there's always going to be high expectations from the inside and the outside. That's just part of it.

"When you have big goals like that, you have to take it game-by-game and you can't look too far ahead. That's my approach."

Fox is also preparing for a big summer with the USA, under the management of ex-Chelsea boss Emma Hayes, as they hope to go far at the 2027 Women's World Cup.

"We're starting off strong by playing Spain twice at home in October. This year has been great for us in terms of the opponents and the challenges," she added.

"I feel like we've played a lot of variety with our opponents and it's given us a taste of different environments, different tactics and layers of how we're going to play.

"That's ultimately what you need to do when you want to win a World Cup. In November, we have to qualify. Those are our objectives."

title: New boss Reedijk promises 'brave and intense' Hibs
description: Former Beveren head coach Marink Reedijk vows to develop a "brave, intense and committed" Hibernian team after becoming the club's new manager.
fullText:
Former Beveren head coach Marink Reedijk has vowed to develop a "brave, intense and committed" Hibernian team after becoming the club's new manager.

The Dutchman, 35, replaces David Gray, who was sacked eight days ago after a difficult start to the term for the Scottish Premiership outfit.

Reedijk has spent the last two seasons with Beveren, earning promotion to the top flight last season after an unbeaten campaign before leaving in the summer.

He previous worked in academy roles at Ajax and West Bromwich Albion, and with the senior teams at KSV Roeselare, Vitesse and Anderlecht B.

Hibs say Reedijk - who is "honoured" to be appointed - arrives with a reputation for attacking football and building a strong team culture.

"I can feel the ambition and see the clarity of what the club is trying to achieve," he said. "That was a big part of what attracted me here.

"I want us to be an assertive team. A team that gives everything, plays with purpose and gives our supporters something to really get behind."

Latest Hibs news, analysis and fan views

Get Hibs news notifications in the BBC Sport app

Reedijk will be assisted by Rogier Molhoek at Easter Road, with the club hailing his arrival as "an exciting moment".

Hibs are currently 10th in the Premiership, with two wins from their opening seven matches, and endured a gut-wrenching Conference League play-off exit.

Under Gray, they finished third in 2024-25 and fifth last term, with the departed manager also leading them to November's League Cup semi-finals, where they will face city rivals Hearts.

Sporting director Malky Mackay insists Reedijk's recruitment is not about "changing the direction" of their footbal strategy, but is about "continuing to evolve it".

"We believe Marink is an excellent fit to take the team forward," he added.

"We began this process with a clear idea of the type of team we want to continue to build and the qualities we wanted from our next manager. Marink's philosophy, his work with players and his leadership style are strongly aligned with that.

"His teams are proactive, high energy and dynamic. What also stands out is his ability to develop individuals and create a strong collective environment."

The new boss is not much older than Hibs trio Grant Hanley, Martin Boyle and Joe Newell.

He never played in the professional ranks and his experience as a head coach is from three years in the Belgian second tier.

However, his 'invincibles' run to the title last season, 28 wins and four draws, certainly grabbed attention - as did his decision to step down rather than lead Beveren in the top flight.

Reedijk, who has worked under Thomas Letsch and Phillip Cocu, has a philosophy doctorate in sports coaching and his methods lifted Beveren four places to fourth in his first campaign at the club after a debut term at Anderlecht Futures in the same division.

He spoke of "quality and potential" in a Hibs squad that has looked stale, risk-averse and unimaginative in recent weeks.

Hibs have shown glimpses of what they are capable of with good wins away to Rangers and Dundee, while a stirring second-half display at home to Gent, joint top of the Belgian Pro League, was undone by a calamitous climax.

Reedijk will have a Spanish training camp and four Premiership outings to get Hibs firing before a derby at Hampden, a huge showdown that will most definitely require the bravery and intensity he seeks.

Ross: Decent appointment, time will tell if it's the right one. His credentials and philosophy sits well with me and what we want to achieve. Welcome and all the best.

Lee: Another young manager! Let's get behind him, and the team and give him a chance to show what he is capable of. I hope it works out, because if it doesn't, beyond the dugout is where the spotlight should be.

Tony: Brilliant, good to have someone in quickly. Not a great knowledge of the guy but from what I've read he likes an attacking team with wingers so that's a positive. Will be good to see what he can do with the current squad. It probably won't solve it quickly but let's see.

Alan: Reedijk inherits a good squad that has been under-performing - most obviously since the European disappointment. If he can get off to a good start, particularly at Hampden (!?), he will gain a great deal of goodwill. Good luck to him.

Fraser: Exciting appointment, and something different. Can't accuse the board of not trying with this appointment

Forbes: Time will tell whether he is the right choice or not. Hopefully he does well although his lack of managerial experience is a concern despite doing well at Beveren.

Duncan: Best of luck to the guy, but this is our 15th manager in 20 years. And I can count on the fingers of one hand the number that have done a good job. When will we learn that maybe the manager isn't the problem?

Malcolm: How does this guy have a record of knowing Scottish football? This is going to be another waste of time with relegation coming our way. What was wrong with Steve Clarke?

title: Teenager Ohashi overcomes Covid to set world record
description: Shin Ohashi, 17, claims his second gold medal of the Asian Games with a world record in the 200m breaststroke.
fullText:
Japanese teenager Shin Ohashi broke the 200m breaststroke world record at the Asian Games, despite contracting Covid-19 in the build-up.

Ohashi, 17, won in two minutes 4.83 seconds to comfortably break the previous record of 2:05.48, which was set by China's Qin Haiyang at the 2023 World Championships.

Ohashi is the second teenage prodigy to make headlines during these Games after China's Yu Zidi, 13, won her third gold on Wednesday.

It is his second gold of the Games after he shared the 100m breaststroke title with China's Dong Zhihao earlier this week.

"Regarding Covid, after all, there was a part where it created a little anxiety for me mentally," Ohashi said after his victory.

"But, conversely, physically I think it was good that I was able to properly rest my body as a period ​of recovery."

Ohashi won five golds at the World Junior Championships last year, with France's Leon Marchand, the sensation in the pool at the 2024 Paris Olympics, describing the youngster as a "scary" prospect.

Meanwhile, Zhang Zhanshuo, 19, won his sixth gold of the Games as China won the 4x100m freestyle relay.

Sarah Bonar and Hannah Ramsay also come into the starting line-up as interim head coach Dave Butcher makes four changes following the 66-14 defeat by New Zealand.

title: From ruin to a (Red) Bull market - how Prem became hot property
description: Prem Rugby seemed on the brink of disaster after Worcester, Wasps and London Irish went bust, but there is renewed confidence and fresh money in the league.
fullText:
Simon Massie-Taylor pulled up outside Newcastle's Kingston Park stadium, and saw fear.

The unannounced arrival of Prem Rugby's chief executive at one of the league's clubs had rarely been a good sign.

Massie-Taylor started the role in January 2022. In the 18 months that followed, Wasps, Worcester and London Irish, with finances stretched out of shape by Covid, had flamed out of the English top flight.

"When those clubs were going into administration, the common denominator was their leadership leaving the room," remembers Massie-Taylor.

"The owners, the chief executives, everyone went.

"So it was basically up to me, [Rugby Players Association general secretary] Christian Day and [Rugby Football Union director of legal and governance] Angus Bujalski to go in and say, 'we're terribly sorry, this is what's happened, this is what it means for you'.

"Telling anyone that they've lost their job is one of the worst bits of having a job. But when it comes to sport, for the people that work in those clubs, it's not just a job, it's a way of life. It was horrible."

So when Massie-Taylor pitched up at Newcastle last year, with the club limping from payroll to payroll, onlookers feared the worse.

"Some of the players and staff, when they first saw me, thought I was this grim reaper figure coming to deliver another bad news story," he said.

Instead he ushered Newcastle's staff into a room decked out in the blue and silver branding of Red Bull.

Backed by a hype video filled with signature extreme sport stunts, executives from the energy drink giant, fresh off a flight, spelled out a grand vision for the Prem's bottom club.

"There were people in that room in tears, it was pretty special," said Massie-Taylor.

That investment was a pivot point for the league.

Massie-Taylor remembers how low the bar was to buy into the Prem in his first few, stressful years. "It was 'do you exist, have you got a criminal record, do you actually have any money?," he says.

But Red Bull's arrival, sealed and delivered in August 2025, marked a sea change.

Since then Black Knight - the owners of Premier League side Bournemouth - have bought up Exeter Chiefs, billionaire industrialist Sir James Dyson has taken a 50% share of Bath and financier Steve Zander has made a multi-million pound investment into Northampton Saints., external

More outside investment is expected soon, with Gloucester and Leicester among those in conversations.

"Investor interest in the league has increased significantly in the last 12 months, certainly the last six," says Massie-Taylor, who convened a summit for prospective buyers in London in June and is heading to the United States in October to press flesh and make the case.

His confidence is shared by more impartial experts.

Matthew Wheeler helped broker Red Bull's takeover of Newcastle, but his specialist investment group A&W Capital has made deals across a variety of sports and media.

"I don't think you're drunk from the Kool-Aid to have belief in the Prem, there definitely is a momentum behind it," he says.

Andrew Umbers is a co-founder of Oakwell Sports Advisory, which had a similar role in Exeter's takeover.

"We put Exeter in front just over 110 sports investors and we had interest probably from around 30," he says. "That interest came from North America, Asia and continental Europe."

It is quite the difference from when Massie-Taylor would entertain enquiries from anyone with proof of identity, a clean chargesheet and a positive bank balance.

There are a few factors that are happy coincidence, rather than canny design.

The value of sports teams generally has risen steeply. The sale of the LA Lakers for a record $12.5bn (£9.3bn) this summer is the prime example.

Wheeler puts the spike down to the guaranteed eyeballs sport attracts in a fragmented media world, its relative resistance to disruption by artificial intelligence as a product and the prestige and scarcity value of owning a sports team.

Prem Rugby was also on an upward growth trajectory before the Covid pandemic hit. Even with the loss of three teams, a return to normality has allowed the league to rediscover that groove.

A brand of the heft of Red Bull getting involved in the league, undoubtedly sparked interest elsewhere.

Friday 25 September - Saturday 19 June

Commentary of every Prem Rugby game is available on BBC local radio, via BBC Sounds or the BBC Sport website.

However, proactive changes have played a part.

An independent financial monitoring panel has kept across all Prem club finances for the past couple of seasons, and is designed to prevent dangerous levels of risk and spending. That has reassured investors.

With a funding deal with the Rugby Football Union and broadcast partnership with TNT Sports locked in for several seasons, there is stability for the foreseeable.

A calendar shift, external has meant England internationals are available more often to their clubs, raising the wattage on the domestic game's star power.

And, while Massie-Taylor won't say it himself, he has inspired confidence. A former investment banker, he understands what prospective buyers are looking for.

"He's done a good job," says Wheeler.

"The governance is important because the first thing an investor wants to know is can they rely on the management and is the league going to be well run.

"You may be buying into an individual team, but you're really buying into the league.

"You can have the most successful team you want, but if the league's not successful, it doesn't mean anything."

Massie-Taylor's most important decision might be his most controversial.

He backed the ring-fencing of the league, scrapping relegation and bringing new teams in via a tender process rather than achievements on the pitch.

This season is the first to be played out without even a hint of jeopardy at the bottom of the table.

It has been unpopular with fans.

While some see a betrayal of sporting tradition, the change gives Prem Rugby a point of difference over lower-level football sides competing for the same investment.

No possible drop down the leagues, no danger of a distressed asset.

"It is a real thing for US investors," says Massie-Taylor.

"There was a fear and, to some extent, a handbrake on investment because of that financial jeopardy."

It is just one aspect of the league that makes prospective American buyers comfortable.

The upper and, from this season, lower limits on how much Prem clubs can spend on players' salaries are common in Stateside sport, as is the equitable sharing of media revenues.

There has also been a shift to centralise deals and maximise revenues.

A proposal to have one kit manufacturer for the whole league - something seen in America's 'big four' leagues (NBA, NFL, MLB and NHL) - has been floated in the past.

"For an investor, owning a Prem Rugby team is more is more like owning an NFL team than it is like owning a Premier League football team [in that regard]," says Wheeler.

It was noticeable that Brett Gosper, formerly the head of World Rugby, now leading NFL Europe, was on hand at Prem Rugby's investor summit to underline those parallels.

The combination of features of a franchise league, with the long rivalries and established, loyal fanbases that a start-up competition lacks, makes the Prem a rare prospect.

"American investors are interested in under-commercialised sport, below the tier-one leagues such as Premier League, NFL or the IPL, that are at a turning point in their cycle," says Umbers.

"We think Prem Rugby is one of those."

"Rugby is not a big sport in America, so there has got to be some education going on," he says.

"But will American investors be interested once they understand the dynamics? Yes."

Massie-Taylor knows the margins are narrow.

A 10-team league cannot afford any more clubs to go under. There are financial debts and a dependency on owner generosity across the league.

But he heads to America with momentum.

"We've proved there's opportunity going forward," he says.

"The thing that's niggling us now is the fear that we don't make the most of it. That's the pressure we all feel to really crack on."

It isn't just the players aiming to start the season fast.

title: Unanswered questions for English teams after Women's Champions League returns
description: Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City start bids for European glory in unconvincing fashion.
fullText:
The Women's Champions League returned this week and with it came a host of unanswered questions for the ambitious English trio involved.

Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City all have designs on winning the competition and, on the face of it, got their campaigns off to solid starts.

Arsenal and Chelsea both have three points after narrow home wins while City recovered from 2-0 down for a creditable draw at heavyweights Bayern Munich.

But scratch deeper, and this was an unconvincing week, particularly given last season's finalists Barcelona and Lyon both opened with commanding victories.

Are the Women's Super League clubs equipped to challenge this season? What still needs addressing? And who has the best chance of lifting the trophy in Warsaw next May?

Last season, Manchester City exploited their absence from European competition to romp to the Women's Super League title.

In returning to the elite tier this season, their squad will face greater tests, and that was immediately true when 2025-26 semi-finalists Bayern Munich raced into a two-goal lead.

But Andree Jeglertz's team gave an immediate indication they belong at this level by recovering to draw 2-2, with summer signings Beth Mead and Carlotta Wamser justifying their arrival at the champions with their first goals for the club.

That was crucial given usual goalscorer Khadija Shaw surprisingly proved fallible in missing a penalty.

When she inevitably finds her shooting boots, City should be just fine in this competition.

Man City fight back from two down to thwart Bayern

With only two goals and five points from three matches, it has been an inauspicious start to the season for Arsenal, who have been bullish in targeting trophies.

Up against Danish minnows HB Koge, it was not just the Disney+ TV coverage of the game that was marred by glitches.

Arsenal's expected goals tally of 1.93 does not tell the story of a performance that was dominant with the ball, but they only fashioned two shots on target against a side they were expected to beat comfortably.

Boss Renee Slegers made a raft of changes, including resting Alessia Russo, but the eight forwards she ultimately featured struggled to breach the resolute visitors' backline, with the Gunners requiring a 95th-minute penalty to steal the points.

Dismissing lower-ranked teams at the start of competition has been an Achilles' heel for Arsenal and, while they did win, tougher tests await and Slegers needs to find a solution.

Ad break in Women's Champions League was unscheduled

Wasteful Arsenal need late penalty to beat Koge

A brilliant goal from Wieke Kaptein handed Chelsea victory on their opening night in what was a promising attacking performance from the Blues.

Summer signing Melvine Malard was bright in her pre-planned 45-minute appearance, while Alyssa Thompson's electric display showcased what she could offer in her second season at Stamford Bridge.

With Ellie Carpenter playing behind Thompson, Chelsea's right side could be a potent weapon as they strive to return to the summit of English football - and, in reality, they ought to have added a couple more goals against Austria Vienna.

However, there were concerns for Sonia Bompastor. Shorn of injured captain Erin Cuthbert and with Keira Walsh substituted early, they ceded control in midfield to the Champions League debutants.

Indeed, Vienna came close on a number of occasions to taking a deserved point, hitting the post and having more shots than their esteemed opponents.

Although Chelsea have only conceded one goal in four matches this season, the fragility on display could cost them against more clinical opponents.

Chelsea win Champions League opener but Walsh injured

As English clubs stuttered through their first games, last season's finalists Barcelona and Lyon both made a statement.

First to play were the French giants at Servette in Switzerland, where they won 8-0, with Marie-Antoinette Katoto scoring a hat-trick as they racked up 31 shots and hit the woodwork.

Holders Barcelona actually went behind at home to Paris FC but swiftly turned the game around and scored four before half-time, ultimately running out 5-2 winners.

Ominous signs from the Champions League favourites.

title: Drinking at football matches - would fans welcome it?
description: Andy Burnham has long championed a repeal of the ban which prevents football supporters from drinking alcohol in the view of the pitch. But do fans even want it?
fullText:
When UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham embarked on his trip to the United Nations in New York, he might not have been expecting a question about football fans drinking alcohol in grounds.

Burnham firmly believes the law that prevents supporters from having a beer at their seat during a match is outdated.

It's a position the Everton supporter has long held, and when asked was happy to reaffirm.

"I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination," said Burnham, who feels football fans are singled out compared to those of other sports and events.

There is no suggestion this is about to become official government policy, and last year MPs rejected a Conservative amendment to the Football Governance Bill that would have forced ministers to launch a formal consultation on scrapping the rule.

That was, of course, before Burnham returned to Downing Street.

It is a complicated and divisive issue, about not just safety. But is it something that match-going supporters actually want?

Drinking alcohol at football grounds in England and Wales has been strictly controlled since the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act was introduced in 1985.

It was brought in to counter escalating hooliganism through the 1970s and into the 1980s.

The ban impacts clubs in the Premier League down to the National League. While beer can be sold, it must be consumed in areas that do not have a view of the pitch.

Yet fans who support teams in the National League North and South and below can drink alcohol around the pitch.

The ban is more strict in Scotland, with a law in place since 1981 that alcohol is only available in hospitality areas and not for other fans.

It was initially imposed following a riot during the 1980 Scottish Cup final between Rangers and Celtic at Hampden.

However, attitudes have been changing in recent seasons.

It was lifted as part of a pilot scheme last year, with several Scottish clubs selling alcohol in clearly defined, monitored areas of the stadiums. It started with lower-level clubs, eventually being extended to the Premiership.

The Scotland national team joined the trial for the friendlies against Japan and Curacao earlier this year. It has been extended to games against Switzerland on 29 September and Slovenia next month.

The Women's Super League in England has just completed two seasons of successful trials and the rule preventing drinking in the stands has now been removed by the league's governing company, WSL Football.

The women's game is not governed by the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act, enabling the competition organiser to make the change.

Is there support for the move within English football's corridors of power?

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in August the competition had not "got a specific view" and "we'd need to give it some really careful thought".

The English Football League, however, issued a statement on Thursday that said it would be "receptive to discussions around reviewing the current legislation".

It added member clubs had already provided "a mandate to lobby for appropriate reform" which had "not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding".

The Football Supporters' Association has for some time backed changing the law.

Like the prime minister, it considers it to be unfair on football fans.

"I think it is outdated," FSA chairman Tom Greatrex told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme.

"If you go to watch football in Germany or in other places around the world, then it's perfectly acceptable.

"It is civilised and appropriate. There's no reason why that shouldn't be the case for football fans, as it is for fans of rugby league, watching Oasis, or anything else that happens often in the same stadiums in the same seats."

The FSA's position is that clubs should have the choice, in consultation with supporters, to sell alcohol.

Clubs might want to offer it in all stands, others in designated areas, while a few might choose not to do so at all.

Other sports offer designated alcohol-free sections, something that football clubs may wish to copy for some families and supporters who do not consume alcohol because of their religion.

The FSA acknowledges this, but believes having the option to make such decisions is important.

It believes relaxing the law would be more popular the further down the leagues you go, where alcohol sales could potentially provide a crucial additional income stream.

The UK Football Policing Unit rejected the suggestion, arguing alcohol plays "a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour" and that "other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour" that football does.

Yet for Greatrex, there is already proof police are not open to ideas through their previous opposition to safe standing.

Before it was introduced four years ago, Mark Roberts, who has been the national lead for football policing since 2014, told the BBC it would make it "easier to throw missiles, engage in hate chanting, racism, sneak alcohol in, take cocaine".

"[The police] were telling everybody that we couldn't have standing at football again, that it would jeopardise safety, " Greatrex said.

"Actually, what we saw then was a controlled, managed pilot projects to get that re-established.

"There hasn't been the level of disorder that some of the police sources were saying there would be. I think the police should have more of an open mind and engage in this in a sensible and mature way."

For many match-going fans, however, the prospect of beer being thrown and potential anti-social behaviour outweighs the opportunity to watch a game with a pint.

Dave, a Chelsea fan from Twickenham, told Nicky Campbell on BBC Radio 5 Live, that he was "100% against it".

"Have a look at some of the footage you see on social media at Boxpark, for instance. A goal goes in and there is beer and lager thrown everywhere," he said.

"I don't want to go round stinking of other people's beer and there is a fashion among certain supporters to throw their beer everywhere.

"If people can't go without drink for a 45-minute period there is something the matter with them."

Adrian, from Leicester, claimed it would be the "worst idea you could come up with".

"There is enough trouble with other things in football, with the flares, drug taking and other things," he added. "You throw the alcohol in as well. Football is tribal whereas other sports they aren't."

But Ryan, a Wolves fan in Banbury, said "a solution that suits everybody" is to provide designated areas for drinking in stands.

Football is in the only sport in the UK which faces restrictions on the consumption of alcohol.

Some of these sports have issues with alcohol-related and anti-social behaviour, but none have the same reputation as football.

The restrictions differ around Europe.

There is a strict ban in the top two divisions of Spanish football, where only alcohol-free beer can be sold outside of hospitality areas. It can, however, be taken to seats.

In the German Bundesliga, there is no ban on drinking at your seat. So relaxed is the approach to alcohol at games that you will even find people selling bottles of beer from shopping trolleys outside grounds.

In the Italian Serie A it is similarly as relaxed, though to a limit of 5% ABV. Some games which are designated "high risk" have sales suspended in and around the stadium.

In France, the Evin Law was introduced in 1991 which is pretty much in line with Scotland, as far as football is concerned. Alcohol cannot be sold at any sports event, other than in VIP areas.
