title: Fury v Joshua announced for 11 December in Cardiff
description: Cardiff's Principality Stadium will host Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury's all-British heavyweight fight on 11 December.
fullText:
Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will contest their long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.

The bout, more than a decade in the making, will be broadcast globally on Netflix.

BBC Sport understands the main event could take place in the early hours of Saturday morning in the UK, with organisers considering a late start to cater for audiences in the United States.

Joshua and Fury will come face-to-face at a news conference in London on Wednesday, 30 September, as the build-up begins to one of the most anticipated fights in British boxing history.

"I am inspiring a generation," Joshua, 36, posted on Instagram. Fury, 38, is yet to comment on the announcement.

The event is being promoted as a collaboration between Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and UFC chief Dana White.

"Two of the best heavyweights of this generation, finally in the ring together," Alalshikh said.

"This will be one of the biggest fights in boxing history. I am very happy to make this fight happen for the fans."

The former two-time world champions had already signed contracts for the bout earlier this year, but the date and venue had yet to be confirmed.

London's Wembley Stadium and New York's Madison Square Garden were the frontrunners to stage the fight, but both presented issues before Cardiff recently emerged as an alternative.

The Principality Stadium has hosted late-night boxing before, including Joe Calzaghe's fight with Mikkel Kessler in November 2007, which began at 01:00 GMT.

Welsh Rugby Union and Cardiff Council officials welcomed the fight, saying it would reinforce the city's reputation for staging major events and could bring a significant economic boost, although some operational details still need to be finalised.

Joshua had been pushing for the fight to take place in the UK and has got his wish.

"Forever indebted to the UK public for their support of Anthony Joshua. We couldn't have got this over the line without you," his promoter Eddie Hearn said.

It is notable that White, who fronts Zuffa Boxing, is involved in the promotion.

"For more than a decade, boxing fans have been clamouring for the heavyweight showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. Together, they bring 66 wins, 52 knockouts and multiple heavyweight world titles into the ring," White said.

"On December 11, two of the biggest heavyweights of this generation finally collide - and the winner will take a significant place in heavyweight history."

There was no official statement from Hearn or Fury's promoter Frank Warren in the official news release sent by Netflix. Hearn had previously said he did not want White to be involved in promoting the fight.

A major fight in Cardiff taking place in the early hours might seem unusual, but there is precedent for UK events being scheduled around American television audiences.

Ricky Hatton's career-defining victory over Kostya Tszyu at Manchester's MEN Arena in June 2005 began at about 02:00 local time, allowing US broadcaster Showtime to show the fight on Saturday evening.

Less than a year later, Welshman Calzaghe's unification fight against Jeff Lacy at the same arena was staged at a similar hour. Calzaghe's 2007 victory over Kessler in Cardiff was also influenced by the US television schedule.

Mixed martial arts has gone even later. Michael Bisping's UFC title defence against Dan Henderson in Manchester in 2016 began deep into the night, with the fighters making their way to the octagon at about 04:45 local time.

When the UFC returned to Manchester in 2024, the UFC 304 main card began at 03:00 BST - corresponding with its traditional 22:00 start on the US east coast, with Briton Leon Edwards fighting Belal Muhammad in the main event just after 05:30.

The precise timing of Fury-Joshua has yet to be announced and promoter Eddie Hearn has played down suggestions it could begin as late as 03:00 GMT.

A ringwalk around 01:00 or 02:00 GMT would place the fight at 20:00 or 21:00 respectively on the US east coast.

For years, British boxing has debated who would win, watched negotiations collapse and wondered whether Fury and Joshua would ever actually share a ring.

Now, finally, there is a date and a venue. It's happening.

In many ways, the uncertainty of recent weeks was the Fury-Joshua story of the past decade in miniature.

In 2020, the two camps agreed the basis of a two-fight deal. In 2021, contracts were signed for an undisputed heavyweight contest, only for Deontay Wilder's successful arbitration case to force Fury into a third fight with the American. Then, in 2022, Joshua accepted a 60-40 split to challenge Fury, but that attempt also fell apart.

Joshua gets the British fight he wanted, organisers are given a stadium capable of staging a huge event in December and broadcasters can tailor it towards American audiences.

There is also an intriguing subplot in White's involvement. While it does not necessarily tell us who wielded the most influence behind the scenes, his involvement underlines just how many powerful figures were involved in finally putting this fight together.

What matters most for supporters is that Fury-Joshua will happen in Britain. There are some fights that are about more than purses, broadcast deals and site fees. This is one of them.

British fans have followed every twist: the world-title wins, the defeats, the comebacks, the rivalries and, above all, the failed attempts to make this contest.

Now they will have the chance to travel to Wales and say they were there. Tens of thousands will descend on the Principality Stadium for what will be one of the biggest nights British boxing has staged in years.

And somewhere among them may be a youngster attending their first fight, watching two of Britain's most recognisable sportsmen make their walks to the ring and deciding they want to lace up a pair of gloves themselves.

The fight may have arrived years later than many wanted but Fury-Joshua can still leave that kind of legacy.

title: Ex-England striker Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021
description: Former England striker Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021, by a man who has subsequently been jailed for three years.
fullText:
Former England striker Andy Carroll has revealed he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021.

The 37-year-old, who was automatically granted anonymity as a victim of sexual assault, has made the details public in an autobiography titled 'Owning it'.

The incident took place at Carroll's home, during his second spell with his hometown club Newcastle and led to the perpetrator being jailed for three years.

Carroll, now a player/co-owner of non-league club Dagenham & Redbridge, says he decided to include the incident in his book "at the very last minute" after discussing it with his girlfriend Lou Teasdale.

A friend of his former partner, who was away at the time, was set to stay over after coming to his home to watch a boxing match.

Carroll says the incident occurred while he was sleeping and he then threw the man out of the house, before knocking him unconscious as he tried to return.

Carroll, who also played in the Premier League for Liverpool and West Ham, called the police and was "sobbing" in the arms of his children's nanny.

The unnamed attacker was found guilty of sexual offences and placed on the sex offender register. Carroll testified in court, a process he says was "humiliating and embarrassing and absolutely horrendous".

Carroll wrote: "I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now.

"Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not. I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet.

"Scary to talk about but it's made [me] the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it."

Carroll, who won nine England caps, added: "What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I'd think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football… The trauma of what happened to me hasn't gone away."

Carroll joined Dagenham in July 2025 and has made six appearances in the National League South this season.

title: Is this really the Premier League's 'Bermuda Triangle'?
description: Do the stats back the social media meme that Bournemouth, Brighton and Brentford form a Premier League 'Bermuda Triangle' where teams lose points?
fullText:
It's the place where points are lost and never to be seen again, according to a popular social media meme.

Draw a line from Brighton to Bournemouth to Brentford and back down to Brighton again and you will have formed the Premier League's very own "Bermuda Triangle".

Those three clubs have developed a reputation for taking points off the traditional Big Six - Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham.

Recent results have only fuelled the narrative and helped to push the tongue-in-cheek theory.

On Friday night, Brentford beat Chelsea 3-0. Less than 24 hours later, Brighton outclassed champions Arsenal, albeit by the same scoreline - though it was a victory that could arguably have been even more emphatic had David Raya not produced a couple of smart saves.

Bournemouth, meanwhile, pushed Liverpool all the way before falling to a gritty 1-0 defeat, with Alisson forced into a brilliant recovery stop to deny the Cherries an early opener.

Those are the sort of performances that stick in supporters' minds and help explain why the theory has taken hold.

Since the start of the 2024-25 season, Brighton have been the best-performing non-traditional Big Six side against Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Man City, Manchester United and Spurs, taking 42 points from 26 games - an average of 1.62 points per match.

The Cherries are not far behind, collecting 35 points from 26 matches, or 1.35 points per game.

Brentford, however, have taken 22 points from 26 matches, averaging 0.85 points per game. Newcastle (1.46), Nottingham Forest (1.46) and Aston Villa (1.38) have all matched or outperformed the Bees against the traditional Big Six over the same period.

In other words, the clubs most commonly grouped together by the meme have produced very different levels of success against elite opposition.

Brighton and Bournemouth have consistently taken points off the Premier League's heavyweights. Brentford's record is less convincing.

In fact, the Opta data suggests Brighton are the main reason the theory has gained such traction.

Since Fabian Hurzeler took charge, only Kenny Dalglish's Blackburn have recorded a better points-per-game return against the traditional Big Six among managers of non-Big-Six clubs with at least 10 matches.

The popularity of the Bermuda Triangle idea may say as much about perception as results.

When it comes to recruitment and spending, Bournemouth, Brighton and Brentford operate in a different world to the Premier League's biggest clubs. They cannot simply outspend Arsenal, Liverpool or Manchester City.

That makes their victories more memorable. Upsets also tend to linger longer in the memory because they fit a familiar story: well-run clubs outperforming opponents with significantly greater resources.

The meme is not entirely without foundation, although the evidence is considerably stronger for Brighton and Bournemouth than it is for Brentford.

Brentford's overall record is weaker, although a series of eye-catching victories under Thomas Frank and now Keith Andrews have helped cement their reputation as a difficult opponent for elite clubs. And the start to this season has helped: their Chelsea success added to by an opening day 3-0 rout of Spurs.

But the numbers do not support a three-club phenomenon quite as clearly as social media might suggest.

If there is a Premier League Bermuda Triangle, Brighton sit firmly at its centre.

The Seagulls' record against the traditional Big Six is not merely impressive by modern standards. According to Opta, it is one of the best any non-Big-Six club has produced in the Premier League era.

The only catch is that the evidence points less to a triangle and more to one standout club, with Bournemouth providing strong support and Brentford helping to supply some of the moments that keep the theory alive.

title: Feaunati returns as England brace for Black Ferns onslaught
description: Maddie Feaunati returns to bring big-game experience and dynamism to the back row as England take on a resurgent New Zealand at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.
fullText:
Maddie Feaunati returns to bring big-game experience and dynamism to the back row as England take on a resurgent New Zealand, their closest challengers at the top of the world rankings, in front of more than 50,000 fans at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.

Feaunati comes in at number eight, with Alex Matthews shifting to blind-side flanker and Abi Burton to the bench.

The three starters all featured in England's Women's Rugby World Cup final win against Canada, one year ago on Sunday.

England, whose 39-match winning streak was halted by a 26-26 draw against Canada last weekend, make their other changes in the front row.

Props Mackenzie Carson and Sarah Bern come in to start with Hannah Botterman and Maud Muir poised to add power off the bench.

Bryony Field, whose involvement in the international set-up before this autumn was limited to age-grade appearances half a decade ago, retains her place at starting hooker ahead of May Campbell.

Amy Cokayne and Connie Powell are both missing through injury, while Lark Atkin Davies has only recently given birth.

England's backline remains unchanged with Helena Rowland at inside centre and Jess Breach, Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and Ellie Kildunne making up the back three.

Natasha Hunt, Tatyana Heard and Emma Sing are the specialist backs on the bench.

Saturday, 26 September, 15:00 BST

Live on BBC iPlayer and BBC Sport website and app, with accompanying live text commentary

"We're moving forward in the right direction whilst building depth in our cover," said head coach John Mitchell.

"New Zealand are playing good rugby at the moment and it's no surprise to see them raise their standards.

"Test matches against the best teams in the world are what we relish and look forward to, especially at Allianz Stadium."

New Zealand were the last team to beat the Red Roses, upsetting the tournament favourites in the final of the previous Women's Rugby World Cup in November 2022.

England have won the teams' three meetings since - most recently running out 49-31 winners in October 2024 - but the Black Ferns have won all seven Tests they have played this year under new coach Whitney Hansen.

"Our players are built different, we're made for these moments," said Hansen, who is the daughter of former All Blacks coach Steve Hansen.

"We've continued to grow each week and we're excited to put our rugby identity to the test against England, who are currently number one in the world. "

Among Hansen's selection is wing Ayesha Leti-I'iga, who scored two tries in her team's World Cup final win over England, and teenage full-back Braxton Sorensen-McGee, who was one of the stars of the 2025 tournament.

title: Transphobia Isn’t Winning Votes. But It Is Making Our Lives Much Worse.
description: Gillian...
fullText:
Trans people must now live out another election cycle knowing our friends, family, coworkers, and neighbors are being flooded with agitprop designed to dehumanize us.

Last week, the conservative group American Principles Project sent a memo to GOP candidates running in the 2026 midterms about one of the party’s biggest attack issues this cycle: transgender rights. In the memo, the APP, which focuses its political work heavily around anti-trans themes, assured these candidates that the transphobic advertisements and messaging it has sold them on for nearly a decade “can still be used to move persuadable voters.”

But then the group pivoted. It warned that this hate-filled strategy on its own “may not be sufficient” without a “compelling message on the economy,” an issue that ranks as the top priority for voters—unlike trans people and our healthcare, which typically have much lower saliency.

One memo from one group may not seem that important. But APP has spent years convincing Republican campaigns and donors about the potency of anti-transgender attacks against Democrats. This is despite the fact that transphobia-themed attacks have failed to seal the deal in competitive statewide and House races in 2019, 2020, 2022, 2023, and 2025. Their apparent success in 2024 was more likely a fluke, deployed against a weakened candidate on a shortened timeframe with a deflated base trying to carry the baggage of another president whose popularity was sunk by the rising cost of living.

The group’s warnings are also bearing out in the polls thus far this year; even after heavily investing in anti-trans advertising in key midterm races across the country—and getting substantial outside assistance from figures like Elon Musk, whose super PAC is spending $100 million in advertisements almost solely focused on demonizing trans people in many of these races—Republicans stand a real chance of losing the House and potentially even the Senate.

While it makes meek references to “economic populism” to ward off voters’ increasing embrace of “the false promise of socialism,” APP seemingly knows very well that an obsessive focus on niche cultural grievances is not enough to blind voters to the reality of the economy most Americans are enduring.

Yet, while the electoral threat that anti-trans attacks pose to Democrats is overstated, where this strategy has been successful is in rendering transgender people as politically isolated as we’ve ever been—decreasing the public’s support for our legal and social equality and foregrounding the most emotional issues (like the rights of the minuscule number of transgender athletes) over the more profound, material forces that actually shape trans people’s daily lives, namely access to affordable healthcare, safe schools, jobs free of discrimination, and the ability to go about our lives with dignity.

Trans people in battleground states must now live out another election cycle knowing that their friends, family, coworkers, and neighbors are being flooded with agitprop designed to dehumanize us. Some of the ads being paid for by Musk in states like Texas and Ohio present such a cartoonish depiction of transgender life or activism that they’ve literally used AI to generate caricatures of trans women who don’t exist.

As I said, real-life trans people mostly have the same day-to-day concerns about their lives as any other Americans. But the core thesis of Trumpism is one of forced scarcity—the belief that your struggle and suffering must be the fault of someone different from you. It proposes that if we can simply make trans people—or immigrants or Muslims or Black people or women—suffer, then the lives of “everyday” (read straight, cis, white) people will surely improve. But as APP’s memo suggests, that promise is collapsing in real time, presenting an opportunity for Democrats to turn the tables on anti-transgender attacks in the context of Trump’s many broken promises.

What Trump assured the American people in 2024 is that their dissatisfaction with the Biden administration was because Biden and Kamala Harris were either too old, too incompetent, or too focused on transgender people and our rights. But now that Donald Trump is president, he has banned trans athletes, gone after doctors and hospitals that provide trans healthcare, purged trans people from the military and any mention of them from much of the federal government, and done everything in his power to deny trans people and our families any modicum of dignity or autonomy over our own lives. Has that lowered your rent? Has that put gas in your car? Has the ritual humiliation and dehumanization of transgender people helped give your children a brighter future?

Some Democrats are still embracing a (likely doomed) effort to negate the anti-trans attack ads through some combination of retreat and triangulation. I understand that it is generally a mistake to expect politicians to be brave. Many strategists and advisers would suggest pols aren’t furthering the political isolation of trans people with these triangulations but simply reflecting public opinion—and that an unreliable ally is better for trans people than a reliable enemy.

But there is another option between the retreat of some candidates this year and the silence these attacks often met in past election cycles. As APP makes clear, the goal of these ads is carving a division between the interests of the broader public and the interests of transgender people ourselves. But Trump, Musk, APP, and their allies on the campaign trail have shown that our fates and interests have never been more intertwined, with the country being robbed and immiserated by the same people harboring a dangerous obsession with the rights and lives of less than 1 percent of the population. They know this isn’t working; all we need to do is connect the dots for everyone else.

Between the reemergence of right-wing red-baiting and Donald Trump’s use of the chilling National Security Presidential Memorandum–7 to criminalize left political organizing, we’re seeing McCarthyism reborn before our eyes. 

This assault on democracy cannot be ignored or wished away. Resisting it requires bravery in the face of threats and repression, a steadfast commitment to the truth, and the unwavering belief that we can—and will—overcome this darkness.

We must have an independent media that sets the record straight, unearths corruption and abuses of power, and advances a politics of justice and dignity for all if we’re to win this fight.

That’s why I’m writing to you today. This September, The Nation needs to add 100 monthly donors to sustain our progressive journalism. Your contribution makes the next investigative report, the next truth-speaking column, and the next pathbreaking essay all possible. 

I hope you’ll support our work with a recurring donation today. If you donate $10 or more a month, we’ll send you a brand new “Hands Off the Free Press!” sticker to recognise your commitment to our cause. Please, donate today.

Onward,

Katrina vanden Heuvel
Editor and Publisher, The Nation

title: A Premature Farewell to the Ignominious Speaker Mike Johnson
description: Joan...
fullText:
If Democrats win the House in the midterms, as expected, Mike Johnson won’t hold the gavel in any meaningful way again.

Is it too soon to say farewell to Speaker Mike Johnson? The Democrats are almost universally expected to win the House in November’s midterms, which would mean we’ve essentially seen the last of him in that role. Assuming these expectations are correct, there might even be debate over whether he gets the title of GOP minority leader. And while there will be a lame-duck session of the 119th Congress after the election, that’s shaping up to be a festival of recriminations, the last stand of GOP members who just lost their seats, thanks at least in part to Johnson.

What an ignominious tenure he has had. Remember, Johnson wasn’t the Republicans’ first choice as speaker when they retook the House. He wasn’t even their fourth. Kevin McCarthy won in January 2023, after more than a dozen votes, but was forced to resign nine months later. The House GOP then fielded three other representatives—Steve Scalise, Jim Jordan, and Tom Emmer—none of whom could get the votes. Finally, the pious Johnson, with his schoolboy looks and his empty legislative record, became the chosen front man for a fractious House GOP caucus, united only behind Trump.

Johnson may seem mild-mannered, but I found his early statements as speaker scary. “People are curious, ‘What does Mike Johnson think about any issue under the sun?’” he said in his first interview with Fox News’s Sean Hannity. “I say, ‘Well, go pick up a Bible off your shelf and read it. That’s my worldview.’” The Nation’s Katha Pollitt lamented his “18th-century values.” But I didn’t expect Johnson to be able to accomplish much, and that turned out to be correct.

Only two weeks ago Johnson was seen boasting, at Donald Trump’s fake “midterm convention,” that the 119th Congress was “the most productive in 80 years.” By most available metrics, that’s untrue. According to GovTrack, the 119th Congress has enacted 429 pieces of legislation, compared with 619 in the 118th Congress and 1,236 in the 117th. The fact-checking site Snopes rated Johnson’s claim “false.”

What else can Johnson claim as a legacy? He tried to bottle up legislation calling on the Trump administration to release the Jeffrey Epstein files, but had to put it to a vote because so many Republicans were fed up with the stonewalling. He needn’t have worried, because the Justice Department released those files so haphazardly and incompletely that Congress has so far been unable to make a case for additional prosecution measures.

In September, after dodging questions about caucus member Max Miller of Ohio, accused of abusing his wife (who is, awkwardly, the daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno), he stood up for Miller. “He has been a great member of Congress,” Johnson told CNN’s Manu Raju. “He has some issues in his personal life he’s working through.” Maybe he’s counting on Miller’s vote in January.

Johnson does deserve some credit—I’d call it blame—for presiding over the longest government shutdown in history. Oh, and one more thing: shepherding Trump’s “One Big [Destructive] Bill” to a party-line reconciliation victory. Some of the bill’s worst program cuts, to Medicaid and the SNAP program, won’t be fully felt until after the election. The bill’s architects and stewards, like Johnson, thought that was politically wily. What they didn’t predict was that states and counties would begin preparing for the cuts this year, so we’re already seeing sharp increases in childhood hunger and healthcare needs. That will not help vulnerable Republicans in November.

When the House returns for its lame-duck session after the midterms, it could take up AI or cryptocurrency legislation, but that’s highly unlikely. In fact, Republican Representative Thomas Massie and Democratic Representative Ro Khanna announced in mid-September that they will have enough votes to force a vote on their Epstein Files Transparency Act II, which would give Epstein’s victims, as well as state and local prosecutors, access to more information in those files. Massie will almost certainly have more support for his move to impeach scandal-ridden Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. If November is a complete disaster for Republicans, both of those pieces of legislation could be a vehicle to punish Trump, and Johnson.

It’s actually fun to imagine the GOP blame game that will follow a midterm drubbing. One issue alone: Johnson’s backing Trump’s ridiculous midterm convention, which saddled vulnerable members with two nights of deadly presidential narcissism. Johnson was a headliner, but NPR found that fewer than half of GOP candidates in competitive House races were alongside him on the list of speakers at the Dallas event. Will the losers who come back to the lame-duck session be anxious to do their speaker’s bidding?

Between the reemergence of right-wing red-baiting and Donald Trump’s use of the chilling National Security Presidential Memorandum–7 to criminalize left political organizing, we’re seeing McCarthyism reborn before our eyes. 

This assault on democracy cannot be ignored or wished away. Resisting it requires bravery in the face of threats and repression, a steadfast commitment to the truth, and the unwavering belief that we can—and will—overcome this darkness.

title: England cannot imitate Spain's success, says Gordon
description: Anthony Gordon believes England cannot copy Spain's example and must use their own strengths to end a 60-year wait to win a major tournament."We can't keep looking at other countries and trying to be like them, because we're not them - we're English and we have our own strengths which they don't have, so maybe we start playing the way we're good at," said Gordon.
fullText:
Anthony Gordon believes England cannot copy Spain's example and must use their own strengths to end a 60-year wait to win a major tournament.

Barcelona winger Gordon was part of the Three Lions squad that again fell short at the semi-finals of the World Cup, while Spain went on to be crowned world champions for the second time.

The 25-year-old has made a fine start to life in Spain since his move from Newcastle in May but ahead of England's Nations League showdown against Spain at Wembley, he thinks there are clear differences between the football cultures of both countries.

"We can't keep looking at other countries and trying to be like them, because we're not them - we're English and we have our own strengths which they don't have, so maybe we start playing the way we're good at," said Gordon.

"I'm speaking from a point of view where I feel like we are trying to replicate Spain.

"Because I'm in Spain, I know we have just as good players, but they have different qualities, so why are you trying to make those players the same as the Spanish players? Because the Spanish players lack the things that we have and vice versa."

Gordon put his country on the cusp of a first World Cup final since 1966 when he opened the scoring against Argentina in the last four, but his withdrawal 11 minutes later changed the course of the game.

Thomas Tuchel replaced him with defender Ezri Konsa as part of a raft of defensive-minded substitutions and England paid for a lack of attacking threat as Argentina struck twice in the final 10 minutes.

"I was (surprised), being totally honest," Gordon added on the substitution. "Only because I'd just scored, so I'm the type of player that, I've said before, I'm really good when I play off adrenaline.

"When I score, I normally don't have many bad games because I get into an untouchable mode of confidence. It makes me feel on top of the world. Especially in that moment, on that stage, I felt really good."

Gordon said he may never get over the disappointment of that defeat but is hoping England use their hurt to spur them on to glory eventually.

"(The) scar doesn't have to be a negative one because it might lead us to victory in the next tournaments," he explained.

"I think any time you lose anything of value in life –- whether it be a person or something like a match or anything you really want to have or win or anything of large value -– you'll never be the same person.

"It leaves a scar, but that scar doesn't always have to be a negative one. You can be a better person for it. You can learn different things about the world, about yourself."

title: Wisconsin's Abu Sama, Emerson Mandell questionable on B1G availability report
description: The Big Ten released its initial availablity report for the Wisconsin-Penn State football game Sept. 26. Here is who made the list.
fullText:
MADISON – The Wisconsin Badgers listed 13 players on its initial availability report for their game with No. 14 Penn State on Sept. 26.

The big news came from the Nittany Lions, who officially listed standout receiver Koby Howard as out for the game. The sophomore leads Penn State in catches (12), receiving yards (344) and average yards per catch (28.7). The nature of the injury is unspecified.

Wisconsin, on the other hand, lists four players as out for the game: receiver Jaylon Domingeaux, defensive lineman Xavier Ukponu (arm), cornerback Cai Bates (undisclosed) and offensive lineman Michael Roeske (undisclosed). None of those injuries has been disclosed, but Domingeaux has been on the sidelines at games with a cast on his arm and Ukponu has been seen with his arm in a brace.

The Badgers questionable players include running back Abu Sama, who said Sept. 22, that he missed last week's game due to a shoulder issue and would be ready to play this week.

Here is the rest of the report:

Questionable: Sama, receiver Malachi Coleman, running back Bryan Jackson, right guard Emerson Mandell and tight end Ryan Schwendeman. Mandell, who is missed all of fall camp (foot), played for the first time last week. Coleman is recovering from what an apparant head injury.

Probable: linebacker Mason Posa, receiver Eugene Hilton, quarterback Danny O'Neil and right tackle Kevin Heywood.

For the past three seasons, the Big Ten has posted availability reports two hours before games.

The process is more extensive this year. Reports will be available four times each week, beginning three days before the game. The process continues with updates two days and one day before the matchup. The deadline for teams to submit their information is 7 p.m. (central) each day.

The gameday availability report will be announced two hours before kickoff.

Listed players will fall into five categories for the first three reports of the week: probable, questionable, doubtful, out or out (1st Half). The designations on the gameday reports are game time decision, out, and out (1st Half).

Badgers coach Luke Fickell said UW followed the injury reporting process during the first three games, though no information was released.

"I wouldn't have wanted to just start something new come Week 1 of the Big Ten," he said. "So I think we decided we're going to go about doing the things the way we need to be able to do them so it's not something new to us."

title: Arsenal early Premier League favourites – players to watch
description: Well, it had to happen didn’t it. No sooner were the pundits, bookies, and football fans in general, talking about Arsenal potentially going unbeaten this season and bringing back a new and updated ...
fullText:
Well, it had to happen didn't it. No sooner were the pundits, bookies, and football fans in general, talking about Arsenal potentially going unbeaten this season and bringing back a new and updated version of the 'Arsenal Invincibles', they go and get destroyed 3-0 by Brighton.

Fans of Premier League football are in for a long few weeks now, as we find ourselves gearing up for the first international break of the season. After a dismal display last weekend however, Arsenal fans will likely welcome this break as it will give them a chance to regroup, and will allow key players a chance to shine for their countries.

Despite such a poor showing against Brighton, The Gunners are still in a very strong position, and despite slipping to 2nd in the table, they're still strong contenders for another title. In fact, they are still favourites amongst most bookmakers, and when you look at the calibre of their players, it's easy to see why.

Arsenal Players to Watch this Season

With odds of 1/1 with both BOYLE Sports and Ladbrokes, the bookmakers clearly still have faith in The Gunners for the rest of the season.

But which players could prove instrumental in Arsenal's title defence this season? Let's take a look, shall we?

Since joining Arsenal, proficient German forward/attacking midfielder Kai Havertz has had a somewhat frustrating time, due largely to injuries.

Last season, the German netted 7 goals from 24 appearances. Compare that with the season before it, where he scored 15 goals from 36 appearances, and you can understand his frustration. Despite suffering injuries, he was still able to find the net on big occasions. He scored for The Gunners against PSG in the Champions League final, becoming the first ever German to score in two Champions League finals. He also scored in the Community Shield final, when Arteta's team defeated Man City 3-0.

As the German now returns to fitness, his precision passing, coupled with his two-footed ability, mean he'll certainly be one to watch this season. With 2 Premier League goals from 5 matches, he also looks set to better last season.

Another player who has been instrumental in Arsenal's title hopes has been England international, Bukayo Saka.

Currently, Saka has netted 3 times for The Gunners out of 5 appearances, which has hopefully answered any questions that people may have had regarding his fitness following injury.

Saka is a real handful for defenders due to his pace and accuracy. When he's not slotting goals in, he's usually whipping them into the box, as we saw for England during the World Cup, particularly during the Mexico game.

Saka is a Gunner through and through. A product of their youth academy, he's a testament to grass-roots football and emphasises everything there is to know and love about the beautiful game. It's clear he loves playing for his team, and it shows each time he steps on the pitch.

Although his last two seasons have been subdued by his standards, he's on course to regain that infamous form of 2023/24, which almost secured them the title.

The current Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard is another player to watch closely this season, for obvious reasons.

Odegaard, who captains both Arsenal, and his beloved home country of Norway, is a real playmaker of a midfielder. Despite questions being raised over his role in the club, he's gradually silenced his critics thanks to 2 goals from 5 games in the Prem.

Does he score the most goals? No, but he's about so much more than that. His passing is pin-point accurate, he's racked up plenty of assists, and as he regains his form following injury, his linking up with Saka and Havertz is going to be crucial if The Gunners want to make it two on the bounce.

If there's one plater that shone for England during the World Cup, that was not named Kane or Bellingham, it was Declan Rice. Despite dealing with a nagging injury (this seems to be a common theme for Arsenal) he was still able to put in some incredible balls and help England to reach the semis.

Last season, many believe he was largely responsible for Arsenal securing the title, and honesty, it's hard to argue with that assessment. A set-piece specialist through and through, Arteta's squad looked absolutely lethal during set-pieces, and Rice's balls being whipped into the box (stop laughing, we're all adults here) were the reason why. It wasn't always the most exciting style of play, but it helped them end the drought.

Rice currently has 2 assists to his name, though you can rest assured that come Spring, that number will be much higher.

fullText:
When highlighting how challenging a week of away fixtures Aberdeen had ahead of them earlier this month, there is no doubt Stephen Robinson would have signed up for a place in the League Cup semi-finals and four Premiership points from visits to Kilmarnock, Motherwell and Hibernian.

The trip to Easter Road yielded one of those points and a timid second-half display cost them all three having taken the lead and seemingly been sitting comfortably only for Northfield's Martin Boyle to once again score against his hometown club.

It was Boyle's 10th against the Dons with this one coming from the spot after an inexplicable Jack Milne challenge.

However, there is a much more positive spin on things at Pittodrie as we go into the newly extended September/October international break.

When the club football gets back under way in just over a fortnight, Aberdeen have a much more favourable schedule, although with that comes the pressure of expectancy.

Three out of their next four matches are at home against St Johnstone, St Mirren and Falkirk with a trip to Dundee United in among that.

The fans will hope to win all four of those but if the Dons can produce a return in the region of between eight and 10 points, Robinson will be content with how things are going.

The recent emergence of Findlay Marshall has been pleasing for the supporters. It looked like the 20-year-old was heading for the exit door, but he has grasped his opportunity and been one of their top performers over the past 10 days.

For those who watched the midfielder's performances for Arbroath during his loan spell last season, it will come as no surprise and he looks to have a bright future.

People in the north-east like nothing more than a local excelling and Marshall will be hoping to keep his place in what seems to be a slowly improving Aberdeen side.

title: Kylian Mbappe reveals what Antonio Rudiger is really like at Real Madrid
description: Although the summer was overshadowed by the arrival of several glittering new names into the Real Madrid team, one player for whom this time was also decisive was the center-back Antonio Rudiger.Like ...
fullText:
Although the summer was overshadowed by the arrival of several glittering new names into the Real Madrid team, one player for whom this time was also decisive was the center-back Antonio Rudiger.

Like Dani Carvajal and David Alaba, the German defender was also set to run out of his contract during the summer, and things were looking bleak for him for most part of the last season as he struggled with injuries. However, unlike these two players, the Merengues decided to give him a one-year extension, and he can prove to be a decisive player for Jose Mourinho this season.

This is not only because of the unique skills that he brings on the pitch, but also because of his role in the locker room. Being one of the most experienced players in the team, he is a highly respected player, while it is also clear that the players also love him.

As Diario AS has reported, one of these players, Kylian Mbappe, talked about Rudiger and his relationship with his teammates as he appeared in a recent interview. The Frenchman admitted that the German often comes off as peculiar, but is a very kind person behind the scenes:

"I think many fans think he is a little crazy. But that is his way of playing. Antonio is the best example of why you should not judge people solely by how they behave on the pitch. Of course, he is crazy on the pitch, because of the way he goes into challenges and behaves. But in the dressing room, he is completely different. He is a kind and attentive person."

There is no doubt that Antonio Rudiger has a very unique personality, and usually comes off as a ferocious player on the field. However, as Kylian Mbappe highlighted, he is a kind and affable person behind the scenes, something that has also been confirmed by some of the video clips coming out on social media. Furthermore, his leadership and experience would also be needed as Real Madrid once again look to navigate through a difficult spell after the derby defeat.

title: Bill Simmons claims LeBron James was going to join Cleveland Cavaliers but ‘something happened’
description: Bill Simmons claims that LeBron James was on the verge of joining the Cleveland Cavaliers, but something unexpected stopped the move. Many expected James to return to the Cavaliers for a third and final stint with the team that drafted him in 2003.
fullText:
Bill Simmons claims that LeBron James was on the verge of joining the Cleveland Cavaliers, but something unexpected stopped the move.

Many expected James to return to the Cavaliers for a third and final stint with the team that drafted him in 2003.

However, much to many people's surprise, James snubbed them in favour of signing with their Eastern Conference rivals, the Philadelphia 76ers.

Speaking on his podcast, Bill Simmons discussed LeBron James joining the Philadelphia 76ers despite rumours suggesting he was going to sign with the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Simmons then claimed that James joining the 76ers was a decision motivated by championships, before noting that something fell apart during his negotiations with the Cavaliers.

"It was the decision he made to try and win the title. I don't think there's any other reason he went there. It's not like, 'Oh I've always wanted to play for the 76ers.'

"But he was going to Cleveland. I don't know what happened. I can't wait for the story. Something happened."

The rumours suggested that LeBron James was going to leave the Los Angeles Lakers and join the Cleveland Cavaliers.

James had left the Cavaliers in 2018 to join the Lakers, after his second stint ended with four NBA Finals appearances and an NBA championship win in 2016.

With the Cavaliers struggling to reach the NBA Finals since his departure, despite multiple winning seasons, suggested that he could be the difference-maker for them.

However, in the end, James decided to join the 76ers instead. Unlike the last time he spurned the Cavaliers in 2010, there wasn't as much ill will from the fans towards LeBron for his decision.

James brought the franchise their one and only championship in 2016, cementing his status as the greatest player in the history of the franchise.

While Cavs fans won't love seeing James on another Eastern Conference contender, they know that he delivered on his promise to the franchise and brought them a championship in the past.

For fans, this adds an extra element of excitement and investment for the games between the Cavs and 76ers this season.

title: MUFC now preparing to cut ties with long-serving Red who’s already caused problems this term as replacement lined up
description: The general feeling behind the scenes at Manchester United is that Luke Shaw will be leaving when his contract expires in June 2027.According to TeamTALK, the club have not ruled out offering Shaw an ...
fullText:
The general feeling behind the scenes at Manchester United is that Luke Shaw will be leaving when his contract expires in June 2027.

According to TeamTALK, the club have not ruled out offering Shaw an extension, but it would only be on a short-term basis – presumably akin to the one-year deal, plus a 12-month option, that Harry Maguire signed before 2026/2027 began.

Alas, the 31-year-old is seemingly planning for pastures new.

He is currently United's longest-serving player following his £30 million move from Southampton in 2014, yet, remarkably, he only hit the milestone of 300 Premier League appearances last time out against Fulham.

Shaw's unrelenting injury problems have plagued his Red Devils career and, while it's no fault of his own, it has made him far too unreliable to depend upon.

Even this campaign, where he is the only out-and-out senior left-back in the side, he has missed three games already due to an unspecified fitness problem.

To put it into perspective, Shaw has accumulated 329 appearances for United across all competitions over the last 12 years. Bruno Fernandes, who joined in January 2020, has amassed 334.

It's said that United have identified a feasible replacement for Shaw ahead of his release in the form of Tyrick Mitchell.

The Crystal Palace star, 27, is also out of contract at the end of the season, so INEOS will undoubtedly be enticed by the fact they won't have to pay anything to bring in the Premier League-proven defender.

Mitchell himself would reportedly 'find it hard' to decline an offer from United, though he is also being targeted by Liverpool, who may make a more lucrative financial proposal.

title: 3 keys to a Cincinnati Bengals victory vs. the Pittsburgh Steelers
description: Generating pressure on Aaron Rodgers will be key to the Bengals walking out of Pittsburgh with a win.
fullText:
One of the NFL's fiercest rivalries renews this week when the Cincinnati Bengals head to the Steel City to face the Pittsburgh Steelers.

If the Bengals are to win and start the year 3-0, here are three keys to getting it done in Pittsburgh.

The Steelers still have a ton of talent on the defensive side of the ball, specifically with their ability to rush the passer with their defensive line. One way to limit the impact of that defensive line is to establish the running game early.

A quality rushing attack from Cincinnati will keep players like TJ Watt, Alex Highsmith, Nick Herbig, Cameron Heyward, Derrick Harmon, and others from teeing off on Joe Burrow and the Bengals' passing attack. It will also open up play action for the big plays down the field to the Cincinnati playmakers.

Chase Brown ran the ball 20 times for 80 rushing yards. A lot of those carries came late in the game with the Bengals having a two-possession lead. He also had an explosive run called back earlier in the game, on a very questionable holding call. If that run was factored in, that would have put Brown over 100 yards during the game.

The Bengals had an astounding 41 total pressures versus Houston in week two. The revamped defense is getting contributions from so many different players. Led by the sheer gravitational pull of Dexter Lawrence in the middle, this Bengals defense is looking legitimate.

Meanwhile, the Steelers have allowed 28 pressures through two games. Will the Steelers offensive line be able to keep Aaron Rodgers upright on Sunday? Or will this Bengals defense continue being a matchup nightmare for opposing offenses? If the Bengals generate pressure at a high rate on Aaron Rodgers, they will have opportunities to create turnovers. That pressure could end up determining the outcome of this one.

It was Joe Flacco instead of Joe Burrow, but Ja'Marr Chase went off for 16 receptions and 161 yards during week 7 last season against Pittsburgh. After having just 2 catches for 12 yards in week 1, the Bengals made more of an effort to get Chase involved during week 2. He finished the game with 7 receptions, 75 yards, and 2 receiving touchdowns. That was with the Bengals playing conservatively on offense to finish the game with a two-possession lead during the second half.

With the Steelers potentially without Joey Porter Jr. again this week, Chase could be in line for another monster performance this week. Establishing the run early will help the entire offense, but there will be times when the Bengals need to let Ja'Marr Chase just be Ja'Marr Chase. Good things happen when the ball goes his direction. I think the Bengals will find ways to get him involved early and often.

title: Phillies’ 7-Year Veteran Celebrates Rare MLB Feat With New Team
description: The Philadelphia Phillies have received a remarkable update on a long-time pitcher who left the organization.
fullText:
The Philadelphia Phillies entered the season with one of baseball's deepest starting rotations and the club has managed some turbulence and changes to retain that strength amid another playoff push.

With Cristopher Sanchez setting a franchise record earlier this season, Zack Wheeler fighting through a return from offseason surgery and Aaron Nola and Andrew Painter finding their strides, Philadelphia's rotation depth has remained a significant part of its postseason plans.

Under president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski, starting pitching has long been the Phillies' calling card. And that included the career start of a player who has now earned a notable career accomplishment with his new team.

Former Mets Backstop Suddenly Ends Career Just 8 Days Before Season Finale

Zach Eflin, who spent the first seven seasons of his career with the Phillies before moving on to the Tampa Bay Rays and then the Baltimore Orioles, has officially reached 10 years of MLB service time.

The Major League Baseball Players Association (MLBPA) marked the occasion with an announcement on social media.

The milestone carries particular significance because reaching a decade of service requires much more than simply having major league talent. Players must remain healthy and productive enough to spend years in the majors while navigating injuries, roster decisions and the natural turnover of professional baseball.

When it comes to Eflin, many Phillies fans will take the moment to remember his dependability and contributions across many years in Philadelphia.

"Throughout history, fewer than 10% of Players have possessed the combination of talent, health, resilience, perseverance and good fortune to achieve the feat," MLBPA noted in the announcement. "Eflin was selected by San Diego in the first round of the 2012 draft and debuted with the Phillies four years later. Eflin spent his first seven seasons in Philadelphia before stints in Tampa Bay and Baltimore. The Florida native has pitched in over 200 games and accumulated more than 900 strikeouts."

Eflin's Philadelphia tenure included several different stages of his development, including the start of what became a standout career in the majors.

Eflin's biggest transformation came after he moved away from an approach centered on overpowering hitters and instead leaned more heavily on his sinker and curveball, thanks in large part to the Phillies' development system. That adjustment helped him become a more effective major league starter, including a 2020 season in which he posted a 3.97 ERA and 10.9 strikeouts per nine innings.

Injuries interrupted his time with Philadelphia, including season-ending knee surgery in 2021. But he later became an important part of the Phillies' 2022 postseason bullpen, posting a 3.38 ERA across 10 and two-thirds playoff innings.

After the 2022 season, Eflin left Philadelphia and signed a three-year, $40 million contract with the Rays. Now, more than a decade after being drafted, the former Phillies pitcher has reached one of baseball's most exclusive career milestones.

title: A Readable UseToggle
description:
A boolean `useState` that hands back `on` / `off` / `toggle` instead
of a raw setter, so call sites read as intent. Every function, and
the controls object itself, stays referentially stable, safe to
pass as props or list as effect dependencies without retriggering
anything downstream.
fullText: useState(false) gives you setValue, so every call site ends up spelling out setValue(true), setValue(false), setValue(v => !v). Wrap it once instead, and the intent - on, off, toggle - moves to the call site. The setters and the object holding them stay stable across renders, so they pass cleanly as props or effect deps. @itsnas panel.tsxExpand allHide line numbersCopy codecodepanel.tsx'use client' function AdvancedPanel() { // @src/code/use-toggle const [isOpen, panel] = useToggle() // panel.off keeps one identity across renders, so it's an honest // effect dep: this runs when isOpen flips, not on every render. useEffect(() => { if (!isOpen) return const onKey = (e: KeyboardEvent) => { if (e.key === 'Escape') panel.off() } document.addEventListener('keydown', onKey) return () => document.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey) }, [isOpen, panel.off]) return ( <> <button onClick={panel.toggle} aria-expanded={isOpen}> Advanced settings button> {isOpen && <fieldset>{/* … */}fieldset>} ) }mainNas (@itsnas)'use client' interface UseToggleControls { on: () => void off: () => void toggle: () => void } /** * A boolean useState with named setters instead of a raw one: * `on`/`off`/`toggle` read as intent at the call site instead of * `setValue(true)`/`setValue(false)`/`setValue(v => !v)`. Both the * individual functions and the controls object itself are * referentially stable across renders, so passing them as props or * effect dependencies doesn't retrigger anything downstream. */ export function useToggle( initialValue = false, ): [boolean, UseToggleControls] { const [value, setValue] = useState(initialValue) const on = useCallback(() => setValue(true), []) const off = useCallback(() => setValue(false), []) const toggle = useCallback(() => setValue(v => !v), []) const controls = useMemo( () => ({ on, off, toggle }), [on, off, toggle], ) return [value, controls] }mainNas (@itsnas)

title: A new report from Europe raises serious alarms about orbital collisions
description: I think we are going to lose the ability to use certain orbits."
fullText:
The 2013 sci-fi blockbuster film Gravity, starring Sandra Bullock and George Clooney, popularized the notion of the Kessler syndrome. In the movie, Russia shoots down a defunct satellite and creates a cloud of debris, leading to serious tension in orbit.

The movie is fantastic, a true thriller, and while some liberties were taken with the depiction of outer space, the basic premise of a cascading series of collisions rendering orbits too cluttered with debris to be usable is valid. The idea was first proposed by NASA scientists Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais nearly half a century ago.

Still, the movie was science fiction, right?

Well, a lot has changed since Gravity‘s release. At the time that theatergoers were sitting on the edges of their seats and watching Bullock dodge debris, there were only about 1,000 active satellites in orbit. Today, that number is closer to 17,000, according to CelesTrak.

The preponderance of this growth has been driven by SpaceX’s Starlink constellation, which now has approximately 11,000 satellites in orbit, with many thousands more on the way. And SpaceX is not alone in the race to provide Internet from space. Amazon has launched hundreds of satellites, with thousands more to follow. Multiple Chinese Internet constellations are likewise in progress.

Then there are the orbital data centers, which may produce hundreds of thousands of satellites.

We’ve written a lot about these constellations, and they have generated a bunch of questions. Most prominent among them: Just how sustainable is all of this? Will we see the Kessler syndrome play out in real time? Here are some answers.

It depends on who you ask, so let’s start with the glass-half-empty and glass-half-full outlooks.

Starting with the pessimists: A few years ago, one of the world’s experts in orbital debris, University of Texas at Austin professor Moriba Jah, told Ars that he worries a lot about the consequences of satellites and debris in low-Earth orbit.

“I think we are going to lose the ability to use certain orbits because the carrying capacity is going to get saturated by objects and junk,” Jah said. ” I also predict that we will see a loss of human life by (1) school bus-sized objects reentering and surviving reentry and hitting a populated area, or (2) people riding on this wave of civil and commercial astronauts basically having their vehicle getting scwhacked by an unpredicted piece of junk. I predict that both those things are going to happen in the next decade.”

At the other end of the spectrum is the person almost solely responsible for the remarkable growth in satellites over the last decade, SpaceX founder Elon Musk. His attitude has largely been that space is big, and things will probably be just fine. For example, during a SpaceX-produced interview this summer at the company’s Starlink terminal factory in Bastrop, Texas, Musk said, “Space is really big. It’s not like space is gonna get crowded. Space is enormous. If you actually look at it relative to the Earth, the satellites are so tiny you can’t even see them.”

So in one way of thinking, very, very bad things are coming. In another, everything’s fine. Where does the truth actually lie?

One of the most credible sources for this kind of information is the European Space Agency, which has long studied space debris and its impacts on various orbits.

Fortunately, it just released its annual Space Environment Report a week ago. The European agency has produced such a report over the last decade to provide a transparent overview of global space activities and assess the quality of efforts to preserve the sustainability of spaceflight.

There are some striking—and concerning—changes this year. For example, the European report has dramatically increased its projections of future satellites in this year’s report after reassessing the current trajectory of large constellations.

“The notable increase in the index this year is primarily driven by the substantially larger future population resulting from the current extrapolation scenario,” the report states. “In particular, the growing influence of large constellations highlights the limitations of traditional mitigation approaches when applied to future traffic at unprecedented scales. At the same time, the results are affected by the limited availability of detailed and verifiable information on future deployment plans, operational practices, and end-of-life strategies of these systems.”

More satellites mean an increasing probability of collisions, which helps to push us toward a Kessler-like scenario.

As part of the report, the European scientists modeled a number of different scenarios. Assuming that satellite launches continue to increase—by far the most likely trend—even if operators continue to follow best practices in terms of disposing of older satellites and avoiding collisions, the orbital environment will still become significantly more cluttered.

“The extrapolation of our current behavior, which assumes the continuation of explosion in orbits at current rates, adherence by constellations to at least the minimum desirable post-mission disposal success rates, and continuation of the currently estimated post-mission disposal success rates for all other objects, leads to an unstable environment with collision rates increasing exponentially,” the report states.

In its technically precise language, the European Space Agency is essentially saying we’re on a road that could ultimately lead to something like the Kessler syndrome. Such a scenario, with a dramatic growth in constellations using best practices for satellite disposal, looks like this in terms of collisions in orbit.

It does indeed start to look pretty dicey by mid-century.

Also worth noting: The projections in ESA’s 2026 report do not include the new category of orbital data centers, as they exclude projects “still being prepared” for launch. It remains unclear whether these mega-megaconstellations of data centers in space will prove to be economically viable, but if they do, they could be the ultimate tipping point for orbital sustainability.

The European Space Agency talks a lot about the need for responsible behavior, and in managing its massive Starlink constellation, SpaceX has been responsible. The company has been effective at deorbiting satellites that lose functionality and at managing a constellation of thousands of satellites. It’s an unprecedented task that the company has learned, on the fly, to carry out at a scale no government or company has attempted before.

We know from mandatory reporting to the Federal Communications Commission that SpaceX is frequently moving satellites around in orbit, making small but precise maneuvers to avoid collisions. Five years ago, its (much smaller) constellation made about 500 such maneuvers a month. During the most recent reporting period, through May 2026, that number had jumped to nearly 35,000 per month. That comes to one maneuver every 75 seconds.

It is important to characterize these properly. Each maneuver is not a “near miss.” Rather, SpaceX has significantly lowered the probability threshold to trigger a collision avoidance maneuver. The NASA standard for maneuver is 1-in-10,000. At the outset of Starlink, though, SpaceX used a 1-in-100,000 threshold and has since become even more conservative, with a threshold of 3-in-10 million, according to a 2025 letter to the FCC.

So it’s clear that SpaceX is not operating its Starlink constellation in a cavalier manner. But it’s also clear that the company’s constellation, and those like it, are cause for significant concern going forward.

No credible experts are saying that the Kessler syndrome could happen imminently—a single collision won’t set off a Gravity-style cascade.

But space is getting more crowded, particularly orbits from 520 km to 1,000 km above Earth. A 2025 paper by Hugh Lewis and Kessler (yes, that Kessler) found that some orbital bands in this region have already reached what is known as a “collisional-runaway threshold,” which is to say that any serious collisions there may create new debris faster over time than debris would be naturally removed by the pull of gravity, down into Earth’s atmosphere.

Another concern comes from spent “rocket bodies,” upper stages from rockets that were not properly disposed of after launch. This was more common in decades past, but some launches today still do not reserve enough propellant to properly deorbit a second or third stage. These school bus-sized stages are particularly problematic at altitudes of 840 and 975 km, said LeoLabs space debris expert Darren McKnight. They are winging around uncontrolled, of course. And the higher the altitude, the longer the debris hangs around, from decades to centuries.

Finally, because there is so much stuff flying around orbit, it would be relatively easy for bad actors to start shooting missiles at satellites in low-Earth orbit, creating debris fields that could potentially wipe out communications and cause massive financial damage. The probability of Kessler syndrome becomes much higher if humans start deliberately blowing things up in space. Did we mention that Iran recently became the ninth country to put a domestically built satellite into orbit?

In the near term, it seems unlikely that space will become unusable. But it will likely become more and more expensive to operate there when considering avoidance technology, people to manage all of this, and propellant for maneuvers. And finding launch windows that avoid known debris will become more difficult.

Longer term, perhaps as early as 15 years from now but more likely longer, a Kessler-syndrome type outcome may start to become increasingly plausible.

title: I built AgeDB, a database for AI agents to store context and data
description: An analytical database built for agents to use directly: columnar storage, a vectorized query engine, and MCP as a first-class interface - sivsivsree/agedb
fullText:
A database your AI agent can talk to, that tells you how it read the question and says
so when it can't answer.

AI agents collect things as they work: leads, prices, support tickets, research notes.
AgeDB gives them somewhere to keep those records and lets them ask questions in plain
English, such as "which companies look most likely to convert?". It runs on your machine as
one small program. There is no SQL to write, and no extra AI call is made to understand the
question.

The last answer is the point. A system that answered from one table would return a
confident, incomplete number. AgeDB refuses, says why, and the agent can ask a narrower
question.

Status: v0.1, single node, 308 tests, written in Rust. AgeDB is a working name and may
change.

There is no language model inside. Plain-language questions are parsed in-process by
deterministic rules. That takes about 17 microseconds per question on a laptop (Apple M1,
release build). The same question over the same schema always gives the same plan, and
nothing is sent anywhere. The agent calling AgeDB is usually already a language model, so
AgeDB does not add a second one to every question.

There are two starting points. Neither is proven yet.

If an embedded database your agent already uses serves you well, that is a legitimate
answer. See How it compares.

Business correctness. A valid plan can still:

Column descriptions and default aggregations reduce this, and the echoed plan is how you
catch it. AgeDB knows only the business definitions your schema states.

Column-level authorization. sensitive hides a column from select *, from schema
context and from error suggestions. Any key that may query the table can still select
the column by name. Keep data a caller must never see in a separate table, database or
tenant.

A hard time limit. The time budget is checked between batches and between execution
stages. It is cooperative: a single sort or merge step already running finishes first, so
a query can overrun its budget by the length of that step.

High availability. AgeDB v0.1 runs on a single node.

A well-built existing stack can do much of this. PostgreSQL or DuckDB, with schema discovery,
a read-only role and validated SQL, also rejects unknown columns and bounds queries. There is
also direct competition:

MCP plus analytics plus semantics is not, on its own, a reason to choose AgeDB.

Models will keep getting better at writing SQL, so "models struggle with SQL" is not a
durable reason to exist. Enforced permissions, consistent definitions and predictable
behaviour across models might be. Whether they are worth adopting a new dependency for is
what the evidence plan tests.

Most of what is distinctive about AgeDB sits above storage.

The engine exists for three reasons:

Those are easier to guarantee when the executor is ours. That is a design reason, not
evidence that users need it. Adopting AgeDB today also means adopting its recovery, upgrade
and maintenance story, which is younger than any established database's.

So the next experiment is to put the same validated interface over an established engine
(DuckDB) as a second backend, and see which one users choose. The custom engine stays only
if users show they need what it does differently.

Requires Rust 1.90 or newer (rustup). There are no other dependencies,
no server to install, and no Docker.

See the whole thing work in about 40 seconds:

An agent launches the process and talks JSON-RPC over the pipe:

/mcp implements the MCP Streamable HTTP transport (revision 2025-06-18):

Every request still needs its API key.

The same server also speaks REST:

The operator guide, including config files, scopes, limits and troubleshooting, is in
docs/usage.md.

There are fourteen tools, no query language, and no escape hatch. There is deliberately no
execute_arbitrary_query:

data_query accepts plain language or a structured plan:

Either way, the response carries the plan that ran, so an agent can check the
interpretation and reuse or adjust it:

And when it cannot answer, it says so with a code the agent can branch on:

The plain-language layer handles:

Anything else is refused with the available columns listed. That refusal is the cue for the
calling agent to send a structured plan instead.

Every front end converges on one validated Query IR. Natural language, structured plans
and any future front end lower into the same representation. It is validated once, in one
place, before anything executes.

ARCHITECTURE.md has the design rationale, on-disk formats, the
concurrency model, and the list of what is deliberately missing.

The numbers in ARCHITECTURE.md track the engine
against itself from change to change. Ingest is measured with WAL fsync off, and there is no
competitor run alongside it. They are useful for catching regressions. They prove nothing
about adoption.

The benchmark that matters is not built yet. It asks whether an agent using AgeDB completes
real analytical tasks more accurately, cheaply and safely than the same agent using a
well-configured alternative. The plan is to use the same model, the same data and the same
task set on both sides, with equivalent metadata and reasonable configuration for the
alternative, and to measure:

The harness and the results will be published whichever way they come out.

AgeDB has solid engineering and no customer evidence yet. No external team uses it every
week. The next 30 days are about finding out whether one should, not about adding features.

If the gate is not met, the direction changes. The most likely change is the validated
interface over an established engine.

Every change must keep these green. CI runs all of them on each pull request:

Tests must be deterministic. Where data is generated, seed it (see Rng in

title: ACTx486 turns a podcast or video into a responsive AI conversation
description: Karina Nguyen and Jakub Zegzulka's research demo lets viewers direct synthetic versions of Elon Musk and Joe Rogan, but each interaction takes minutes to generate.
fullText:
ACTx486 makes the appeal and risk of interactive synthetic media visible in the same demo: viewers can steer familiar people through new scenes, while the team acknowledges that responses take minutes and its safeguards remain incomplete.

Karina Nguyen (@karinanguyen) and Jakub Zegzulka (@jakubzegzulka) introduced ACTx486 on September 23rd, a research demo that lets viewers interrupt a podcast, ask questions and direct changes to the scene. The exchanges shown so far were generated in advance, and a complete turn takes minutes.

https://x.com/karinanguyen/status/2102806675174687176

The pair built the demo around an episode of The Joe Rogan Experience featuring Elon Musk. ACTx486 combines clips from the original recording with generated segments showing the two men speaking and responding. The project labels generated sections on screen and says the simulated faces, voices and words are synthetic. Neither man said the generated dialogue, and the project is not affiliated with the show or its hosts.

The demo relies on viewers recognizing familiar people in a conversation that never happened. Its creators say they chose the episode because its subjects are recognizable and the risks are easy to see: a system that puts new words in a trusted person's mouth could make falsehoods more convincing.

Viewers can ask the simulated Musk for Los Angeles recommendations tailored to a viewer profile, request an answer in Italian, ask to visualize life on Mars or direct a change to the scene. The site also says the system can generate diagrams, carry changes across turns and send useful information to a phone. These are descriptions of the team's demo, not evidence of a deployed service or measured user demand.

ACTx486 routes a request through research, response writing and scene generation, according to the project. The published examples were made in advance. The team says it hopes to bring an ideal response under six seconds, a target it has not reached. Today, the demo runs more like a production pipeline than a live conversation. A real-time version would also need to address the computation, review and delay involved.

Nguyen's published biography describes work on post-training, model behavior and early products at Anthropic, followed by AI research and product work at OpenAI. Zegzulka's portfolio documents interaction-design work on Meta's Orion augmented-reality glasses and Apple's emerging-technology projects. The demo reflects those backgrounds in its focus on directing a scene through conversation rather than putting a chat window beside a video.

The creators say they started with existing media rather than a blank prompt. The original recording provides the scene's pacing and context; viewers can ask questions or alter moments without inventing the whole experience. ACTx486 calls the viewer a "microdirector" and leaves open how much control viewers should have over a work shaped by its original creator.

The safeguards described on the site cover a narrower set of cases than the demo's capabilities. ACTx486 says the simulation avoids using later parts of the episode, completes research before responding and declines personal and political questions on the real person's behalf. The team also says it needs a broader trust-and-safety layer for media that speaks as someone else. In the examples, authentic footage sits alongside invented speech in a real person's voice and invented lines based on public information. On-screen labels mark where the footage changes; the project does not claim those labels resolve the risks of synthetic likenesses.

ACTx486's website describes the project as a research demo and offers an email request form. Its creators say they are publishing it to develop safeguards in public. For now, the project has shown pre-generated scenes, not a responsive medium. Making it responsive will require much faster generation and safeguards that hold up when viewers can steer a recognizable person's likeness in unpredictable directions.

title: AMD Upstreams AVX10_V2_AUX Support into LLVM Clang 24
description: In addition to AMD working on AVX10_V2_AUX support for the GCC compiler, this summer they also posted AVX10_V2_AUX support for the LLVM/Clang compiler
fullText:
AMD Upstreams AVX10_V2_AUX Support Into LLVM Clang 24

In addition to AMD working on AVX10_V2_AUX support for the GCC compiler, this summer they also posted AVX10_V2_AUX support for the LLVM/Clang compiler. As of yesterday that enablement was merged for LLVM 24 for that important step toward AI Compute Extensions (ACE).
AVX10_V2_AUX adds dedicated data processing and format conversion for helping accelerate AI workloads. This adds onto AVX10 with instructions for converting standard data types to compressed data formats like FP4 and FP6, additional OCP microscaling formats, new rounding modes, and more. AVX10_V2_AUX is part of the AI Compute Extensions (ACE) worked on by both Intel and AMD as part of the x86 Ecosystem Advisory Group.
Engineers from both Intel and AMD have worked on various bits of software around the AI Compute Extensions with AMD engineers seemingly responsible for the AVX10_V2_AUX work.
Merged to LLVM 24 Git on Monday was the initial AVX10_V2_AUX ISA support and is being exposed with the Clang compiler via the new -mavx10v2aux compiler flag. The AVX10_V2_AUX implementation spans 15k lines of new code over 20 patches. See the LLVM pull request for those curious about any other details of this implementation.
LLVM/Clang 24.1 stable should be out around next March so we'll see what more work from the Intel/AMD x86 Ecosystem Advisory Group makes it into this next open-source compiler release.
