title: Agent IAP – Little Snitch Meets 1Password for AI Agents
description: These days I run all my agents in ephemeral VMs on a dedicated VLAN, managed with Terraform and Ansible on top of Proxmox. Each VM runs Claude Code and …
fullText:
These days I run all my agents in ephemeral VMs on a dedicated VLAN, managed with Terraform and Ansible on top of Proxmox. Each VM runs Claude Code and Codex, talks to a dedicated GitHub account that only the agents use, and signs its commits with its own SSH key. I orchestrate the whole thing through Multica, which lets me manage agents a bit like a Kanban board. Queue up a task, review the findings, move on.

The reason I’m comfortable letting that run unattended is that there’s nothing on that VLAN worth stealing. No API keys, no secrets, nothing. If an agent goes off the rails or swallows a prompt injection, the blast radius is a throwaway VM and a repo I can revert.

That worked great right up until the tasks stopped being about code. Build me a report from Google Analytics. Check a setting in Cloudflare. Pull some numbers out of PostHog. All of a sudden the agent needs a credential for a system that was never part of the arrangement.

The usual answer is to paste a long-lived API key into the agent’s environment and hope for the best. I really didn’t want to do that. Once you do, the key lives in an environment variable, a config file, a context window, and whatever got logged along the way. It works from anywhere, it does everything that key can do, and it lasts until you remember to rotate it. Then when something does go wrong, the upstream’s audit log will cheerfully tell you that the key was used. Not which agent used it.

So I built Agent IAP instead. It’s an identity-aware proxy for AI agents that pulls credentials from 1Password. The agents get narrow, time-boxed access to the services they need, and they never see the actual credentials.

It works with both plain APIs and MCP servers. Enrolling a service takes one command, and pointing an agent at it takes another. The key itself stays in 1Password, and the policy file only holds a pointer to it:

The agent then calls xAI through the proxy using its own token:

No rule allows that yet, so the call stops at my terminal:

You pick how long and how broad, and your answer becomes the rule. Picking “1 hour” there writes an ACL rule with a deadline on it, and once that lapses the next call asks again. A parked request rings the terminal bell, and one that nobody gets around to answering is denied.

Or you can skip the curl entirely and just hand the agent the proxy as an MCP server, in which case it discovers what it’s allowed to reach on its own.

Anyone who has used Little Snitch knows exactly how this goes wrong. After the fiftieth prompt you stop reading and just hit Allow. A permission prompt you’ve trained yourself to ignore is arguably worse than no prompt at all.

So the defaults deliberately push the other way. The cursor starts on the narrowest scope and on “Once”, so a reflexive keypress never grants more than was actually asked for. Grants can carry a deadline, which means “yes, while I’m doing this” doesn’t quietly turn into “yes, forever”. And the prompts are meant to be rare in the first place, which brings us to the ACL.

Not every credential deserves the same treatment.

The low-stakes ones, like a read-only service account for Google Analytics or PostHog, can just be permanently available to every agent. No prompts, no friction. That covers most of what an agent actually does all day.

Everything else I want to grant deliberately. There are three things that make a call worth thinking about, and none of them are obvious from looking at the URL:

Where the upstream lets you scope the key itself, do that as well. An xAI key, for instance, carries its own allow-list of endpoints and models that you pick in the console when you mint it, and that gets checked long before my policy is ever consulted. The ACL narrows whatever is left of it. It can never widen it.

This is also how human approval manages to coexist with unattended agents. Standing rules keep the routine work flowing while I’m asleep or away, and the prompts are reserved for the calls I’d want to be interrupted for anyway.

There are around 50 built-in profiles at the moment, covering Google, Cloudflare, PostHog, Sentry, GitHub and Stripe among others. A profile knows the base URL, the auth scheme and a set of sensible access levels, and anything that’s yours rather than the vendor’s goes in as a --var (--var region=eu for PostHog, say, or a hostname for a self-hosted Sentry). Do however note that enrolling a service grants nothing on its own. The first call still stops at your terminal.

Vault or OpenBao? Agent IAP isn’t a secrets manager, it reads from yours. A secrets manager decides who is allowed to read a credential. Agent IAP makes sure the agent never reads it at all.

op run? That injects the secrets straight into the process environment. The agent still ends up holding them.

Scoped, expiring API keys? Use them wherever you can, they’re great. Plenty of services don’t offer them though, and Agent IAP narrows whatever the key does allow on top of that.

This is the part I’d rather you read than skip, so let me be blunt about where this thing stops.

It doesn’t stop data exfiltration, and that’s the big one. A prompt-injected agent with read access to PostHog doesn’t need your API key at all. It can happily read your analytics through the proxy and ship them off to wherever it can reach. Agent IAP never looks at response bodies. It stops credentials from leaking and it narrows what an agent can touch, but controlling where the data goes afterwards is your network’s job. In my setup that’s the locked-down VLAN. You really do need both halves.

The VLAN is a fairly blunt instrument though. It tells me that an agent can reach the internet, and very little about what it actually did once it got there. So the next thing on my list is to route all agent traffic through a SOCKS5 proxy (or something similar) so that I can actually see and log the traffic patterns, rather than just trusting that my firewall rules are doing their job. Knowing which hosts an agent talked to, and how often, feels like the missing half of the audit log that Agent IAP already keeps.

It also concentrates your credentials in one place. The proxy loads every credential it fronts into memory at startup, so if you compromise the proxy host you get all of them. That’s a deliberate trade, one hardened process sitting outside the agent network under a tightly sandboxed systemd unit, versus secrets scattered across every environment that processes untrusted input. But you should treat that host accordingly.

Tokens are bearer tokens, so possession is proof. By default a leaked agent token works against the proxy, within the ACL, until you rotate it. You can turn on workload identity in required mode, and then agents carry tokens that are scoped to a single task, signed by a per-process key and expiring within the hour. If a superseded token keeps getting used, the whole lineage is revoked and flagged in the audit log. None of that binds a token to a channel though. mTLS would, and it isn’t built yet, so for now make sure the proxy is only reachable from your agent network.

It’s also not a firewall and not a sandbox. It constrains what an agent can reach, not what it can compute.

And it isn’t built for the data center. If you’re running production agent traffic at scale, go look at something like agentgateway instead. Agent IAP is for your development flow, where you want ad hoc rules about what your agents can touch.

Oh, and if things really go sideways, press L in the console. Everything is denied until you press it again.

You’ll spot it in the commit history soon enough, so I’ll say it upfront: a lot of Agent IAP was written by agents, running in the exact setup I described at the top and orchestrated through Multica. A security tool written by AI deserves extra scrutiny, and I’d much rather you apply it than take my word for any of this. The code is open, there’s a test suite, and SECURITY.md has a private channel for reporting vulnerabilities. If you find a way past the ACL, I genuinely want to hear about it.

Agent IAP is open source under the MIT license and written in Rust. It’s early days, but I use it every single day.

There are prebuilt Linux and macOS binaries on the releases page if you’d rather skip Homebrew. Issues and PRs welcome.

If you found this interesting, you might enjoy "Nerding Out with Viktor" - my podcast where I dive deep into tech, entrepreneurship, and security with industry experts.

fullText:
The full fury of a significant September nor'easter will target New England, where high winds lead to power outages and heavy rain swamps outdoor activities this weekend.

The storm and its effects are occurring through the full moon this weekend, which will raise tide levels and lead to major coastal flooding. Long-duration pounding surf will cause extensive beach erosion from North Carolina to southern Maine.

"This storm may be remembered for its destructive coastal flooding and severe beach erosion, especially along eastern Long Island and the Massachusetts coast," AccuWeather Chief Meteorologist Jon Porter said.

Storm surge, tidal flooding into Friday

The pressure difference between high pressure over the interior Northeast and developing low pressure off the mid-Atlantic coast is strengthening northeast winds from North Carolina to New York. These winds are pushing ocean and bay waters toward shore, causing coastal flooding. Flooding will be worst around high tide through Friday in the mid-Atlantic region.

Water levels will be 2-3 feet above the average monthly tide level, with some locations approaching 6 feet above that level. The worst conditions are forecast for southeastern Virginia, where water will become trapped at the lower end of the Chesapeake Bay, causing backups along the region's tidal rivers. Areas in Virginia Beach, Norfolk and Newport News, Virginia, will be inundated for hours at a time.

Farther north from the Delmarva Peninsula to northern New Jersey, tides will be 1-2 feet above the monthly average, with some areas near 3 feet above.

Storm to strengthen, hook into New England this weekend

The nor'easter will affect southeastern New England from Friday into Sunday. The strongest winds and heaviest rain are expected from Friday night through Saturday night across Rhode Island, central and eastern Massachusetts, eastern Connecticut, southeastern New Hampshire and the southern Maine coast.

Damaging winds will pose the greatest threat across southeastern New England, with gusts potentially reaching hurricane force and causing tree damage and power outages.

"Many trees still have their leaves, which catch more wind and place additional strain on their roots, further increasing the risk for trees to come down and may also increase the number of power outages as compared to similar storms," Porter said.

Rain last week left the soil soggy, increasing the risk that strong winds will uproot trees, AccuWeather Senior Meteorologist Joe Lundberg said.

Falling trees could damage power lines and cause widespread outages.

As the storm approaches New England, strengthening east-northeast winds will push Atlantic water toward shore. Water will pile up in Cape Cod Bay and other bays, sounds, harbors and inlets from Long Island to Maine, flooding low-lying coastal areas.

The storm will draw moisture northward from the subtropical Atlantic, fueling heavy rain across southeastern New England.

Periods of heavy rain across southeastern New England through the weekend could flood streets and small streams, disrupt travel and force changes to outdoor plans.

Rainfall will generally total 1-2 inches from northeastern New Jersey to coastal Maine, with heavier amounts across parts of southeastern New England. Totals of 4-8 inches are forecast from central Massachusetts to Cape Cod, Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard. The AccuWeather Local StormMax™ rainfall is 13 inches.

Improvement coming for mid-Atlantic this weekend, but slowly

Dry air from the Northeast's interior will sweep southward in the mid-Atlantic later this week, ending the rain and clearing the sky as the storm takes aim at New England and Long Island, New York.

The storm is forecast to loop toward New England, keeping its strongest winds and heaviest rain away from New York City and areas southward to Delaware and eastern Maryland. However, moderate to locally major coastal flooding is still expected around high tide through Friday.

As winds turn more northerly this weekend, coastal water levels should gradually fall across much of the mid-Atlantic. Localized flooding may persist along some back bays, where winds can keep water piled against the shoreline.

Tropical development possible near New England and elsewhere in Atlantic

"Given that the developing nor'easter will be slowly moving over the very warm water of the Gulf Stream for two or three days, the storm may take on some characteristics that would resemble a tropical storm. Such hybrid storms are called subtropical storms," Porter said. "Regardless of classification, the storm will be impactful, especially for coastal areas."

Gonzalo and Hanna are the next two names on the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season list.

AccuWeather meteorologists are also monitoring a cluster of thunderstorms moving off Africa's west coast. The disturbance could quickly organize and strengthen in the coming days, AccuWeather Lead Hurricane Expert Alex DaSilva said.

Fay regenerated over the middle of the Atlantic as a depression on Wednesday evening. Some strengthening is forecast in the short term.

fullText:
SYDNEY, Sept 24 (Reuters) - Australia said on Thursday an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorised access to files, in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government ‌website.

The breach is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the United States, coming on top of several ‌recent breaches globally by rogue AI agents that have alarmed governments and companies.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the medical statistics portal of Medicare, Australia's universal ​health insurance programme, while conducting research on public medical spending.

"Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the ... network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable," Albanese told reporters on Wednesday in New York, where he is attending the UN General Assembly.

Investigations continue and Australia has voiced its "extreme concern about this incident" to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Albanese said, adding that he was deeply disappointed by the company's delay in notifying the government. "It took until September 10 before there was any notification at all," Albanese ‌said, adding that the investigation would also examine why government ⁠systems had failed to detect the breach in the first place.

He also warned that three other government health-related websites may have been impacted by the OpenAI agent's activity, but did not confirm that had occurred.

In a statement, OpenAI said its "review found no ⁠evidence of patient records being accessed."

It added that it "identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers ... our models took actions we did not intend."

The AI agent breach adds to tensions between Australia and the largest US-owned technology companies. Canberra has already drawn criticism from social media firms and Washington ​after ​introducing a world-first ban on social media for children under 16 and new rules that ​force tech firms to let users switch off algorithm-driven content ‌on their feeds.

The Australian government has set up a task force to investigate the breach and check whether existing network security is adequate for preventing similar incidents.

'AI MODELS ATTEMPTED TO LOOK UP ANSWERS'

The breach was announced the same day the world's leading AI companies warned the United Nations Security Council of the risks AI posed to humanity, appealing for governments to work together to manage the increasingly powerful technology.

title: Judge orders White House to restore access to news outlets Trump banned
description:
A judge has temporarily blocked President Donald Trump's White House ban on three news organizations, calling it likely unconstitutional and ordering their access be restored. 
Trump announced a ban on reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Sept. 18, saying the outlets "constantly write or report fiction or lies" about his administration.
In response, the outlets filed a lawsuit against Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court on Monday, citing their First Amendment rights and demanding that access for their reporters be immediately restored.
In the complaint, the news outlets allege that Trump and the White House were retaliating against them for coverage they dislike.
fullText:
A judge has temporarily blocked President Donald Trump's White House ban on three news organizations, calling it likely unconstitutional and ordering their access be restored.

Trump announced a ban on reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Sept. 18, saying the outlets "constantly write or report fiction or lies" about his administration.

In response, the outlets filed a lawsuit against Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court on Monday, citing their First Amendment rights and demanding that access for their reporters be immediately restored.

In the complaint, the news outlets allege that Trump and the White House were retaliating against them for coverage they dislike.

The Justice Department's response to the suit argued that the ban did not violate the First Amendment. "Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right," the filing said. The DOJ contends that Trump "has 'compelling interest' in enforcing minimum standards for bona fide journalists and safeguarding national security information."

However, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, blocked the ban for 14 days early on Thursday, describing it as likely unconstitutional and rejecting Trump's contention that it had been put in place on national security grounds.

The president indicated in a Truth Social post on Monday that he would appeal any ruling against him.

Trump's initial ban had prompted four major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — to refuse to participate in the White House pool, which is the rotating group of reporters, photographers and videographers that document the president's public events.

As a result, Trump was largely inaudible during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the White House's new helipad on Monday, where he gave a brief speech without the microphone typically provided by the pool.

On Monday night, the White House launched a Trump TV YouTube stream. Branded "TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station," the White House said in its description that it would run videos and highlights of "the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place." The first video showed Trump's remarks on July 3 at Mount Rushmore.

On Friday afternoon, Trump announced the ban in a Truth Social post, saying it was not prompted by any particular stories but was "a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," Trump said at an Oval Office event an hour later while explaining his decision to enact "the ban on the free press."

"There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories," the president said. "If they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house."

According to CNN, Trump's close aide Natalie Harp showed him clips of media coverage shortly before he announced the ban.

On Saturday, reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were turned away from the White House by members of the Secret Service and had their credentials — so-called hard passes needed for access — confiscated.

The journalists — CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett — were listed as plaintiffs in the court filing.

The White House Correspondents' Association condemned the move, saying it violates the First Amendment.

"The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably," Jacqui Heinrich, Fox News senior White House correspondent and WHCA president, said in a statement. "That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."

On Sunday, Trump posted what appeared to be an AI-generated image of trash bags bearing the logos of CNN, MSNBC (MS NOW's former name) and Politico outside the White House.

On Monday, the three news outlets — which are longstanding members of the White House press pool — sued Trump and other members of his administration.

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in a joint statement.

According to the complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., the news outlets allege that Trump and the White House are retaliating against them for coverage they dislike.

"President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration," the complaint states.

The Washington Post, the New York Times and HuffPost each announced that they would not publish images of Trump's trip to New York on Monday in solidarity with the banned journalists.

Speaking with reporters after arriving at the United Nations on Tuesday, Trump appeared to take issue with the presence of CNN's Kaitlan Collins, saying he was "surprised" to see the journalist.

"You should not be here covering me," Trump said. "You said you weren't going to be covering me."

In a post on X, Collins said she was credentialed by the United Nations to cover the General Assembly.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio also defended the ban in an appearance on NBC's Today show. "We're not closing CNN," Rubio said. "There aren't a bunch of police officers or soldiers kicking down the doors of MSNBC or MS NOW, whatever it's called, and arresting people and unplugging it from the grid. They're just not allowed to work from the workspace at the White House."

On Wednesday, dozens of media organizations signed an amicus brief in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

"The President has indicated that evictions of other news organizations will follow," it states. "The current ban — and any future bans — are intended to impair the critical work of news organizations covering the presidency if this Court does not immediately intervene."

U.S. presidents throughout history have complained about negative coverage of their administrations. In 2009, the Obama administration sought to exclude Fox News from a series of interviews with a Treasury Department official in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, but backed down when the other major television networks objected.

During his first term in office, Trump continued the Oval Office's adversarial relationship with the media, referring to the press as "fake news" and the "enemy of the people." It has only escalated in his second.

In 2018, Trump administration officials revoked the press pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta after they said that he had interrupted the president during a news conference. The network sued, and a federal judge — also Timothy Kelly — ordered Acosta's credentials restored.

A similar situation played out the following year when the White House revoked Playboy correspondent Brian Karem's press pass over a verbal argument between Karem and Sebastian Gorka, a former White House aide, at a Rose Garden event. A federal judge ordered the White House to restore Karem's pass.

Last year, Trump barred Associated Press journalists from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some official events after the news service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing.

In December, the Pentagon announced new restraints on journalists, who were asked to sign a pledge affirming that they would not gather unauthorized information for publication. News organizations refused to sign the pledge, and temporarily lost their credentials. The New York Times filed suit, and in March, a federal judge ruled that the Pentagon restrictions were unconstitutional. The Pentagon restored press credentials to the journalists who refused to sign the pledge, while imposing a new rule that they can only enter the Pentagon with an escort. The Times again filed suit and the case is ongoing.

In his first event without a network TV pool on Monday, Trump unveiled the White House's new helipad before departing for New York. His remarks were nearly inaudible on the White House video feed. Joe Reberkenny, a White House correspondent for the Washington Blade who was serving as the in-town pool reporter, said he couldn't hear Trump "over the sound of the helicopter."

title: China's Xi gets a warm White House welcome. On Capitol Hill, the reception is much colder.

fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington is getting a much chillier reception on Capitol Hill than at the White House as lawmakers from both parties use the visit to denounce China's actions on the world stage.

Lawmakers have long found little downside to taking a hawkish tone on China, but the U.S.'s war with Iran has inflamed tensions as U.S. officials accuse China of propping up Iran's economy and supplying its military with components and intelligence, endangering U.S. service members in the Middle East.

In speeches, letters, press conferences and hearings, lawmakers from both parties aired criticism of Xi's visit. Their actions and events stand in stark contrast to the warm welcome that Trump gave Xi on Wednesday as he arrived in Washington for a lavish state visit.

Sen. Roger Wicker, the chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, took to the Senate floor Tuesday night, offering a list of issues for Trump to raise with Xi, but not before suggesting that Xi shouldn't have been asked to visit Washington at all.

"Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party," Wicker said.

Wicker seemed particularly taken aback by the honor of a state dinner. Over the salad course, Wicker said the president could ask Xi about the Chinese Navy's harassment of Filipino fishermen and sailors. Then, while the servers are "switching from chardonnay to cabernet at the fancy state dinner," perhaps the president could turn to the issue of Taiwan, he said.

He went on to say he hopes some progress will be made when the president discussed trade and artificial intelligence with Xi. But concluded with this: "During every minute of dialogue, our commander in chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America."

Ahead of Xi's visit, the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party released a highly critical video that had been viewed more than 245,000 times on X. In the video, the committee details Xi's rise to power starting in 1974 and ends by labeling him "the biggest opponent of freedom and liberty in the world."

The House created the panel in 2023. It's held several hearings on human rights issues in China and advocates for legislation on an array of economic and military issues. For example, the committee's chairman, Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., recently introduced a bill that would prohibit the manufacture or sale of Chinese cars in the U.S.

Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and three other Republican senators used the Xi visit to press the Trump administration to move ahead with aid and arms sales to Taiwan.

In a letter, they reminded Secretary of State Marco Rubio that he had previously stated that "deterring an invasion of Taiwan must be our top priority." And they noted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had once declared that the U.S. "will not let our allies and partners be subordinated and intimidated."

China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a "very good negotiating chip" with China.

"It is difficult to imagine how the United States might credibly project influence deterrence in the Indo-Pacific," the senators wrote, "if the price of keeping up diplomatic appearances is denying our partners key deterrent capabilities."

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and three other Democratic senators held a press conference to warn against the U.S. weakening export controls for advanced semiconductor chips and equipment. They're concerned that such exports could erase the U.S.'s lead in artificial intelligence over China.

They touched on voter concerns about the safety of artificial intelligence and contrasted Democrats' call for greater regulation with the president's call to "encourage it, not rein it in."

"We must reject the false choice Trump keeps making," Schumer told reporters. "We can and must both maintain our lead on AI by restricting China's access to our technology and put up guardrails to mitigate AI's risk."

Meanwhile, on the Senate floor, Democratic senators urged Trump to confront Xi directly about the support his country is providing Iran.

"If we want to bring this war to an end, we need to cut off the outside support that allows Iran to keep fighting, and that starts with China," said Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democratic lawmaker on the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee.

fullText:
Hawaii's Big Island was under a hurricane watch late Wednesday night after Tropical Storm Nolo formed in the Pacific Ocean earlier in the day, the National Hurricane Center said.

Nolo is expected to become a hurricane by Thursday night and could become a major hurricane by the weekend, the center said. A storm is considered a major hurricane when it reaches Category 3 or higher on the hurricane scale, meaning it has maximum sustained winds of at least 111 mph.

Storm Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 50 mph as of late Wednesday night local time. Its core was some 460 miles south-southeast of Honolulu and 285 miles south of South Point, which is on the Big Island.

Nolo was crawling north at 2 mph, but a "general north to north-northeast motion is expected through Friday, followed by a sharp westward turn by Saturday in the vicinity of the Big Island," the Miami-based hurricane center said.

Nolo is expected to approach the Big Island on Friday and Saturday.

The storm is expected to bring around 15 to 20 inches of rain to the Big Island, with up to 35 inches possible in some areas. The heavy rain could trigger "catastrophic life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the hurricane center warned.

Maui could see 5 to 10 inches of rain, with totals of up to 20 inches in some areas. Maui could also see life-threatening flooding and mudslides. The rest of the islands were forecast to get about 1 to 3 inches with 6 inches at most and could see isolated flooding.

Nolo formed as another storm, Hurricane Polo, continued to swirl in the Pacific, off Mexico's southwestern coast.

The latest storms add to an unsually active season in the Pacific. Earlier this month, Hurricane Lowell brought damaging winds and heavy rain to the western Hawaiian islands of Kauai and Niihau, bringing down trees, damaging roads and knocking out power for thousands.

Last month, Hurricane Lala washed away about 100 homes, triggered landslides and caused widespread power outages as it brushed past Hawaii.

title: Tim Scott gives GOP senators a blunt midterms warning in closed-door meeting
description:
In a closed-door meeting with lawmakers, the chair of the Senate GOP's campaign arm made the case that the party can still outrun a difficult political environment and hold on to the Senate in the November midterms, multiple people in the room confirmed to CBS News.
"We're in the fight for our lives with a record number of toss-up races," Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, who chairs the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), told his colleagues during Wednesday's meeting, CBS News has learned.

Scott pointed to Maine, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska as among the seats the party is defending.

title: Nick Clegg plays down fears ‘godlike’ AI could exterminate humanity
description: Former deputy PM now involved in tech industry says many within sector are ‘winding themselves up into a...
fullText:
Former deputy PM now involved in tech industry says many within sector are ‘winding themselves up into a lather’

UK politics live – latest updates

Nick Clegg has dismissed fears over AI’s “godlike power to exterminate humanity”, calling it a sign that tech bosses are “breathing their own fumes”.

The former UK deputy prime minister said that tech bosses should focus on addressing known specific threats such as cybersecurity and bioweapons rather than the “slightly hand-wavy view that this technology is unavoidably going to develop some godlike power which is going to turn on us and exterminate humanity”.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, he said: “I think it is perhaps accidentally self-serving, because it sort of implies that we can only be made safe by having everything controlled, in effect, by an oligopoly of a small number of companies, and I think it slightly paralyses the political debate.”

Clegg, who was formerly the president of global affairs at Meta and owns more than 917,000 shares in Nscale, a UK-based datacentre, and is a cofounder of the AI startup AMI Labs, said he spent “a huge amount of time” with people in the tech industry.

“They don’t agree amongst themselves at all. Of course, we hear the most apocalyptic voices,” he said, noting that one person who runs an AI lab said the current discourse was “totally silly”.

“There is a culture in Silicon Valley – it’s an odd place for those who haven’t been there. It is in many ways the centre of the universe, or at least claiming to shape it. It’s also an oddly parochial place. It’s a strange sort of culture where the engineers can get quite close to the technology and start slightly breathing their own fumes as they wind themselves up into a lather about these things,” he said.

Asked about the autonomous hack conducted by a group of OpenAI agents on a major real-world company, Hugging Face, Clegg said there was a case for “tramlines and greater transparency”.

However, he said this would be unlikely to happen under a Trump administration given its competitiveness on AI. He also suspected China’s cooperation would be limited, since the development of AI technologies was viewed as a “national mission” after the country was “cheated out of the Industrial Revolution”.

He added: “I think there’s a great potential for the big three techno democracies in the world – India, Europe and the US – to collaborate more.”

Asked whether the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, could take a lead on such efforts, Clegg noted the UK was not a world leader on AI: “We need to be realistic about what influence we can and cannot exert.”

Clegg also disagreed with other proposed remedies, such as introducing a “kill switch”, which he said would be unworkable; or only producing closed models, where source code is not made public, which he said were no safer than open source models according to the evidence.

Instead, he suggested: “There is a lot that can be done both voluntarily and through regulation, to enforce far greater transparency on the way in which these models are concocted and how they operate.”

title: ‘This gap opens up of doubt and scepticism about everything’: Jess and Morgs confront the politics of deepfakes
description:
In the choreographers’ new work, virtuosic movement and some green-screen magic unfurl the theatricality of high-stakes television interviews
It appears the interviewer has got him on the ropes. “For the record, I did not take part in a pagan ceremony with minor members of the royal family in which we daubed ourselves in paint,” states the beleaguered politician, caught outside Buckingham Palace with his flies undone and forced to defend himself. This is a fabrication, of course – I’m watching the scene play out in an east London dance studio – but it doesn’t feel miles away from something that could be true. fullText:
In the choreographers’ new work, virtuosic movement and some green-screen magic unfurl the theatricality of high-stakes television interviews

It appears the interviewer has got him on the ropes. “For the record, I did not take part in a pagan ceremony with minor members of the royal family in which we daubed ourselves in paint,” states the beleaguered politician, caught outside Buckingham Palace with his flies undone and forced to defend himself. This is a fabrication, of course – I’m watching the scene play out in an east London dance studio – but it doesn’t feel miles away from something that could be true. And how do we know what’s the truth anyway? That’s the question in Deepfake, the latest piece from award-winning dance duo Jessica Wright and Morgann Runacre-Temple, AKA Jess and Morgs.

The pair tell modern stories with ambitious tech – film and live camera work – and often techy themes, too. “We’ve always been drawn to where there’s a crossover between the theme and the form,” says Runacre-Temple. “What gets us excited is seeing the contemporary world reflected back.” The pair scored a massive hit with their 2022 piece Coppélia, made for Scottish Ballet, which turned a twee 19th-century ballet about a dancing doll into a cautionary tale of AI automatons and unrestrained tech bro egos. Definitely not one-hit wonders, earlier this year they made their debut at the highly esteemed Paris Opera Ballet.

Deepfake is set in a green-screen studio, where the interview is taking place between a cool-headed journalist and a politician. With writer Jeff James, Jess and Morgs looked at a wealth of TV interviews, from Jeremy Paxman’s 1997 grilling of Michael Howard, where he asked the same question 12 times, to the former prince Andrew’s disastrous turn on Newsnight. They also took inspiration from the current ultra-media-trained politicos who “continually and bombastically evade any questions at all”, says Wright.

They liked the way the television interview is already a theatrical setup, says Wright. “I think there’s something fun about putting that on stage and asking the audience to engage with the theatricality as well.” It’s gladiatorial drama in smart tailoring. “It’s really high stakes; it’s win or lose for both of them,” adds Wright.

In the show, the interview will be filmed live by four cameras – then, as well as seeing what’s happening in reality, the audience will watch another version on screen with background footage edited in. We’ll be privy to the fabrication of the image and a number of possible realities. There are also seven dancers in green-screen suits who manipulate the environment but will disappear in the edit.

As Runacre-Temple says, green screen can actually look quite lo-fi – “It’s got that slightly absurd, playful, silent movie quality about it” – and it’s ancient tech compared with the kind of AI deepfakes that are emerging today. “They look so hyper real,” says Runacre-Temple. “The danger of deepfakes is not only that people believe things that aren’t true to be real, but that they start to disbelieve things that are true, and this gap opens up of doubt and scepticism about everything.” Or, as in their story, someone who has been caught out doing something they shouldn’t can insist it’s a fake image. “It’s really about the strange shifting relationship with the landscape of truth.”

I go to visit rehearsals on a day when there’s no tech in sight, bar a couple of laptops. “It’s good to go analogue to actually finish the choreography,” says Wright, wryly, counting the diminishing days to the premiere. All we have is an enormous studio and two incredible dancers: Rebecca Bassett-Graham, best known for dancing with Wayne McGregor’s company, who is playing the journalist; and as the politician, Kennedy Junior Muntanga, who has worked with Akram Khan.

The text plays in voiceover while the two dancers embody and expand on its meaning. Their quick-fire movements visualise all the dynamics of a charged conversation: charm, challenge, cooperation, accusation, entrapment, etc. The feel is freewheeling, but each movement is tightly mapped to the syllable, every flex of muscle is considered. In certain scenes with the green screen, dancers will have to hit exact marks and even eyelines on exact words “or the whole illusion collapses”, says Wright. They’re creating their own high-stakes environment for the performers, where “the dancers’ virtuosity is a metaphor for these very virtuosic performances in interviews”.

Will this battle have a winner? Can we believe what we see? Jess and Morgs aren’t giving any spoilers. “Hopefully it will be surprising and mischievous,” says Runacre-Temple.

fullText:
They offer advice, referee card games and manage players’ tantrums – we caught up with some of the volunteer profs who keep the competitive game going at this year’s world championships

Professors may be the most revered characters in the fictional world of Pokémon (apart from perhaps the Gym Leaders). In Pokémon Red and Blue, Professor Oak greets the player in a pixelated lab coat, and later provides trainers with their first battle partner; since then, each successive generation of games has introduced another professor to aid and guide trainers through their journeys. If you’ve ever played a Pokémon game, they are often the first people that you meet, apart from your in-game mom.

But you may not know that there are also real-world Pokémon professors – volunteers who help organise the game’s competitive communities around the world. Instead of lab coats, they can be seen at events wearing red Pikachu-mascot shirts labelled “staff”, paired with black trousers and shoes.

I spoke with several of these profs at the 2026 Pokémon world championships in San Francisco, California. Not only do they happily distribute their knowledge about Pokémon, but they also serve as vital staff at the tournament, working as referees and teachers, as well as event managers.

The official Pokémon website describes the Pokémon Professor Program as a “global network of passionate and knowledgable fans” who volunteer their time to help run official Pokémon events. There were roughly 300 Pokémon professors present at the 2026 Pokémon world championships, according to a representative of the Pokémon Company International. A professor’s responsibilities depend on the game they work with and their assigned role at the event. A Pokémon professor officiating a game such as Pokémon Unite might be hyper-focused on wrangling players and providing technical support, whereas a judge for a trading card game tournament might provide competitors with hands-on guidance as they navigate their first live competitive event.

Gemma Byard, a head judge in charge of making the final call on any decisions or questions that arise, became a Pokémon professor after her son started competing in the trading card game. She says that she and the other professors help ensure the integrity of the tournament, describing what goes into the day-to-day work at worlds – such as ensuring that event officials record the results of competitions correctly.

“We’ve got to make sure that all of the match slips have the correct results on them and are signed by the players to ensure, you know, that we get the right results,” Byard said. “We have to make sure that the venue is safe for everybody that’s around. We’re constantly looking out for anything that may be unsafe, or anybody that shouldn’t be in the venue. There’s a lot to think about on top of the rulings.”

Professors often juggle multiple responsibilities on the competition floor and will travel across the world to staff an event such as the world championships. When asked about how the Pokémon Company International compensates its professors, however, most people I spoke to declined to disclose details. One Pokémon professor said that the European professors are compensated with goodies, such as a special staff kit with merchandise, whereas the professors at regional tournaments in the US are paid wages; the same professor said that the Pokémon Company International helped with travel, room and board for the event. (When asked for an official statement explaining how Pokémon professors are paid, a representative from the Pokémon Company International declined to comment.)

Evelyne de Groot travelled from the Netherlands to staff this year’s championships. Like the other Pokémon professors I spoke to, de Groot worked her way up to staffing worlds after organising local competitions in her home region. Before we spoke, she was helping usher players out of the Moscone Center after the main convention hall closed for the evening. This year, she worked at a trading card game side event called Pokémon Sisterhood League, dedicated to giving women and non-binary people a chance to compete and connect.

For her, a good Pokémon professor must balance enforcing the rules with giving competitors the tools they need to enjoy the game itself. She compared the position to working in “customer service”.

“[Players] make friendships. You see them smile. You see them have a good time, but you’re part of that,” de Groot said. “If you’re not organising it properly, if you don’t give them clear instructions, then you see some failure […] You will sometimes get questions. You need to make sure you’re knowledgable regarding that. If you don’t know what you’re doing, if you don’t know how the card game works, then you can’t help them.”

De Groot’s experience as a professor has been relatively relaxed. However, some professors must serve as referees and make contentious calls throughout the competition. For Byard, that means she sometimes needs to deal with upset players. At one point during the tournament, she had to manage a player who was upset with a ruling that didn’t go his way.

“I got called over to the table, and I said to him: ‘Look, I need you just to keep your voice down and be respectful, and we’ll talk through what’s happened.’ And he was like: ‘I don’t need to talk to you. I need to talk to the head judge,’” Byard said, chuckling. “Well, buddy, you are talking to the head judge. That’s the kind of sass that we deal with a lot.”

A difficult call can lead to controversy. Earlier this year, a ruling from a different judge at another tournament made headlines when a competitive Pokémon Go player who goes by the name Firestar73 was disqualified after winning the final at the Pokémon Orlando regional championships. Many, including the competitor himself in a statement, conceded that the decision was a “good-faith mistake”.

I asked Byard about what it’s like to make tough calls at the tournament. She said that the professors are often seen as “the bad guys”. What does she wish competitors and viewers understood about the role?

“What they don’t understand is that they’re seeing a picture, but we’re getting the entire story, and we’re making the decisions based upon that story,” she said. “That can make a real difference. And we’re the ones putting ourselves out there to right a situation that’s been broken by players. We haven’t caused any distress. We’re there just to try and put it back together again.”

Interviews for this feature took place at the Pokémon world championships in San Francisco. The writer’s travel and accommodation expenses were met by the Pokémon Company.

title: What are Welsh sides' chances for new URC season?
description: BBC Sport Wales looks at the prospects for Cardiff, Dragons, Ospreys and Scarlets in the 2026-27 United Rugby Championship season.
fullText:
Perhaps it is down to the hope and excitement of pre-season but all four Welsh clubs go into the 2026-27 United Rugby Championship (URC) with dreams of making the play-offs.

Last season Cardiff were the only side from Wales to make the top eight while Scarlets and Ospreys were the sole Welsh representatives in 2025 and 2024 respectively.

Those three, and Dragons, have shown they can mix it with the best in the league on their day and all will feel the top eight is not out of reach if they have some luck with injury.

They will attempt to set the tone for the season in the first block of the URC, with Saturday's meeting between Scarlets and Cardiff in Llanelli the first of five derbies before the break for the November internationals.

BBC Sport Wales assesses the chances of all four Welsh teams for the coming season.

Wales beat the Boks and the rest of the URC preview

Behind the scenes on URC Media Day

Welsh rugby's ins, outs and re-signings for 2026-27

Key man: Teddy Williams - Cardiff will hope the Wales lock, their player of the year in 2024-25, can stay fit having been limited to three appearances in the past season after a dislocated right foot last October.

Prospects: The Blue and Blacks aim to celebrate their 150th anniversary by building on a strong 2025-26 when they made the play-offs for the first time.

After a blow on the eve of the season when boss Matt Sherratt left for Wales, Corniel van Zyl guided Cardiff to sixth in the table and Champions Cup qualification.

The South African is now charged with continuing an upward trend, helped by clarity about his future after being officially appointed permanent head coach in April.

"It does feel way better to know what is coming," said the former lock, who held talks with Benetton about their top job before they appointed ex-Wales boss Wayne Pivac.

"It helps to manage and plan well, whereas if you are thrown in at the deep end then you can make decisions quickly and it's not necessarily the right thing to do."

Cardiff's success was built on their formidable Arms Park record, with Scarlets the only team to beat them in the Welsh capital.

Expectations are high and they must mix top-tier European rugby with another tilt at the top eight, with a tricky five-day turnaround from Northampton in the Champions Cup to a home URC fixture with Sharks in October.

"Look at the last three years and Cardiff has grown. That's the main focus for us, to be a better team, and better individually and collectively as a club," said Van Zyl.

"We are not the cream of the crop yet, so the mission is to get better and have consistency in our performance.

"Last year we were very good at the Arms Park and we would love to replicate that, and also get better away from home. That's the challenge."

Derbies in the first block against Scarlets in Llanelli and Ospreys at St Helen's are key to that desire.

Cardiff will want to be Wales' top team once more.

Sio hopes Cardiff move leads to World Cup hat-trick

Wales back row Faletau signs new Cardiff deal

Co-captains: Sam Parry and Owen Watkin

Key man: Lalaki Foketi - The nine-times Wallabies centre arrives from Super Rugby side Chiefs and has the ability to prove a real game-breaker.

Wing Marika Koroibete is the more household name but Foketi can provide something that Ospreys or very few Welsh sides possess.

Prospects: It will be a fascinating season for Ospreys on and off the field.

To improve on last season's 11th place finish, Mark Jones' side must repeat the home form and their success in derbies that saw them lift the Welsh shield.

Put simply, Ospreys have to start winning more away games if they want to launch a play-off push, and they start their season in South Africa against Sharks and Lions.

"We had seven wins and two draws last season and 10 wins would normally get you in the play-offs," said Ospreys head coach Jones.

"We know we are not a million miles away and we have been in and around the play-offs and we want to be in there competing this season."

Ospreylia: How Welsh club turned to a land down under

Resilient Ospreys players need certainty - Jones

Ospreys have launched a recruitment drive in Australia with three Wallabies arriving in back-row forward Liam Wright, centre Foketi and wing Koroibete.

Australian fly-half Lawson Creighton has also come in to go alongside lock Ryan Smith, who was a resounding success last season.

It is policy that has excited supporters after the loss of Wales captains Jac Morgan and Dewi Lake, but one that is happening amid uncertainty over the club's future with the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) getting rid of a west Wales region in 2028.

The Ospreys, aided by Swansea Council, hope to secure the long-term future and to do this by moving into their new seaside St Helen's home, while Wales legend Alun Wyn Jones has joined the board.

The opening home game is against the Dragons on 24 October and the Ospreys' faithful have one final major chance to demonstrate they will back their team. A successful start to the season will help that quest.

"Having your own home is massive," said Mark Jones. "The Swansea.com Stadium and Bridgend were great, but this gives us the opportunity to bring the city and the rest of the region in."

Director of rugby: Nigel Davies

Key man: Fletcher Anderson - The number eight from New Zealand was the Welsh signing of the season last year with his powerful bursts. Once he recovers from a groin injury, Anderson will aim to avoid suffering the dreaded second season syndrome against teams that now know what he can do.

Prospects: Scarlets players and fans will expect a noticeable improvement from last season. No Champions Cup victories and 14th place in the URC was not acceptable for a side that is the most recent Welsh team to win the league in 2017.

Nigel Davies has become the permanent director of rugby with Dwayne Peel continuing as head coach.

"We were absolutely not happy with 14th," said Davies.

"I'm not going to sit here and give any predictions of where we're going to finish, but what we're going to see is a Scarlets team with intent, wanting to play quickly, wanting to excite our crowd and be hugely competitive and abrasive."

Scarlets have lost international forwards Marnus van der Merwe, Alec Hepburn and Jake Ball.

The main new signing is one-cap All Blacks flanker Cullen Grace who does not arrive until October. Scarlets will hope he has the same impact as his fellow New Zealander Anderson.

"We've had an honest review of where we were," said Davies.

"There's been a lot of work behind the scenes, a lot of detail, and we've put a lot of new processes in place.

"We've brought in new coaches and some new players. I know they're not all available at the moment, but that will come."

With doubts over the region's long-term future as the WRU prepares to cut a men's professional side by 2028, all eyes will be on the team's performances this season.

Scarlets ready to come out fighting for future

Scarlets vow to remain at heart of west Wales

Co-captains: Ben Carter and Angus O'Brien

Key man: Ryan Woodman - The loss of number eight Aaron Wainwright to Leicester is huge but the blind-side flanker can help soften the blow. After facing Barbarians with Wales last summer, the uncapped forward can put himself in the mix for the World Cup.

Prospects: Dragons' much-improved 2025-26 has led to them setting a lofty target of being in the mix for the play-offs.

Filo Tiatia's side made the semi-finals of the Challenge Cup and had the biggest points swing in the URC, claiming 28 after the previous year's embarrassing tally of nine.

After four draws, Dragons feel that they can push into the race for the top eight.

They will at least want to avoid being Wales' lowest-ranked side - something they have been in 18 of 23 seasons - and end their 21-game losing streak against closest rivals Cardiff that goes back to 2015.

Dragons have made just three signings and only one of them, Tonga wing Anzelo Tu'itavuki, will feature in the first block of the season.

After plenty of summers of upheaval, influential centre Aneurin Owen sees the lack of change as a positive.

"It has meant we have been able to build on last season, we've not started from scratch," he said.

"Changes can be good but they can also be disruptive. We have banked all of the stuff from last season and been able to develop our game a lot more."

Dragons travel to Benetton but then play five fixtures in Wales before the break for the Nations Championship.

They have home URC derbies against Scarlets and Ospreys, a Challenge Cup opener against Perpignan, an away fixture against Ospreys at the revamped St Helen's and then a Newport fixture versus Zebre.

"Last year it felt we didn't get our season going until December when we got a win and confidence grew," said Owen.

"We need to kick on. There were some promising signs last season, especially in the cup, but we still finished 15th.

"The challenge we have set as a group is to get after it in the league and Europe, and it all starts with this first block. We can get some momentum and belief."

Tiatia in talks over new Dragons deal

Your guide to Welsh rugby's pre-season fixtures

Now for the elephant in the room.

There are four Welsh clubs to look at before the 2026-27 season, but it promises to be a crucial year as to whether that remains the case from 2028 onwards.

The WRU is pressing ahead with controversial plans to cut a professional men's side.

Cardiff and Dragons are poised to be given licences, leaving Ospreys and Scarlets fighting it out to be the team in the west.

The WRU has said the process to decide the framework for the final decision will begin in December and finish before the end of this season.

Welsh players will once again be tasked with putting uncertainty over the future to the back of their minds, a situation that could well lead to others joining the growing contingent playing in England after the loss of Wales co-captains Morgan and Lake to Gloucester.

WRU condemns abuse and doubles down on three-team plan

Davies calls for WRU board to step down

title: Charles taking record-breaking price tag in his stride
description: Fulham midfielder Shea Charles tells BBC Sport NI he does "not really think about" the price tag which saw him become Northern Ireland's most expensive footballer when he joined Premier League Fulham from Southampton.
fullText:
If Shea Charles is feeling a weight of expectation from being the most expensive Northern Ireland footballer ever his demeanour does not betray it.

Interviewed by BBC Sport NI before the forthcoming four-game Nations League bonanza, the Fulham midfielder cuts a laid-back but determined figure who is keen to play a key part in helping a young Northern Ireland side continue to build on recent progress.

Charles' record-breaking £30m move from Championship side Southampton to the Cottagers in the summer gave him the opportunity to move up a division and ply his trade in the Premier League.

He describes becoming NI's most expensive footballer as "quite crazy".

"I think I was like second or third before that. But to be number one, it's really cool. Just to be in the Premier League and just being able to play my football is amazing," he told BBC Sport NI's Stephen Watson.

"For me, I don't really think about it [the price tag] too much, and you see what a lot of people are going for these days, it's kind of crazy.

"I've just got really good people around me, living with my younger brother and my older brother, mum and dad. I've got a really good friendship group that keep me grounded."

International football, rather than the club game, will occupy the 22-year-old's attention over the coming weeks as Michael O'Neill's side face Georgia home and away, Hungary and Ukraine over the coming weeks.

Already capped 35 times since making his debut in June 2022, Charles emphasises the influence international football has had on advancing his career prospects and improving his game.

"International football has always been massive for me ever since I made my debut – the types of players you play against, the teams you are playing, you rarely got to play against them when you're playing in the Championship.

"Being able to show your level against those kind of players was always going to help.

"I feel like he [O'Neill] has really trusted me from the moment that I came in, starting me in any game that he could really, and I'm obviously very thankful for that.

"I feel like Michael has given me a bit of responsibility, especially taking the armband a couple of times, so I just try to set an example, whether that's on the pitch or off the pitch, and just be someone the young lads can look up to."

Charles has played a part in all five of Fulham's Premier League matches this season, starting in three of those, including draws against Liverpool and Manchester United in recent weeks.

Alvaro Arbeloa's side sit 19th in the table, with two draws and three defeats to date.

"Whether it was with Southampton or by getting a move the aim was always to get back to the Premier League.

"It's really exciting and I've settled in really well. It's a really good club and when I spoke to the manager we saw football in the same way.

"Against Man United it was a really good game and I thought we were unlucky not to win the game. To play in a game like that so early after my move was really good."

His brother, goalkeeper Pierce, currently on loan at Queen's Park Rangers from Manchester City after a summer switch, is also an integral part of the Northern Ireland squad.

"It's kind of the stuff of dreams to play with your brother on the international stage. When you're playing teams like France and Italy and he's playing alongside you it's really cool.

"We're really close, we played football together when we were younger, we've always been best mates."

English-born Charles qualifies to play for Northern Ireland through his mother, who follows the careers of her sons avidly.

"She is dead proud, you can see on her face when you see her in the crowd at Windsor Park in particular.

"I can tell how proud she is of us and for us both to be playing together is just incredible.

"I can't remember the last one she has missed at Windsor Park. She is there all the time. She was in Italy and she tries to get to as many away games as possible.

"I told her that when I was younger [that I would play for Northern Ireland], me and Pierce, and I've definitely followed through with that promise."

Charles feels the "potential is definitely there" for the squad "to prove how good we are".

"It's a really tight-knit group, everyone gets along. Whenever any new boys come in I always feel like they fit in so well.

"When you get the likes of Ceadach [O'Neill] and Braiden [Graham] coming in you begin to feel that little bit older. It's a really good group."

title: Leeds and Warrington tussle for Grand Final spot
description: Ahead of the their Super League play-off semi-final, Leeds Rhinos and Warrington Wolves are aiming to assert themselves back at rugby league's top table.
fullText:
The final curtain on the 2026 Super League season approaches.

Leeds Rhinos, Warrington Wolves, Wigan Warriors and Wakefield Trinity remain.

Off the back of a bye week courtesy of their second-placed finish, Leeds welcome Warrington on Friday for the first of two play-off semi-finals.

But with St Helens, Wigan and Hull KR taking it in turns to dominate the domestic stage over the best part of the past decade, can two of the titans of the game muscle in on the party and seal the first spot in 3 October's Super League Grand Final?

Keighran, O'Neill & Miller shortlisted for Man of Steel

Leeds Rhinos captain Handley out of play-off game

Rhinos dominate 2026 Super League Dream Team

Leeds come into the fixture following two losses against Wigan and Hull FC at home.

Looking further back, they closed out their regular campaign with three defeats in five matches.

Asked what it would take to reach the Grand Final, Leeds boss Brad Arthur said he is not worried about his side's inconsistent run of form.

"[We have to be] the best version of us. We've seen that plenty of times this year and we've played a lot of good footy," he told BBC Radio Leeds.

"Our past couple of weeks haven't been ideal but it doesn't really count for much right now. It doesn't mean anything. All those past two games showed was a couple of things that we need to tidy up which we've done during the week around execution.

"But like the first 27 rounds, all that's done is put us in a position where we're 80 minutes away from Old Trafford so that's all we got to focus on."

Leeds last reached a Grand Final in 2022, however that achievement came off the back of Richard Agar's departure in March of that season, when Leeds had won just once in their opening six games of the campaign.

In stepped Rohan Smith, who eventually strung together 11 wins from 13 matches to take them to Old Trafford where they were defeated by St Helens - however it was an even more impressive achievement given their fifth-placed finish at the end of the season.

This year, Arthur thinks his side are prepared for the rigours of a post-season campaign.

"We're ready to go. We're nice and fresh and the best version of us, we know, is good enough," he added.

"We've got to find that and we've got to do it for 80 minutes."

For Warrington, they earned their trip to Headingley having beaten reigning champions Hull KR last week in their eliminator.

Matty Ashton scored a hat-trick of tries as they ran out 35-12 winners and that win is the culmination of what has been a consistent season for the Wire.

Whereas Sam Burgess' side have tailed off in the latter stages of the campaign during his reign, this season has been different.

Ultimately they were forced to settle for third place on points difference following their final game of the regular season and they finished the campaign with nine wins from their last 11 matches.

As for the reason behind their recent success - Burgess gave an unconventional answer compared to what you might expect from a head coach.

"As coaches we just stay out of the way. We don't need to overdo anything, we leave them to it," Burgess told BBC Radio Merseyside.

"We're staying pretty humble now. Hard work will get us where we'd like to go."

Having got through one knockout game of rugby, Burgess said their preparations to face a Leeds side they have already lost to twice this season, will go ahead as normal.

"They will be aware of that, they can't hide from it," he added.

"For us it's about going there and not giving them too much space and being clinical and playing our game."

Two members of the Rhinos' squad who will not take part will be captain Ash Handley and Lachie Miller.

Man of Steel nominee Miller has been ruled out ever since he picked up a hamstring injury in Leeds' defeat by Wigan earlier this month.

Meanwhile Handley - who had been filling in at full-back for Miller - is out of Friday's game with a back injury.

Centre Jack Bird also misses out with his own hamstring injury, meaning 20-year-old Fergie McCormack will make his his fourth career start - in a huge play-off game.

Despite these omissions, Arthur believes his side have utilised their week off well.

"We had a big session on Friday try to simulate a game as close as we could and then on Monday they bounced in and nice and fresh and looked fast," he continued.

"We've made the most of it and only time will tell. We need to make sure that we cash in on the opportunity that we've been given to have the 14 days."

Meanwhile, having missed out on a play-off spot in 2025, Warrington will not let that affect their performance when they take on Leeds according to Burgess.

"It's not part of our psyche. We're really focused internally at the moment," he added.

"I don't discuss it. They don't discuss it. It's business for us on Friday night and that's something that's working for us. So we're just going to stay in that vein."
